knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct inequality-elimination algorithm for coordinate projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To eliminate a variable \(y\) from a finite linear-inequality system, partition the inequalities according to whether the coefficient of \(y\) is positive, negative, or zero. Combine each positive-coefficient inequality with each negative-coefficient inequality using nonnegative multipliers that cancel \(y\), retain the zero-coefficient inequalities, and then discard \(y\). The resulting finite system describes exactly the coordinate projection onto the remaining variables. Repetition eliminates any finite block of variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fourier–Motzkin elimination computes a projection by combining inequalities having opposite signs in each eliminated variable.
assumptions_latex: The input is a finite system of real linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated inequalities define exactly the coordinate projection of the input feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Fourier–Motzkin Elimination

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step syntactic growth before redundancy removal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an elimination step has \(p\) inequalities with positive eliminated-variable coefficient, \(q\) with negative coefficient, and \(z\) with zero coefficient, Fourier–Motzkin elimination produces at most \(pq+z\) inequalities before redundancy removal. Repeated elimination can therefore create large intermediate systems even when the final projection has a short irredundant description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One elimination step creates at most one inequality per positive–negative pair, plus the unaffected inequalities.
assumptions_latex: A Fourier–Motzkin step has sign-class sizes \(p,q,z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unreduced output contains at most \(pq+z\) inequalities.

notation.meaning: Counts of positive-, negative-, and zero-coefficient inequalities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-side transport under a linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear map \(T\), \[T\bigl(\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L\bigr)=\operatorname{conv}(T(V))+\operatorname{cone}(T(R))+T(L).\] Hence a linear image of a finitely generated polyhedron is obtained by mapping its point, ray, and lineality generators; zero and duplicate images may subsequently be removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear projection acts directly on point, ray, and lineality generators.
assumptions_latex: \(V,R\) are finite subsets of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L)=\operatorname{conv}(T(V))+\operatorname{cone}(T(R))+T(L)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^k:Ax+By\le c\}
\]
be a polyhedron. Its coordinate projection is
\[
\pi_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^k,
\ Ax+By\le c\},
\]
and this set is a polyhedron. More generally, every linear image of a polyhedron is polyhedral. Conversely, every polyhedron has such an existential representation, including the case \(k=0\). Hence finite systems with auxiliary variables define exactly the polyhedra after projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating auxiliary variables from finitely many linear inequalities yields a polyhedron, and every polyhedron admits such an existential representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A projection representation of \(P\) is a finite system \[Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+k}:Cx+Dy\leq e\}\] such that \[P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^k,\ Cx+Dy\leq e\}.\] More generally, a linear-image representation is \(P=T(Q)\) for a linear map \(T\); it becomes a coordinate projection representation after adjoining the equations \(x=Tz\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection representation describes membership in a polyhedron by the existence of auxiliary variables satisfying a finite linear system. Equivalently, the represented set is a coordinate projection or linear image of a higher-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\), and \(P\) is polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Projection is existential quantifier elimination: \(x\in P\Longleftrightarrow\exists y\;Cx+Dy\leq e\).
Every linear image \(T(Q)\) equals the projection of \(\{(x,z):z\in Q,\ x=Tz\}\) onto the \(x\)-coordinates.
special_cases_latex: If \(k=0\), the representation is an ordinary H-description of \(P\).
Orthogonal projection onto a subspace is obtained by taking \(T\) to be the corresponding linear projector.
immediate_consequences_latex: Projection does not leave the finite-dimensional polyhedral class.
Different lifted systems can represent the same polyhedron and may have substantially different numbers of inequalities.
boundary_notes: The projection of a general closed convex set need not be closed, whereas finite-dimensional polyhedral projections are polyhedral and hence closed.
Auxiliary variables are existential; uniqueness of a lifting point \(y\) is not required.
A projection representation is not automatically irredundant or size-minimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The size of a polyhedral extended formulation is the number of inequalities in its lifted linear description, with affine equations conventionally not counted. knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An extended formulation of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) consists of a polyhedron
\[
Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^k:Ex+Fy\le g\}
\]
and a specified linear map \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^{d+k}\to\mathbb{R}^d\) such that
\[
\pi(Q)=P.
\]
For the usual coordinate formulation, \(\pi(x,y)=x\), so
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^k,
\ Ex+Fy\le g\}.
\]
The variables \(y\) are auxiliary and need not be uniquely determined by \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended formulation describes a polyhedron as the linear projection of another polyhedron in a higher-dimensional space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial and asymptotic data of a polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron. Valid inequalities are written \(c^\top x\leq\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedra; the object defined is the combined boundary, incidence, recession, and lineality structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial–asymptotic geometry of \(P\) is the structured collection \[\mathfrak G(P)=\bigl(\mathcal F(P),\subseteq,\dim,\operatorname{rec}(P),\operatorname{lin}(P)\bigr),\] where \[\mathcal F(P)=\{P\cap\{x:c^\top x=\delta\}:c^\top x\leq\delta\text{ is valid for }P\},\] \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:x+td\in P\ \forall x\in P,\ t\geq0\},\qquad \operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap(-\operatorname{rec}(P)).\] The order \(\subseteq\) records face incidence, while dimension records rank or codimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The facial–asymptotic geometry of a polyhedron comprises its faces ordered by inclusion and graded by dimension, together with its recession cone and lineality space.
assumptions_latex: \(c^\top x\leq\delta\) ranges over inequalities valid for \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak G(P)=(\mathcal F(P),\subseteq,\dim,\operatorname{rec}(P),\operatorname{lin}(P))\) with the displayed defining formulas.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(P=\{x:a_i^\top x\leq b_i,\ i\in M\}\), every nonempty face is obtained by making a subset of the defining inequalities tight.
The asymptotic part is determined from any H-description by \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad\leq0\}\) and \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{d:Ad=0\}\).
special_cases_latex: For a polytope, \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\), so only the finite face structure remains.
For a polyhedral cone, the origin is distinguished and the asymptotic cone equals the set itself.
immediate_consequences_latex: The face family is finite and closed under intersection.
Every nonempty face has the same lineality space as \(P\).
Strict inclusion of nonempty faces decreases dimension by at least one.
boundary_notes: The tuple records geometric structure, not a unique choice of inequalities or generators.
For arbitrary closed convex sets, the face family or extreme-direction family need not be finite.
The empty face may be included in \(\mathcal F(P)\); its dimension convention must be specified separately if used.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. Let \(c^\top x\leq\delta\) be valid for \(P\), meaning it holds for every \(x\in P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedral faces, including improper faces and their active-constraint descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face of \(P\) is a set \[F=P\cap\{x:c^\top x=\delta\}\] for some valid inequality \(c^\top x\leq\delta\). The face structure is the finite partially ordered set \((\mathcal F(P),\subseteq)\), graded by \(\dim F\). If \(P=\{x:a_i^\top x\leq b_i,\ i\in M\}\), then every nonempty face has the form \[F_I=\{x\in P:a_i^\top x=b_i\ \forall i\in I\}\] for some \(I\subseteq M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is the portion of a polyhedron on which a valid inequality is tight. All faces, ordered by inclusion and graded by dimension, form the polyhedron's face structure; every nonempty face can be described by a subset of active defining inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=P\cap\{x:c^\top x=\delta\}\) is a face, and every nonempty face is \(F_I\) for some active-index set \(I\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A convex subset \(F\subseteq P\) is a face when any segment in \(P\) whose relative interior meets \(F\) has both endpoints in \(F\).
A nonempty face is the solution set of maximizing some linear functional over \(P\).
special_cases_latex: \(P\) and \(\varnothing\) are the improper faces.
Zero-dimensional nonempty faces are vertices; inclusionwise maximal proper faces are facets.
immediate_consequences_latex: The intersection of two faces is a face.
There are only finitely many faces.
If \(F\subsetneq G\) are nonempty faces, then \(\dim F\leq\dim G-1\).
boundary_notes: Different valid inequalities or active-index sets may define the same face.
For lower-dimensional \(P\), dimension and codimension are naturally measured relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\).
A general convex-set face need not be exposed, but every face of a polyhedron admits an active-constraint representation.

notation.meaning: face obtained by making constraints indexed by I tight

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and \(F\in\mathcal F(P)\). Set \(d=\dim P\), with dimensions taken in the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by exposure, propriety, dimension, codimension, and supporting hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face \(F=P\cap\{x:c^\top x=\delta\}\), defined by a valid inequality \(c^\top x\leq\delta\), is classified as follows: it is improper when \(F\in\{\varnothing,P\}\), proper when \(\varnothing\neq F\subsetneq P\), a vertex when \(\dim F=0\), an edge when \(\dim F=1\), and a facet when \(F\subsetneq P\) and \(\dim F=d-1\). Its codimension is \(\operatorname{codim}_P(F)=d-\dim F\). A nonempty proper face is exposed by the supporting hyperplane \(\{x:c^\top x=\delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral faces are classified as improper or proper and by dimension relative to the polyhedron. Vertices have dimension zero, edges dimension one, and facets codimension one. Every nonempty proper polyhedral face lies in a supporting hyperplane that exposes it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The type of \(F\) is determined by whether it is improper and by \(\dim F\) or \(\operatorname{codim}_P(F)=d-\dim F\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A facet is an inclusionwise maximal proper face.
A vertex is a singleton face and hence an extreme point of \(P\).
For \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\), every nonempty face is described by a set of constraints active throughout that face.
special_cases_latex: If \(d=0\), the unique nonempty face \(P\) is improper rather than a proper vertex face.
For a one-dimensional pointed polyhedron, proper nonempty faces are its endpoint vertices, when they exist.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every proper face is contained in a facet.
Distinct faces have distinct affine hulls.
A strict chain of nonempty faces has length bounded by \(d+1\).
boundary_notes: The word edge is normally reserved for one-dimensional faces; an unbounded one-dimensional face may be a ray.
Codimension is relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\), not necessarily to \(\mathbb R^n\).
The empty face has dimension \(-1\) only under an explicit convention.

notation.meaning: dimension of P minus dimension of F

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension and dimensional taxonomy of polyhedral faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of polyhedral dimension, supporting-hyperplane faces, proper faces, and dimension-based face classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polyhedron \(\mathcal X\), \(\dim \mathcal X\) is the maximal number of affinely independent points in \(\mathcal X\), minus one. If \(\mathcal H_{a,b}\) is a supporting hyperplane of \(\mathcal X\), then \(\mathcal F=\mathcal X\cap\mathcal H_{a,b}\) is a face of \(\mathcal X\), and \(\mathcal F\) is itself a polyhedron. A face is proper if \(\varnothing\neq\mathcal F\neq\mathcal X\). A face of dimension \(0\) is an extreme point, one of dimension \(1\) is an edge, and one of dimension \(\dim\mathcal X-1\) is a facet. Every proper face of \(\mathcal X\) lies in \(\partial\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral dimension is one less than the maximum number of affinely independent points. Intersecting a polyhedron with a supporting hyperplane produces a polyhedral face. A nonempty face other than the whole polyhedron is proper; faces of dimensions zero, one, and one below the dimension of the polyhedron are respectively extreme points, edges, and facets. Every proper face lies on the boundary.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal H_{a,b}\text{ is a supporting hyperplane of }\mathcal X\text{ when defining }\mathcal F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F=\mathcal X\cap\mathcal H_{a,b}\text{ is a polyhedral face};\quad \varnothing\neq\mathcal F\neq\mathcal X\Rightarrow\mathcal F\subseteq\partial\mathcal X;\quad \dim\mathcal F=0,1,\dim\mathcal X-1\text{ defines respectively an extreme point, edge, and facet.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a nonempty polyhedron, and let \(F\) be a face of \(P\). The face \(F\) is called proper when
\[
\varnothing\ne F\subsetneq P.
\]
Equivalently, a proper face is neither the empty face nor the whole polyhedron. Under this convention, vertices, edges, and facets are proper faces whenever their dimensions are strictly smaller than \(\dim P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper face is a nonempty face strictly contained in the polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Boundary Decomposition by Proper Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic location of proper faces and localization of relative-boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty polyhedron. Every proper face \(F\) satisfies \(F\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}P\). Conversely, every \(x\in\operatorname{rbd}P\) has a proper carrier face \(F_P(x)\). Hence \[\operatorname{rbd}P=\bigcup\{F:F\text{ is a proper face of }P\},\] and a face meeting \(\operatorname{ri}P\) must equal \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative boundary is exactly the union of the proper faces, and any face meeting the relative interior is the whole polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rbd}P=\bigcup_{F\text{ proper}}F,\qquad F\cap\operatorname{ri}P\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow F=P.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative Boundary Decomposition by Proper Faces

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recursive Hierarchy of Proper Polyhedral Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's nonempty-bounded polyhedron convention and concerns nonempty proper faces; the empty face and the whole polyhedron are not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a \(k\)-dimensional polyhedron in the source's terminology, with \(k>0\). Its \((k-1)\)-dimensional boundary polyhedra are called faces of \(P\), and every face obtained recursively as a face of one of these faces is also called a face of \(P\). Thus \(P\) has proper faces of dimensions \(k-1,k-2,\ldots,0\). A zero-dimensional face is called a vertex, and a one-dimensional face is called an edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-dimensional nonempty bounded polyhedron, the codimension-one boundary pieces are faces, and their faces are recursively faces of the original polyhedron. Zero-dimensional faces are vertices and one-dimensional faces are edges.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a \(k\)-dimensional polyhedron in the source's terminology.
Faces are generated recursively from the codimension-one boundary polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ has proper faces of dimensions }k-1,k-2,\ldots,0;\quad \dim F=0\Rightarrow F\text{ is a vertex},\quad \dim F=1\Rightarrow F\text{ is an edge}.\)

children.top_down_role: Whole-set and convention-dependent extremal cases in the face hierarchy.

assumptions_latex: The empty set is admitted as a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The improper faces of \(P\) are exactly \(\varnothing\) and \(P\).
review_flags: convention_explicit: empty face is included in the face lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-lattice convention including the empty face.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Exposed Faces p. 113
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a nonempty polyhedron, using the convention that \(\varnothing\) is a face. The improper faces of \(P\) are defined to be
\[
\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad P.
\]
Every other face \(F\) satisfies \(\varnothing\ne F\subsetneq P\) and is proper. The whole polyhedron is the maximum element and the empty face is the minimum element of the face lattice ordered by inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the empty face included, the two improper faces are the empty set and the entire polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Improper Faces

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Exposed Faces p. 113
source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternative standard convention affecting the improper-face list.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the extended face-lattice convention, the improper faces of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\) are \(\varnothing\) and \(P\). If the definition of face excludes \(\varnothing\), then \(P\) is the sole improper face and the face poset has no adjoined bottom element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The empty set is improper only under conventions admitting it as a face; the whole polyhedron is always improper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varnothing\text{ excluded as a face}\implies P\text{ is the unique improper face}.
knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Face Convention Boundary

children.title: Exposed Faces
children.top_down_role: Faces selected by supporting linear objectives.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a face of \(P\) if and only if \(F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle\) for some attained, finite linear maximum.

notation.meaning: Maximizers of the linear functional over the polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty faces; the exposing functional may be zero for the whole face.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Exposed Faces p. 113
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty subset \(F\subseteq P\) is an exposed face of \(P\) if there exist \(c\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
\langle c,x\rangle\le\alpha\quad\text{for all }x\in P,
\qquad
F=\{x\in P:\langle c,x\rangle=\alpha\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle\), with a finite attained maximum. Every nonempty face of a polyhedron is exposed. Taking \(c=0\) exposes the improper face \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty polyhedral face is precisely the maximizer set of some linear functional that is bounded above on the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Faces

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Exposed Faces p. 113
source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates proper exposure, whole-set exposure, and the excluded empty face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), \[\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle=P\iff c\perp\operatorname{lin}(P-P).\] Thus every proper face requires a direction whose restriction to \(\operatorname{aff}P\) is nonconstant. An attained argmax set is never empty, so the empty face is not exposed under the attained-maximum convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directions constant on the affine hull expose the whole polyhedron; proper faces require nonconstant directions, and no attained objective exposes the empty face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle=P\iff c\perp\operatorname{lin}(P-P),\quad \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle\ne\varnothing\text{ when attained}.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant and Nonconstant Exposing Directions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior of the Normal Cone Selects the Exact Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes all linear directions exposing a prescribed nonempty polyhedral face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a nonempty face of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), choose \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), and set \[N_P(F):=N_P(x)=\{c:\langle c,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in P\}.\] Then \[\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in P}\langle c,y\rangle=F\iff c\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directions exposing exactly a given nonempty polyhedral face are the relative-interior vectors of that face's normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in P}\langle c,y\rangle=F\iff c\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).

notation.meaning: Normal cone at any relative-interior point of F

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interior of the Normal Cone Selects the Exact Face

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates proper exposure from exposure of the whole polyhedron and excludes the empty face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), the argmax of the zero functional is \(P\), never a proper face. Every nonempty proper face is exposed by a direction whose restriction to \(\operatorname{aff}P\) is nonconstant. The empty face cannot be represented as an attained argmax set. More generally, a vector \(c\) exposes \(P\) exactly when \(c\perp\operatorname{lin}(P-P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper faces require a direction nonconstant on the affine hull; constant directions expose the whole polyhedron, and no attained objective exposes the empty face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle=P\iff c\perp\operatorname{lin}(P-P)\), while an attained argmax is never empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero and Nonzero Exposing Directions

children.title: Supporting-Hyperplane Incidence
children.top_down_role: Incidence between supporting hyperplanes and selected faces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an index set \(I\), possibly empty, such that \(F=\{x\in P:A_Ix=b_I\}\); if \(F\subsetneq P\), then \(F\) is also the incidence set of a supporting hyperplane with nonzero normal.

notation.meaning: Rows of the inequality system indexed by I; I may be empty when F equals P.
A supporting hyperplane with nonzero normal c.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-inequality incidence for every nonempty face, with a genuine supporting-hyperplane description for proper nonempty faces.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Exposed Faces p. 113
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:Ax\le b\}\) be nonempty, and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(P\). There is an index set \(I\) of inequalities, possibly empty, such that
\[
F=\{x\in P:A_Ix=b_I\}.
\]
If \(F\subsetneq P\), then there exist \(c\in\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
P\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\langle c,x\rangle\le\alpha\},
\qquad
F=P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\langle c,x\rangle=\alpha\}.
\]
Thus every nonempty face is determined by simultaneously active inequalities, while every proper nonempty face is the incidence set of a genuine supporting hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face is determined by suitable active inequalities, with the empty index set allowed for the whole polyhedron; every proper nonempty face is also the incidence set of a supporting hyperplane with nonzero normal.
knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Hyperplane Incidence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal carrier face of a point or subset
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(S\subseteq P\). Denote the face family by \(\mathcal F(P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localization of points and subsets within the finite face lattice of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimal carrier face of \(S\) is \[\operatorname{face}_P(S)=\bigcap\{F\in\mathcal F(P):S\subseteq F\}.\] It is the unique inclusionwise smallest face of \(P\) containing \(S\). For a point \(x\in P\), write \(F_P(x)=\operatorname{face}_P(\{x\})\); it is uniquely characterized by \[x\in\operatorname{ri}F_P(x).\] If \(P=\{z:a_i^\top z\leq b_i,\ i\in M\}\) and \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^\top x=b_i\}\), then \[F_P(x)=\{z\in P:a_i^\top z=b_i\ \forall i\in I(x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal carrier face of a subset is the intersection of all faces containing it. For a point, it is the unique face whose relative interior contains that point, and it is obtained by imposing every defining constraint active at the point as an equality.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq P\); for the point formula, \(x\in P\).
For the active-set formula, \(P=\{z:a_i^\top z\leq b_i,\ i\in M\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{face}_P(S)\) is the unique smallest face containing \(S\), and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F_P(x)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite \(S=\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}\), \(\operatorname{face}_P(S)\) is the unique minimal face containing the union of the point carrier faces.
For a point \(x\), the carrier face is the intersection of all supporting hyperplanes of \(P\) that contain \(x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}P\), then \(F_P(x)=P\).
If \(x\) is a vertex, then \(F_P(x)=\{x\}\).
For \(S=\varnothing\), the intersection convention determines whether the carrier is \(\varnothing\) or the least face and must be fixed separately.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two points lie in the relative interior of the same face exactly when they have the same minimal carrier face.
If \(S\subseteq T\subseteq P\), then \(\operatorname{face}_P(S)\subseteq\operatorname{face}_P(T)\).
Facial localization is idempotent: \(\operatorname{face}_P(\operatorname{face}_P(S))=\operatorname{face}_P(S)\).
boundary_notes: The active-index set depends on the chosen H-description, but the resulting carrier face does not.
A constraint active at one point need not define a facet; redundant or implicit equalities may also be active.
For infinite-dimensional or nonpolyhedral convex sets, intersections and exposed-face formulas require separate qualifications.

notation.meaning: minimal face of P containing S
indices of inequalities active at x

source_refs.locator: §3.8, Theorem 3.24 and Proposition 3.25(iii), pp. 101–102

review_flags: The active-set formula should be interpreted using all inequalities active at the point; implicit equalities do not affect the resulting face.

children.top_down_role: Facial carriers associated with individual points.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is exactly one face \(F\) of \(P\) such that \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), namely \(F=F_P(\{x\})\).

notation.meaning: Minimal carrier face of the point x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F_P(x):=F_P(\{x\})\). Then \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F_P(x)\). Moreover, for every face \(G\) of \(P\), \[x\in\operatorname{ri}G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G=F_P(x).\] Thus the relative interiors of the nonempty faces of \(P\) are pairwise disjoint and form a partition of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of a polyhedron lies in the relative interior of exactly one face, its minimal carrier face.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise order characterization of containing faces and equality of facial strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and \(x,y\in P\). For every face \(G\) of \(P\), \[x\in G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_P(x)\subseteq G.\] Moreover, \(x\) and \(y\) lie in the relative interior of the same face if and only if \(F_P(x)=F_P(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face contains a point exactly when it contains that point's carrier face, and equal point carriers characterize a common facial stratum.
assumptions_latex: \(x,y\in P\), and \(G\) is a face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in G\iff F_P(x)\subseteq G,\qquad F_P(x)=F_P(y)\iff\exists H\in\mathcal F(P):x,y\in\operatorname{ri}H.

notation.meaning: Minimal carrier face of x in P

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in S\), let \(F_P(x)\) be its pointwise carrier face. The carrier of the whole subset satisfies \[F_P(S)=\bigcap\{F\in\mathcal F(P):F_P(x)\subseteq F\ \text{for every }x\in S\}=\bigvee_{x\in S}F_P(x).\] Consequently, \(S\subseteq G\) for a face \(G\) exactly when \(F_P(x)\subseteq G\) for every \(x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset's carrier face is the least face containing the carrier face of each of its points.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary calculus of nonempty subset carriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\varnothing\ne S\subseteq T\subseteq P\), then \[F_P(S)\subseteq F_P(T),\qquad F_P(S)=F_P(\operatorname{conv}S)=F_P(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S).\] For every nonempty family \((S_j)_{j\in J}\) of nonempty subsets of \(P\), \[F_P\!\left(\bigcup_{j\in J}S_j\right)=\bigvee_{j\in J}F_P(S_j).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset carriers are monotone, invariant under convex and closed-convex hulls, and turn unions into face-lattice joins.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_P(S)\subseteq F_P(T),\quad F_P(S)=F_P(\operatorname{conv}S)=F_P(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S).

children.title: Polyhedral Codimension Geometry
children.top_down_role: Codimension structure and its connection to irredundant inequalities.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Codimension of a Polyhedral Face
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron of dimension \(d\), and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(P\). Dimensions are taken in the affine hulls of the respective sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedra, including lower-dimensional and unbounded polyhedra; codimension is relative to the containing polyhedron, not necessarily to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The codimension of \(F\) in \(P\) is \[\operatorname{codim}_P F:=\dim P-\dim F.\] Thus \(F\) is a facet precisely when \(\operatorname{codim}_P F=1\). If \(P\) is represented relative to \(\operatorname{aff}P\) by an irredundant system \[P=\{x\in\operatorname{aff}P:a_i^Tx\le b_i,
 i=1,
\ldots,
 m\},\] then every inequality defines the facet \(F_i=P\cap\{x:a_i^Tx=b_i\}\), and every facet of \(P\) occurs in this way. More generally, if \(I(F):=\{i:a_i^Tx=b_i\ \forall x\in F\}\), then \[F=P\cap\bigcap_{i\in I(F)}\{x:a_i^Tx=b_i\},\qquad \operatorname{codim}_P F=\operatorname{rank}_{\operatorname{lin}(P-P)}\{a_i:i\in I(F)\}.\] The rank is that of the restrictions of the active normals to the direction space of \(\operatorname{aff}P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty face F of a d-dimensional polyhedron P, its codimension in P is dim P minus dim F. Facets are exactly the codimension-one faces. In an irredundant inequality description relative to the affine hull, inequalities and facets correspond one-to-one. Any face is obtained by making all inequalities active on it equalities, and its codimension is the rank of those active normals after restriction to the direction space of the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{codim}_P F=\dim P-\dim F\), with facets characterized by \(\operatorname{codim}_P F=1\) and irredundant inequalities corresponding to facets.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{codim}_P F=\dim\operatorname{aff}P-\dim\operatorname{aff}F\).
For an irredundant relative \(H\)-representation, \(F\) is a facet if and only if it is the equality set of exactly one facet-defining inequality, up to positive scaling and affine-hull equations.
special_cases_latex: If \(P\) is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\operatorname{codim}_P F=n-\dim F\).
A vertex of a pointed \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron has codimension \(d\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Any strict inclusion \(F\subsetneq G\) of nonempty faces implies \(\operatorname{codim}_P F>\operatorname{codim}_P G\).
Redundant inequalities need not correspond injectively to facets, whereas a minimal representation has one inequality per facet.
boundary_notes: Ambient codimension \(n-\dim F\) differs from relative codimension when \(P\) is not full-dimensional.
The number of active inequalities can exceed codimension when active normals are dependent or the description is redundant.

notation.meaning: Codimension of the face relative to the containing polyhedron.
Indices of inequalities active everywhere on the face.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The face \(R\) is a ridge of \(P\) if \[\operatorname{codim}_P R:=\dim P-\dim R=2,\] equivalently, if \(\dim R=d-2\). Thus a ridge is a facet of every facet of \(P\) that contains it. In particular, any strict chain from \(R\) to \(P\) through a proper intermediate face has the form \(R\subsetneq F\subsetneq P\), where \(F\) is a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ridge is a face of relative codimension two, hence a facet within every containing facet of the polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\), set \(F_i:=\{x\in P:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\). Irredundancy implies that \(F_i\) is a facet of \(P\). Conversely, every facet \(F\) of \(P\) equals \(F_i\) for a unique index \(i\), up to identifying positive scalar multiples of the same inequality. Thus an irredundant normalized inequality description and the facets of \(P\) correspond bijectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a full-dimensional irredundant inequality description, each inequality supports one facet, and every facet arises from exactly one normalized inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Witness Criteria for an Irredundant Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational tests for indispensability in a finite full-dimensional external description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\] be nonempty and full-dimensional. Inequality \(i\) is indispensable if and only if there exists \(z\) such that \[a_j^{\mathsf T}z\le b_j\ (j\ne i),\qquad a_i^{\mathsf T}z>b_i.\] If the entire description is irredundant, this is also equivalent to the existence of \(x\in P\) satisfying \[a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i,\qquad a_j^{\mathsf T}x<b_j\quad(j\ne i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality is indispensable exactly when deleting it admits a violating point; in an irredundant full-dimensional system, its facet also contains a point where every other inequality is strict.
assumptions_latex: The displayed system is finite and its inequalities are nontrivial.
The strict facet-point equivalence additionally assumes the entire description is irredundant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i\text{ is indispensable}\iff\exists z:\ a_{-i}^{\mathsf T}z\le b_{-i},\ a_i^{\mathsf T}z>b_i.
knowledge_statements.title: Witness Criteria for an Irredundant Inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Affine-Hull Form and Ambient Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension to lower-dimensional polyhedra and the failure of unrestricted ambient irredundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{aff}P\) and write \[P=\{x\in L:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\] using inequalities nonconstant on \(L\). If this relative description is irredundant, its normalized inequalities correspond bijectively to the facets of \(P\). Without restricting to \(L\), an indispensable ambient inequality may instead help enforce \(\operatorname{aff}P\) and have contact set \(P\), so the inequality–facet bijection can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-dimensional polyhedron, the facet correspondence requires an irredundant description relative to its affine hull; indispensable ambient inequalities need not define facets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative irredundant inequalities on L correspond to facets, whereas arbitrary ambient irredundancy need not.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Affine-Hull Form and Ambient Failure Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Witness Criterion for an Irredundant Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tests whether one inequality is indispensable in a finite full-dimensional external description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}
\]
be nonempty and full-dimensional. Inequality \(i\) is irredundant if and only if there exists \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) such that
\[
a_j^{\mathsf T}z\le b_j\quad(j\ne i),\qquad a_i^{\mathsf T}z>b_i.
\]
Equivalently, there exists \(x\in P\) with \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\) and \(a_j^{\mathsf T}x<b_j\) for every \(j\ne i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality is indispensable exactly when deleting it admits a point that violates it; in a full-dimensional irredundant system its facet has a point where every other inequality is strict.
assumptions_latex: The displayed system is finite and contains nontrivial inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inequality \(i\) is irredundant iff the system without it has a point violating it.
knowledge_statements.title: Witness Criterion for an Irredundant Inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Point and Directional Extreme Objects of a Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(K=\operatorname{rec}P\), and let \(L=K\cap(-K)=\operatorname{lin}P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedra. Ordinary extreme points occur only in the pointed regime; extreme recession directions are defined directly for pointed recession cones and modulo lineality otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(v\in P\) is an extreme point if, for all \(x,y\in P\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), \[v=\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y=v.\] A nonzero vector \(r\in K\) generates an extreme ray of a pointed cone \(K\) if \[r=u+w,
\quad u,w\in K\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u,w\in\operatorname{cone}\{r\}.\] For a nonpointed polyhedron, its point-like extreme objects are its minimal faces, each of which is an affine translate \(v+L\); its direction-like extreme objects are the faces of \(K\) having dimension \(\dim L+1\), equivalently the extreme rays of the quotient cone \(K/L\). Thus the extreme objects consist of zero-dimensional faces and one-dimensional recession faces when \(L=\{0\}\), and of their lineality-relative analogues when \(L\ne\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point cannot be expressed as a nontrivial convex combination of two different points of the polyhedron. An extreme ray of a pointed recession cone cannot be decomposed into two cone vectors outside that same ray. If lineality is present, the smallest point-like objects are affine translates of the lineality space, and the smallest nonlineality recession faces have dimension one more than the lineality space; these become points and rays after quotienting by lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extreme objects are characterized by indecomposability under convex or conic combinations, with minimal faces and quotient rays replacing points and rays in the nonpointed regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v\) is an extreme point of \(P\) if and only if \(\{v\}\) is a zero-dimensional face of \(P\).
For pointed \(K\), \(\operatorname{cone}\{r\}\) is extreme if and only if it is a one-dimensional face of \(K\).
special_cases_latex: For a polytope, all extreme objects are vertices; its recession cone is \(\{0\}\).
For a pointed unbounded polyhedron, both vertices and extreme rays may occur.
immediate_consequences_latex: A polyhedron containing a line has no ordinary extreme points.
A polyhedron has only finitely many minimal faces and lineality-relative extreme recession faces.
boundary_notes: A general ray of \(P\) need not be extreme.
In the nonpointed regime, choosing a representative point or direction is not canonical; the affine class or quotient ray is the intrinsic object.

notation.meaning: Lineality space of the polyhedron and its recession cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Extreme-Point Criteria and the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes extreme points in inequality and nonnegative equality forms and gives extreme-point attainment for an attained linear minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be polyhedral. (a) If \(P=\{x\mid a_j^Tx\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\), then \(v\in P\) is an extreme point if and only if \(\{a_j\mid a_j^Tv=b_j\}\) contains \(n\) linearly independent vectors. (b) If \(P=\{x\mid Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), then \(v\in P\) is an extreme point if and only if the columns of \(A\) indexed by \(\{i\mid v_i\ne0\}\) are linearly independent. (c) If \(P\) has at least one extreme point and a linear function attains a minimum over \(P\), then it attains a minimum at an extreme point of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an inequality-form polyhedron, a feasible point is extreme exactly when its active constraint normals contain n linearly independent vectors. In nonnegative equality form, it is extreme exactly when the columns indexed by its nonzero coordinates are linearly independent. If a polyhedron has an extreme point, every attained linear minimum has an extreme-point minimizer.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\mid a_j^Tx\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,r\},\quad v\in P\quad\text{(part (a))}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)\iff\operatorname{span}\{a_j:a_j^Tv=b_j\}=\mathbb R^n;\quad v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)\iff\{A_{:i}:v_i\ne0\}\text{ is linearly independent};\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^Tx\cap\operatorname{ext}(P)\ne\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-point attainment on a line-free polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum attainment at an extreme point for a convex function bounded above on a line-free polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and let \(C\neq\varnothing\) be a polyhedral convex set satisfying \(C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex as a Zero-Dimensional Extreme Face
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(v\in P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedra; the active-normal formulation is intrinsic after restricting normals to the direction space of \(\operatorname{aff}P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(v\) is a vertex of \(P\) when \(\{v\}\) is a face of \(P\), equivalently a face of dimension zero. It is an extreme point when \[v=\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y,
\quad x,y\in P,
\quad 0<\lambda<1\] implies \(x=y=v\). For polyhedra these definitions are equivalent. If \(P\) is pointed and full-dimensional, they are also equivalent to the active-constraint condition \[\operatorname{rank}A_{I(v)}=n,
\qquad I(v):=\{i:a_i^Tv=b_i\}.\] For a polyhedron of dimension \(d\), the relative version requires the restrictions of the active normals to \(\operatorname{lin}(P-P)\) to have rank \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex is a zero-dimensional face. An extreme point is a point admitting no nontrivial expression as a convex combination of two distinct feasible points. For polyhedra these notions coincide. In a full-dimensional pointed inequality representation, they are also equivalent to the active constraint normals spanning the whole ambient dual space; for a lower-dimensional polyhedron, the corresponding rank is taken relative to its affine hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\text{ is a vertex}\iff v\text{ is an extreme point}\iff\operatorname{rank}_{\operatorname{lin}(P-P)}\{a_i:i\in I(v)\}=\dim P\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists a valid inequality \(c^Tx\le\delta\) for \(P\) whose equality set on \(P\) is exactly \(\{v\}\).
The minimal face of \(P\) containing \(v\) is the singleton \(\{v\}\).
special_cases_latex: For a polytope \(P=\operatorname{conv}V\) with irredundant finite generator set \(V\), its vertices are precisely its extreme points.
If \(P\) contains a line, it has no vertices and no extreme points.
immediate_consequences_latex: A pointed polyhedron has at least one vertex.
At a vertex, at least \(\dim P\) active facet normals are needed, although more may be active in a degenerate representation.
boundary_notes: A point on a one-dimensional edge but not at its endpoint is not extreme.
The rank test must account for affine-hull equations when \(P\) is not full-dimensional.

notation.meaning: Index set of inequalities active at the point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Characterizations of Polyhedral Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes extreme points under inequality, equality-and-nonnegativity, and equality-and-bound representations of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be polyhedral and let \(v\in P\). (a) If \(P=\{x\mid a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\), then \(v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)\) if and only if \(\{a_j\mid a_j^{\mathsf T}v=b_j\}\) contains \(n\) linearly independent vectors. (b) If \(P=\{x\mid Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), then \(v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)\) if and only if the columns of \(A\) corresponding to the nonzero coordinates of \(v\) are linearly independent. (c) If \(P=\{x\mid Ax=b,\ c\le x\le d\}\), then \(v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)\) if and only if the columns of \(A\) corresponding to indices \(i\) satisfying \(c_i<v_i<d_i\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality-feasible point is extreme exactly when its active constraint normals span the ambient space. In equality form with nonnegativity or bounds, extremality is characterized by independence of the columns associated with nonzero or strictly interior coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}P&=\{x\mid a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}:&v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)&\iff\operatorname{rank}\{a_j\mid a_j^{\mathsf T}v=b_j\}=n;\\P&=\{x\mid Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}:&v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)&\iff\{A_{:i}\mid v_i\ne0\}\text{ is linearly independent};\\P&=\{x\mid Ax=b,\ c\le x\le d\}:&v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)&\iff\{A_{:i}\mid c_i<v_i<d_i\}\text{ is linearly independent}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded and Recession Types of One-Dimensional Faces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(E\) be a face of \(P\) with \(\dim E=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional faces of finite-dimensional polyhedra, with separate pointed and nonpointed regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-dimensional face \(E\) is called an edge. Exactly one of the following geometric forms applies. It is a bounded edge when \[E=[v,w]=\{(1-\lambda)v+\lambda w:0\le\lambda\le1\}\] for two distinct vertices \(v,w\) of \(P\). It is an unbounded pointed edge when \[E=v+\operatorname{cone}\{r\}=\{v+\lambda r:\lambda\ge0\}\] for a vertex \(v\), a nonzero recession vector \(r\), and an extreme ray \(\operatorname{cone}\{r\}\) of \(\operatorname{rec}P\). If \(P\) is nonpointed, no one-dimensional face exists unless \(\dim\operatorname{lin}P\le1\); when \(\dim\operatorname{lin}P=1\), every minimal face is an affine line parallel to \(\operatorname{lin}P\), not a bounded edge or a pointed half-line. Thus bounded segments and recession half-lines exhaust the pointed regime, while affine lines represent the lineality regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-dimensional face is an edge. In a pointed polyhedron it is either a segment joining two vertices or a half-line starting at one vertex in an extreme recession direction. In a nonpointed polyhedron every nonempty face contains the lineality space. Consequently, if lineality has dimension one, a minimal one-dimensional face is an affine line; if lineality has dimension greater than one, one-dimensional faces cannot occur.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim E=1\) yields a segment, a recession half-line, or—in the one-dimensional lineality regime—an affine line, according to boundedness and pointedness.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For pointed \(P\), an edge is bounded if and only if it has two vertices, and unbounded if and only if it has exactly one vertex.
An extreme ray of a pointed cone is precisely one of its one-dimensional faces.
special_cases_latex: For a polytope every edge is a bounded segment.
For a pointed polyhedral cone every edge is an extreme ray starting at the origin.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two vertices are adjacent exactly when they are contained in a common edge.
An unbounded pointed edge determines an extreme ray of \(\operatorname{rec}P\).
boundary_notes: A general unbounded subset of \(P\) need not be a face or an edge.
Affine lines are excluded from pointed polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme Classes in the Lineality Quotient
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, \(L=\operatorname{lin}P\), and \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\) the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpointed finite-dimensional polyhedra and their intrinsic pointed quotient geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quotient polyhedron is \(\bar P:=\pi(P)\). It is pointed because \[\operatorname{lin}\bar P=\pi(\operatorname{lin}P)=\{0\}.\] An extreme point class of \(P\) modulo lineality is a coset \(v+L\subseteq P\) such that \(\pi(v)\) is an extreme point of \(\bar P\). Equivalently, \(v+L\) is a minimal face of \(P\). An extreme direction class modulo lineality is a nonzero ray \(\operatorname{cone}\{\pi(r)\}\) that is an extreme ray of \(\operatorname{rec}\bar P=\pi(\operatorname{rec}P)\). Equivalently, its inverse image in \(\operatorname{rec}P\) is a face \(L+\operatorname{cone}\{r\}\) of dimension \(\dim L+1\). These classes are independent of the representatives \(v\) and \(r+\ell\), \(\ell\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a polyhedron by its lineality space produces a pointed polyhedron. A point-like extreme object of the original polyhedron is therefore a coset whose image is a vertex of the quotient; this coset is exactly a minimal face. A direction-like extreme object is an extreme ray of the quotient recession cone, represented upstairs by a face consisting of the lineality space plus one additional ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extreme points and rays modulo \(L\) are the vertices of \(\pi(P)\) and the extreme rays of \(\pi(\operatorname{rec}P)\), respectively.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v+L\) is point-extreme modulo \(L\) if and only if it contains no proper nonempty face of \(P\).
\(L+\operatorname{cone}\{r\}\) is direction-extreme modulo \(L\) if and only if its quotient is a one-dimensional face.
special_cases_latex: When \(L=\{0\}\), quotient extremality reduces to ordinary vertices and extreme rays.
When \(P\) is an affine space, \(P/L\) is a singleton and there are no nonzero quotient recession rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every minimal face of \(P\) is a translate of \(L\).
Representative choices made by an orthogonal complement produce the same quotient extreme classes.
boundary_notes: Ordinary extreme points do not exist when \(L\ne\{0\}\).
A complement-based pointed section depends on the chosen complement, whereas the quotient classes are canonical.
review_flags: The source states the equivalent orthogonal-section decomposition explicitly; the quotient notation is the coordinate-free formulation of the same reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Classes in the Lineality Quotient

children.title: Face-Incidence Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial organization of faces and local adjacency.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) denote all its faces, including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite face systems of finite-dimensional polyhedra; incidence is ordered by containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The face-incidence hierarchy of \(P\) is the ranked partially ordered set \[(\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq),\qquad \rho(F):=\dim F+1,\] with the convention \(\dim\varnothing=-1\). Two faces \(F,G\) are incident when \(F\subseteq G\) or \(G\subseteq F\). A cover relation \(F\prec G\) means \(F\subsetneq G\) and no face \(H\) satisfies \(F\subsetneq H\subsetneq G\); for polyhedra this implies \(\dim G=\dim F+1\). The meet and join are \[F\wedge G=F\cap G,
\qquad F\vee G=\text{the unique minimal face of }P\text{ containing }F\cup G.\] Hence \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) is a finite graded lattice, commonly called the face lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces of a polyhedron, ordered by inclusion, form its incidence hierarchy. Comparable faces are incident. A cover is an incidence with no intermediate face and increases dimension by one. Intersections give meets, while the unique smallest face containing two faces gives their join. Including the empty face and the whole polyhedron yields a finite graded lattice ranked by dimension plus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq)\) is a finite graded lattice with meet \(F\cap G\) and join equal to the minimal face containing \(F\cup G\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Hasse diagram of \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) records precisely the cover incidences between consecutive face dimensions.
For \(P=\{x:a_i^Tx\le b_i\}\), nonempty faces correspond to feasible active-index closures ordered oppositely by inclusion of their closed active sets.
special_cases_latex: The rank-one elements are vertices, rank-two elements are edges, and coatoms are facets.
For a polytope, the interval \([\varnothing,P]\) is the entire face lattice.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonmaximal face is contained in a facet.
Every face interval \([F,G]\) inherits a finite graded incidence structure.
boundary_notes: Two intersecting faces need not be incident unless one contains the other.
Distinct active-index subsets can define the same face in a redundant inequality representation.

notation.meaning: Set of all faces of P.
Cover relation in the face poset.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polytope. Write \(V(P)\), \(E(P)\), and \(\Phi(P)\) for its vertices, edges, and facets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The primal skeleton is defined for polytopes; the facet-adjacency graph is the dual codimension-one analogue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The one-skeleton of \(P\) is the undirected graph \[G_1(P):=(V(P),
\mathcal{E}_1),\] where \(\{v,w\}\in\mathcal{E}_1\) if and only if \(v\ne w\) and the segment \([v,w]\) is an edge of \(P\). The facet-adjacency graph is \[G_{d-1}(P):=(\Phi(P),
\mathcal{E}_{d-1}),
\qquad d:=\dim P,\] where \(\{F,G\}\in\mathcal{E}_{d-1}\) if and only if \(F\ne G\) and \(F\cap G\) is a face of dimension \(d-2\). These graphs are the rank-one and corank-one adjacency projections of the face lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-skeleton has the vertices of the polytope as graph nodes and joins two nodes exactly when their segment is a polyhedral edge. The facet-adjacency graph has facets as nodes and joins two facets exactly when their intersection is a ridge, a face two dimensions below the polytope. Both graphs are obtained by retaining selected consecutive levels of the face-incidence hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vertex adjacency is incidence through an edge, while facet adjacency is incidence through a ridge.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v\) and \(w\) are adjacent if and only if some one-dimensional face has exactly \(v\) and \(w\) as its vertices.
Facets \(F,G\) are adjacent if and only if they both cover the same \((d-2)\)-face.
special_cases_latex: For a polygon, the one-skeleton is its boundary cycle, and the facet-adjacency graph is the same cycle.
For a simplex, both graphs are complete graphs on \(d+1\) nodes.
immediate_consequences_latex: The degree of a vertex counts incident bounded edges.
In a simple \(d\)-polytope every vertex has degree \(d\).
boundary_notes: Unbounded polyhedra may have one-dimensional half-line faces that are not represented by a pair of vertices in the ordinary skeleton.
Facet intersections of dimension below \(d-2\) do not create facet-adjacency edges.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\) be full-dimensional and let \(u\neq v\) be vertices. Put \(I(u,v)=\{i:a_i^Tu=b_i=a_i^Tv\}\). The least face containing \(u,v\) is \(F(u,v)=\{x\in P:a_i^Tx=b_i\ \forall i\in I(u,v)\}\), and \(\dim F(u,v)=d-\operatorname{rank}A_{I(u,v)}\). Thus \(u,v\) are adjacent exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}A_{I(u,v)}=d-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two vertices of a full-dimensional H-polyhedron are adjacent exactly when their common active normals have rank d minus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\sim v\iff\operatorname{rank}A_{I(u,v)}=d-1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank characterization of adjacency in a standard-form polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the immediately preceding standard-form setup \(X=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), and let \(x^1,x^2\in\ddot X\) be distinct. Define \(\alpha=\{i:x_i^1>0\text{ or }x_i^2>0\}\). Then \(x^1\) and \(x^2\) are adjacent if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(A_{\cdot\alpha})=|\alpha|-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two distinct extreme points of a standard-form polyhedron, take the coordinates positive in at least one point. The points are adjacent exactly when the corresponding columns of A have rank one less than their number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^1\text{ and }x^2\text{ are adjacent}\iff\operatorname{rank}(A_{\cdot\alpha})=|\alpha|-1

children.title: Face-Flag Incidence Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Nested face chains and local incidence patterns.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron of dimension \(d\), with face lattice \(\mathcal{F}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite chains in the face lattice of a finite-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A face flag of length \(k\) is a strictly increasing chain \[\mathscr{C}=(F_0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_k),
\qquad F_i\in\mathcal{F}(P).\] Its rank set is \(\{\dim F_i+1:0\le i\le k\}\). The flag is saturated when every inclusion is a cover relation, equivalently \(\dim F_{i+1}=\dim F_i+1\). A complete flag is a saturated maximal chain \[\varnothing=F_{-1}\prec F_0\prec F_1\prec\cdots\prec F_d=P,
\qquad \dim F_j=j.\] Two flags have the same local incidence pattern when their rank sets agree and the corresponding containment relations occur inside isomorphic intervals of \(\mathcal{F}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face flag is a nested sequence of distinct faces. It is saturated when no intermediate face can be inserted, so consecutive dimensions differ by one. A complete flag runs from the empty face through one face of every dimension to the whole polyhedron. Rank sets record which dimensions occur and face-lattice intervals encode the local incidence pattern around a partial flag.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flags are chains in \(\mathcal{F}(P)\); complete flags contain exactly one face of every dimension from \(-1\) through \(d\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A saturated flag is a path moving upward along cover edges in the Hasse diagram of the face lattice.
A complete flag is a maximal chain in the finite graded lattice \(\mathcal{F}(P)\).
special_cases_latex: In a polygon, a complete flag has the form \(\varnothing\prec\{v\}\prec e\prec P\).
In a \(d\)-simplex, complete flags correspond to orderings of its \(d+1\) vertices.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every partial flag can be extended to a complete flag.
A complete flag in a \(d\)-polyhedron has \(d+2\) members when \(\varnothing\) and \(P\) are counted.
boundary_notes: A collection of pairwise intersecting faces need not be a flag because comparability by inclusion is required.
The source establishes the graded face hierarchy; the term “flag” is conventional terminology for chains in that hierarchy.

notation.meaning: A chain of faces constituting a flag.

review_flags: Locator supports finiteness, containment, and consecutive face dimensions but does not introduce the word “flag” explicitly.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face flag of \(P\) is a finite sequence \(\Phi=(F_0,\ldots,F_r)\) of faces satisfying \(F_0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_r\). Its length is \(r\). The flag is saturated when no face of \(P\) lies strictly between any consecutive \(F_i\) and \(F_{i+1}\). Thus face flags are precisely finite chains in the inclusion-ordered face lattice.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proper nonempty face flags of \(P\) correspond bijectively to simplices of \(\operatorname{sd}(\partial P)\).

children.title: Maximal Face Chains
children.top_down_role: Dimension-complete chains through the face hierarchy.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a pointed polyhedron of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every maximal face chain has one face of each dimension \(-1,0,\ldots,d\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graded face lattice of a pointed polyhedron
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness ensures that maximal chains begin with a vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be pointed and \(d\)-dimensional. A maximal face chain is a chain \[\varnothing=F_{-1}\subsetneq F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_d=P\] that cannot be enlarged by inserting another face. Every such chain is saturated and satisfies \(\dim F_i=i\) for \(i=0,\ldots,d\). Conversely, any chain containing exactly one face of each dimension from \(0\) through \(d\), together with \(\varnothing\), is maximal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a pointed d-dimensional polyhedron, every maximal face chain contains the empty face and exactly one face of each dimension from zero through d.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Face Chains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends the pointed seed to nonempty polyhedra with positive-dimensional lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a nonempty \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron with lineality space \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) of dimension \(\ell\). Every maximal chain has the form \(\varnothing\subsetneq F_\ell\subsetneq F_{\ell+1}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_d=P\), where \(\dim F_i=i\). Conversely, every such dimension-complete chain is maximal. Thus it has \(d-\ell+1\) strict inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal chain contains the empty face and one nonempty face of every dimension from the lineality dimension through the dimension of the polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every maximal chain has face dimensions \(-1,\ell,\ell+1,\ldots,d\) and \(d-\ell+1\) strict inclusions.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Chains with Lineality

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq G\) are nonempty faces of a polyhedron \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interval \([F,G]_{\mathcal F(P)}\) is graded, and every saturated chain from \(F\) to \(G\) has \(\dim G-\dim F\) inclusions.

notation.meaning: Face-lattice interval between F and G

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graded intervals in polyhedral face lattices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes incidence locally inside a fixed face interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty faces \(F\subseteq G\) of \(P\), define \([F,G]_{\mathcal F(P)}=\{H\in\mathcal F(P):F\subseteq H\subseteq G\}\). This interval records the local incidence pattern between \(F\) and \(G\). It is graded by \(H\mapsto\dim H-\dim F\): whenever \(H_1\) is covered by \(H_2\) in the interval, \(\dim H_2=\dim H_1+1\). Hence every saturated chain from \(F\) to \(G\) has \(\dim G-\dim F\) inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty faces lying between two fixed faces form a graded interval; saturated incidence chains have length equal to the dimension difference.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Incidence Patterns

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A full-dimensional formulation avoiding quotient notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be full-dimensional and let \(F\neq\varnothing\) be a face. For every \(H\) with \(F\subseteq H\subseteq P\), let \(N_P(H)\) be the normal cone along \(\operatorname{relint}H\). Then \(H\mapsto N_P(H)\) is an inclusion-reversing bijection from \([F,P]_{\mathcal F(P)}\) onto \(\mathcal F(N_P(F))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces containing a fixed face are anti-isomorphic to the faces of its normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([F,P]_{\mathcal F(P)}\cong\mathcal F(N_P(F))^{\mathrm{op}}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Cone and Lineality Space of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets, specialized in consequences to polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession cone and lineality space of \(C\) are \[\operatorname{rec}C:=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+\lambda r\in C\ \forall x\in C,
\forall\lambda\ge0\},\] \[\operatorname{lin}C:=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+\lambda r\in C\ \forall x\in C,
\forall\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}.\] They satisfy \[\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C),\] so \(\operatorname{lin}C\) is the largest linear subspace contained in \(\operatorname{rec}C\). The set \(C\) is pointed when \(\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\), equivalently when it contains no affine line. For closed convex \(C\), boundedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction can be added with every nonnegative multiplier to every point of the set without leaving it. A lineality direction permits every real multiplier. The lineality space is exactly the symmetric part of the recession cone and is its largest subspace. A set is pointed when this space is trivial, while a nonempty closed convex set is bounded exactly when it has no nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C)\), with pointedness determined by \(\operatorname{lin}C\) and boundedness by \(\operatorname{rec}C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(r\in\operatorname{rec}C\) if and only if \(C+r\subseteq C\).
\(r\in\operatorname{lin}C\) if and only if \(C+r=C\).
special_cases_latex: For an affine set \(a+L\), both its recession cone and lineality space equal \(L\).
For a polytope, \(\operatorname{rec}C=\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty face of a polyhedron has the same lineality space as the polyhedron.
A pointed unbounded polyhedron has nonzero recession directions but no two-sided lineality directions.
boundary_notes: Closedness is material to the stated boundedness characterization for arbitrary convex sets.
Pointedness does not imply boundedness.

§3.6, “Lineality Space and Recession Cone,” pp. 97–99

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constraint and Generator Descriptions of Polyhedral Recession
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) be nonempty, and suppose also that \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v^1,
\ldots,
 v^p\}+\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,
\ldots,
 r^q\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedra with both half-space and Minkowski–Weyl representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession cone of \(P\) is \[\operatorname{rec}P=\{r:x+\lambda r\in P\ \forall x\in P,
\forall\lambda\ge0\}.\] For the two displayed representations it has the equivalent descriptions \[\operatorname{rec}P=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ar\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,
\ldots,
 r^q\}.\] Its lineality space is \[\operatorname{lin}P=\{r:Ar=0\}=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P).\] Thus recession removes the offsets \(b\) from an \(H\)-representation and removes the bounded convex-hull component from a \(V\)-plus-ray representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone collects all directions along which the polyhedron can be translated indefinitely. In an inequality description it is obtained by homogenizing the inequalities, replacing b by zero. In a Minkowski–Weyl description it is the cone generated by the recession generators. The lineality space is obtained by turning the homogeneous inequalities into equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\operatorname{rec}P=\{r:Ar\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,
\ldots,
 r^q\}\) and \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{r:Ar=0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(r\in\operatorname{rec}P\) if and only if \(P+r\subseteq P\).
If \(x_0\in P\), then \(r\in\operatorname{rec}P\) if and only if \(x_0+\lambda r\in P\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(P\) is a polytope, then \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}\).
If \(P\) is a polyhedral cone, then \(\operatorname{rec}P=P\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The recession cone of a polyhedron is itself a polyhedral cone.
\(P\) is bounded if and only if the homogeneous system \(Ar\le0\) has only the solution \(r=0\).
boundary_notes: The generator family need not be minimal; nonextreme or repeated rays may be present.
The equality \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{r:Ar\le0\}\) assumes \(P\) is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional consequences of the inequality-side lineality formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\neq\varnothing\), and let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\). Then
\[L^\perp=\operatorname{range}(A^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{span}\{a_i:i\text{ is a row index of }A\},\qquad \dim L=n-\operatorname{rank}A.\]

children.title: Pointed-Quotient Reduction
children.top_down_role: Reduction of nonpointed geometry to pointed representatives.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointed Representative and Quotient by Lineality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\), and let \(M\) be any linear complement of \(L\), so \(\mathbb{R}^n=L\oplus M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonpointed polyhedra; both quotient and complementary-section realizations are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The pointed-quotient reduction of \(P\) is the quotient polyhedron \[\bar P:=\pi(P)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n/L,
\qquad \pi(x)=x+L.\] It satisfies \(\operatorname{lin}\bar P=\{0\}\). A complementary pointed representative is \[Q:=P\cap M,\] after translating coordinates if necessary so that the chosen complement meets \(P\). Under the canonical identification \(M\cong\mathbb{R}^n/L\), \(Q\) represents \(\bar P\), and \[P=Q+L,
\qquad \operatorname{rec}P=\operatorname{rec}Q+L.\] For the orthogonal choice \(M=L^\perp\), the representative is \(Q=P\cap L^\perp\), and every \(x\in P\) has a unique decomposition \(x=q+
\ell\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(\ell\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lineality can be removed canonically by passing to the quotient space. The quotient polyhedron is pointed. Choosing a complementary subspace realizes that quotient as a pointed section Q, and the original polyhedron is recovered by adding the lineality space. An orthogonal complement gives a convenient unique representative of each coset, although the quotient itself does not depend on this choice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P/L\) is pointed and any complementary representative \(Q\) gives \(P=Q+L\) and \(\operatorname{rec}P=\operatorname{rec}Q+L\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The fibers of \(\pi|_P\) are precisely the affine sets \(x+L\subseteq P\).
For \(M=L^\perp\), orthogonal projection onto \(L^\perp\) maps \(P\) onto \(Q\) and identifies \(Q\) with \(P/L\).
special_cases_latex: If \(P\) is pointed, then \(L=\{0\}\) and \(Q=P\).
If \(P=a+L\) is affine, then \(P/L\) is a singleton.
immediate_consequences_latex: Minimal faces of \(P\) correspond to vertices of \(Q\).
Faces of \(\operatorname{rec}P\) immediately above \(L\) correspond to extreme rays of \(\operatorname{rec}Q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Lineality Criterion for a Pointed Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for quotienting by a subspace of the lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron with \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\), let \(S\subseteq L\) be a linear subspace, and let \(\pi_S:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n/S\) be the quotient map. Then
\[\operatorname{lin}(\pi_S(P))=\pi_S(L)\cong L/S.\]
Consequently, \(\pi_S(P)\) is pointed if and only if \(S=L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient removes every line exactly when it factors out the entire lineality space; any smaller lineality subspace leaves residual lineality.
assumptions_latex: \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) and \(S\subseteq L\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(\pi_S(P))\cong L/S\), so \(\pi_S(P)\) is pointed exactly when \(S=L\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face-Lattice Correspondence under the Lineality Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial structure of a polyhedron modulo its complete lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n/L\). Every nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\) satisfies \(F+L=F\). The assignments
\[F\mapsto\pi(F),\qquad G\mapsto P\cap\pi^{-1}(G)\]
are mutually inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between the nonempty faces of \(P\) and \(\pi(P)\), and
\[\dim F=\dim\pi(F)+\dim L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting by lineality preserves the nonempty face lattice and subtracts the lineality dimension from every face dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) and \(\pi\) is the quotient map modulo L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonempty face lattices of \(P\) and \(\pi(P)\) are isomorphic, with \(\dim F=\dim\pi(F)+\dim L\).
