knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Classification of Polyhedral Boundedness and Vertex Existence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, \(K=\operatorname{rec}P\), and \(L=K\cap(-K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedra; empty feasible sets are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The boundedness–vertex regime of \(P\) is classified by the pair \((K,L)\): \[P\text{ is bounded}\iff K=\{0\},\] \[P\text{ has a vertex}\iff P\text{ is pointed}\iff L=\{0\}.\] Accordingly, \(P\) lies in exactly one of three regimes: (i) bounded, where \(K=L=\{0\}\) and \(P\) is a polytope with vertices; (ii) unbounded pointed, where \(K\ne\{0\}\) and \(L=\{0\}\), so vertices and extreme recession rays may coexist; or (iii) nonpointed, where \(L\ne\{0\}\), so \(P\) contains lines and has no ordinary vertices, although its quotient \(P/L\) is pointed and has quotient vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is bounded exactly when its recession cone is trivial. It has an ordinary vertex exactly when its lineality space is trivial. This gives three mutually exclusive regimes: bounded polytopes; unbounded but pointed polyhedra, which may have both vertices and recession rays; and nonpointed polyhedra, which contain lines and have no ordinary vertices but retain vertex classes after quotienting by lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\{0\}\) characterizes boundedness, while \(L=\{0\}\) characterizes pointedness and vertex existence.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), boundedness means \(Ar\le0\Rightarrow r=0\).
Pointedness means \(Ar=0\Rightarrow r=0\), equivalently \(A\) has trivial null space after affine-hull reduction.
special_cases_latex: A singleton is bounded and pointed and has one vertex.
An affine line is nonpointed, unbounded, and has no vertex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty polytope has at least one vertex.
Unboundedness alone does not preclude vertices; nontrivial lineality does.
boundary_notes: The equivalence between pointedness and vertex existence is special to nonempty polyhedra and does not hold for all closed convex sets.
An unbounded pointed polyhedron need not have a bounded objective value in every linear direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence Excess of a Polyhedral Face
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\) be a \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron and let \(F\) be a nonempty face. Let \(\Phi_F\) be the set of distinct facets of \(P\) containing \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial facial degeneracy measured using intrinsic facets, so it is independent of redundant copies in a chosen inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial incidence excess of \(F\) is \[\delta_P(F):=|\Phi_F|-\operatorname{codim}_P F.\] The face is incidence-nondegenerate when \(\delta_P(F)=0\), and incidence-degenerate when \(\delta_P(F)>0\). Since a codimension-\(k\) face requires at least \(k\) independent supporting normals, \(\delta_P(F)\ge0\). In an irredundant relative \(H\)-representation, \(|\Phi_F|\) equals the number of facet inequalities active everywhere on \(F\). Degeneracy therefore records excess facet incidence beyond the codimension forced by dimension, rather than mere duplication or scaling of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a face F, count the distinct facets containing it and subtract its codimension. The result is the facial incidence excess. Zero excess is the nondegenerate incidence pattern; positive excess means more facets meet at the face than dimension alone requires. Using distinct intrinsic facets prevents duplicated or redundant inequalities from creating artificial facial degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is facially degenerate exactly when \(|\Phi_F|>\operatorname{codim}_P F\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In a minimal inequality representation, \(\delta_P(F)=|I(F)|-\operatorname{rank}_{\operatorname{lin}(P-P)}\{a_i:i\in I(F)\}\).
For a vertex \(v\) of a \(d\)-polytope, \(\delta_P(v)=|\Phi_v|-d\).
special_cases_latex: A simple polytope has \(\delta_P(v)=0\) at every vertex.
A vertex incident with more than \(d\) facets has positive incidence excess.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive excess permits several different active-facet subsets to span the same normal space.
Facial degeneracy can complicate enumeration because active descriptions of the same face need not be minimal or unique.
boundary_notes: Representation degeneracy caused solely by repeated inequalities is excluded by counting distinct facets.
Incidence excess is not a condition number and does not quantify metric near-dependence of normals.

children.title: Vertex Simplicity Classes
children.top_down_role: Vertex regimes distinguished by local facet incidence.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\) be a \(d\)-dimensional polytope and let \(v\) be a vertex of \(P\). Denote by \(\Phi(v)\) the facets containing \(v\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic simplicity for vertices of finite-dimensional polytopes, with an active-constraint formulation for irredundant descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The vertex \(v\) is simple when it belongs to exactly \(d\) facets: \[|\Phi(v)|=d.\] It is nonsimple when \(|\Phi(v)|>d\). The polytope \(P\) is simple when every vertex is simple. If \[P=\{x\in\operatorname{aff}P:a_i^Tx\le b_i,
\ i=1,
\ldots,
 m\}\] is irredundant, then \(v\) is simple exactly when precisely \(d\) facet inequalities are active at \(v\). Equivalently, the tangent cone at \(v\), translated to the origin and viewed in \(\operatorname{lin}(P-P)\), has exactly \(d\) extreme rays, and the vertex has exactly \(d\) adjacent vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex of a d-dimensional polytope is simple if exactly d facets contain it, and nonsimple if more than d do. A polytope is simple when all its vertices are simple. In an irredundant description, this is the same as having exactly d active facet inequalities. Locally, a simple vertex has an orthant-like tangent cone, exactly d incident edges, and exactly d neighboring vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is simple if and only if \(|\Phi(v)|=d\), equivalently its local edge degree is \(d\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone of dimension \(d\), considered in its linear span.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointed finite-dimensional polyhedral cones; lower-dimensional cones are treated relative to their span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone \(K\) is simplicial when there exist linearly independent vectors \(r^1,
\ldots,
 r^d\) such that \[K=\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,
\ldots,
 r^d\}.\] Equivalently, \(K\) has exactly \(d\) extreme rays, and any choice of one nonzero generator from each extreme ray is linearly independent. The cone is nonsimplicial when it has more than \(d\) extreme rays. If \(R=[r^1\ \cdots\ r^d]\) is expressed in coordinates on \(\operatorname{span}K\), simpliciality is equivalent to \(R\) being nonsingular and \[K=R\mathbb{R}_+^d.\] Thus each \(x\in K\) has a unique coefficient vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^d\) with \(x=R\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A d-dimensional pointed polyhedral cone is simplicial if it is generated by d linearly independent rays. Equivalently, it has exactly d extreme rays. In coordinates on its span, it is an invertible linear image of the nonnegative orthant, and every cone vector has unique nonnegative coordinates in the extreme-ray generators. A pointed cone with more than d extreme rays is nonsimplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is simplicial if and only if it has \(d=\dim K\) linearly independent extreme-ray generators.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists a linear isomorphism \(T:\operatorname{span}K\to\mathbb{R}^d\) such that \(T(K)=\mathbb{R}_+^d\).
A full-dimensional cone \(K=\operatorname{pos}R\) is simplicial when \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is nonsingular.
special_cases_latex: Every one-dimensional pointed cone is simplicial.
The nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb{R}_+^d\) is simplicial.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every face of a simplicial cone is generated by a subset of its extreme rays.
The face lattice of a simplicial \(d\)-cone is Boolean on its \(d\) extreme rays.
boundary_notes: A cone containing a nonzero line is not simplicial under this pointed-cone definition.
A redundant generating list may be linearly dependent even when the cone itself is simplicial; minimal extreme-ray generators must be used.

notation.meaning: Cone of nonnegative linear combinations of the columns of R.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{span}K\) and \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}\), where \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\) form a basis of \(S\). If \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\in S\) is the dual basis, \(\langle u_i,r_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\), then \[K_S^*=\{y\in S:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}=\operatorname{cone}\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}.\] Thus the intrinsic dual of a simplicial cone is simplicial.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal Cones and the Normal Fan of a Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. For a nonempty face \(F\), choose any \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedra; normal cones encode dual objective directions and are constant on relative interiors of faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The normal cone of \(P\) along \(F\) is \[N_P(F):=N_P(x):=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^T(y-x)\le0\ \forall y\in P\},
\qquad x\in\operatorname{ri}F.\] Equivalently, \[c\in N_P(F)\iff F\subseteq\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in P}c^Ty.\] Its relative interior consists of objective vectors whose maximizing face is exactly \(F\): \[c\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\iff \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in P}c^Ty=F.\] The collection \[\mathcal{N}(P):=\{N_P(F):F\text{ a nonempty face of }P\}\] is the normal-cone complex, or normal fan when these cones cover the relevant dual space. Face inclusion reverses: \(F\subseteq G\) implies \(N_P(G)\subseteq N_P(F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cone of a face consists of linear objective vectors maximized throughout that face. Vectors in its relative interior select exactly that face as the optimizer set. Collecting the normal cones over all faces yields the normal-cone complex, which organizes objective space into polyhedral regions. Larger primal faces correspond to smaller dual cones, so the correspondence reverses face inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_P(F)=\{c:F\subseteq\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in P}c^Ty\}\), and the family \(\mathcal{N}(P)\) reverses the face-incidence order.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(N_P(x)=\partial\delta_P(x)\), where \(\delta_P\) is the convex indicator of \(P\).
For \(P=\{y:a_i^Ty\le b_i\}\) and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), \(N_P(F)=\operatorname{cone}\{a_i:i\in I(F)\}\), modulo normals to \(\operatorname{aff}P\) in the lower-dimensional case.
special_cases_latex: At an interior point of a full-dimensional polyhedron, the normal cone is \(\{0\}\).
At a vertex of a full-dimensional polytope, the normal cone is full-dimensional.
immediate_consequences_latex: Linear objectives with coefficients in the same relative-open normal cone have the same optimal face.
Facet normals, active-constraint representations, primal faces, and linear-objective optimality regions are linked by the normal-cone correspondence.
boundary_notes: For an unbounded polyhedron, normal cones need not cover all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\); objectives outside their union may be unbounded above.
For a lower-dimensional polyhedron, every normal cone contains \(\operatorname{lin}(P-P)^\perp\).

notation.meaning: Normal cone of P along the relative interior of F.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar of a Polyhedral Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\). Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral convex set containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional set polarity with the unit-level convention; conic polarity is recorded as the homogeneous special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar of \(C\) is
\[
C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,y\rangle\leq 1\ \text{for every }x\in C\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\leq1\}\), where \(\sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\). Polarity reverses inclusion: for sets \(C_1,C_2\) containing the origin, \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) implies \(C_2^\circ\subseteq C_1^\circ\). Since a polyhedral convex set is closed, the bipolar identity is \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\). If \(C=K\) is a convex cone, positive scaling makes the unit bound equivalent to the homogeneous condition, so
\[
K^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty polyhedral convex set C in Euclidean space that contains the origin, its polar consists of all vectors y whose inner product with every point of C is at most one. It is the unit sublevel set of the support function. Polarity reverses containment, and applying it twice returns C because C is closed and convex and contains zero. For a cone, the defining upper bound becomes zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\leq1\},\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C,\qquad C_1\subseteq C_2\Rightarrow C_2^\circ\subseteq C_1^\circ.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[C^\circ=\bigcap_{x\in C}\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\}.\]
For a cone \(K\), \[K^\circ=\{y:\sigma_K(y)=0\}=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\), then \[C^\circ=\{y:\langle v_i,y\rangle\leq1,5 i\leq m\}.\]
If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\}\), then \[K^\circ=\{y:\langle r_j,y\rangle\leq0,5 j\leq q\}.\]
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar of a polyhedral convex set is polyhedral.
If \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(C^\circ\) is bounded; if in addition \(C\) is bounded, both members of the polar pair are polytopes.
boundary_notes: If a convex set does not contain the origin, the bipolar is the closed convex hull of the set together with the origin, not necessarily the original set.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed polyhedral convex cone. Adopt the nonpositive polar convention \(K^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous polarity, emphasizing the exchange between finite generator and finite inequality descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A conic polar-dual representation pair consists of the mutually polar cones
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\},\qquad K^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle r_j,y\rangle\leq0,5 j\leq q\},
\]
and, equivalently, whenever
\[
K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle a_i,x\rangle\leq0,5 i\leq m\},
\]
one has
\[
K^\circ=\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}.
\]
Redundant generators or inequalities are permitted. Closedness gives \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\), so the generator-to-inequality exchange is involutive at the level of the represented cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic polar-dual representation pair is a closed polyhedral cone and its polar. A finite generating list for the primal cone becomes a finite list of homogeneous inequalities for the polar. Conversely, the normal vectors in a homogeneous inequality description of the primal generate its polar. Applying polarity again returns the original closed cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_j\}_{j=1}^q\Longleftrightarrow K^\circ=\{y:\langle r_j,y\rangle\leq0\ \forall j\},\qquad K^{\circ\circ}=K.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(R=[r_1\ \cdots\ r_q]\), \[K=\{R\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^q\},\qquad K^\circ=\{y:R^\top y\leq0\}.\]
If \(K=\{x:A x\leq0\}\) and the rows of \(A\) are \(a_i^\top\), then \[K^\circ=\{A^\top\mu:\mu\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^n\), \(K^\circ=\mathbb{R}_-^n\).
For a linear subspace \(L\), \(L^\circ=L^\perp\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Facets in an irredundant full-dimensional inequality representation correspond to extreme rays of the polar, and extreme rays correspond to polar facets.
The representation exchange remains valid with redundant rows or generators, although such descriptions do not encode a bijection of individual entries.
boundary_notes: With the nonnegative dual-cone convention \(K^*=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\), one has \(K^*=-K^\circ\).
For infinitely generated cones, closure may be required when recovering a generator cone from inequalities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp role of origin interiority in normalized bounded polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope and define \(P^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in P\}\). Then
\[
P^\circ\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\operatorname{int}P.
\]
If \(0\in P\setminus\operatorname{int}P\), then \(P^\circ\) is unbounded but \((P^\circ)^\circ=P\). If \(0\notin P\), then
\[
(P^\circ)^\circ=\operatorname{conv}(P\cup\{0\}),
\]
so double normalized polarity does not recover \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar is bounded exactly when the origin is interior. A boundary origin yields an unbounded polar, while an excluded origin is adjoined by double polarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^\circ\) is bounded iff \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and \((P^\circ)^\circ=\operatorname{conv}(P\cup\{0\})\).
knowledge_statements.title: Boundedness Boundary for Polar Polytopes

Its normalized polar is \[P^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\ \text{for every }x\in P\}.\] Then \(P^\circ\) is also a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P^\circ\), and normalized bipolarity gives \((P^\circ)^\circ=P\). If \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\), then \(P^\circ=\{y:\langle y,v_i\rangle\le1\text{ for all }i\}\).

children.title: Face-Polarity Duality
children.top_down_role: The order-reversing correspondence between primal and polar faces.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(P^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in P\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face polarity for full-dimensional polytopes with the origin in their interiors; this avoids quotient-space qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty proper face \(F\) of \(P\), its polar face is
\[
F^\triangle:=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\ \text{for every }x\in F\}.
\]
The assignment \(F\mapsto F^\triangle\) is an inclusion-reversing bijection between the nonempty proper faces of \(P\) and those of \(P^\circ\). Its inverse is the same construction in the opposite direction:
\[
(F^\triangle)^\triangle=F.
\]
If \(F\) has dimension \(k\), then \(F^\triangle\) has dimension \(n-1-k\). With the conventional extensions \(\varnothing^\triangle=P^\circ\) and \(P^\triangle=\varnothing\), this is an anti-isomorphism of the complete face lattices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional polytope containing zero in its interior, the face polar to F consists of the points of the polar polytope that pair to one with every point of F. This operation reverses inclusion, is bijective, and returns F when applied twice. The dimensions of paired proper faces add to n minus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F\subseteq G\Longleftrightarrow G^\triangle\subseteq F^\triangle,\qquad(F^\triangle)^\triangle=F,\qquad\dim F+\dim F^\triangle=n-1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For any \(x_F\in\operatorname{ri}F\), \[F^\triangle=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x_F,y\rangle=1\}.\]
The vertices of \(P\) correspond to facets of \(P^\circ\), while facets of \(P\) correspond to vertices of \(P^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: If \(F=\{v\}\) is a vertex, then \[F^\triangle=P^\circ\cap\{y:\langle v,y\rangle=1\}\] is a facet.
If \(F\) is a facet supported by \(\langle a,x\rangle\leq1\), then \(F^\triangle=\{a\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The face lattices of \(P\) and \(P^\circ\) are anti-isomorphic.
The numbers of \(k\)-faces of \(P\) and \((n-1-k)\)-faces of \(P^\circ\) coincide.
boundary_notes: If the origin is on the boundary or outside the polytope, the stated polar need not be a full-dimensional polytope and the dimension formula requires modification.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Use the coordinate order on \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\). A convex corner is a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) that is lower comprehensive: \(0\leq z\leq x\in C\Rightarrow z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative, order-compatible polarity for closed convex corners, also called antiblocker polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The nonnegative polar, or antiblocker, of a convex corner \(C\) is
\[
\operatorname{abl}(C):=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \text{for every }x\in C\}=C^\circ\cap\mathbb{R}_+^n.
\]
It is itself a convex corner. The transformation is order reversing on convex corners and involutive:
\[
C_1\subseteq C_2\Rightarrow\operatorname{abl}(C_2)\subseteq\operatorname{abl}(C_1),
\qquad \operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(C))=C.
\]
Thus convex corners form a polarity class within the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex corner is a closed convex lower-comprehensive subset of the nonnegative orthant. Its antiblocker consists of the nonnegative vectors whose inner product with every point of the corner is at most one. Antiblocking reverses containment, maps convex corners to convex corners, and applying it twice recovers the original corner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{abl}(C)=C^\circ\cap\mathbb{R}_+^n,\qquad \operatorname{abl}^2(C)=C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{abl}(C)=\{y\geq0:\sigma_C(y)\leq1\}.\]
For \(y\geq0\), membership in \(\operatorname{abl}(C)\) is equivalent to validity of the inequality \(y^\top x\leq1\) over all \(x\in C\).
special_cases_latex: For the box \(C=[0,u]\) with \(u\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\), \[\operatorname{abl}(C)=\{y\geq0:u^\top y\leq1\}.\]
For \(C=\{x\geq0:a^\top x\leq1\}\) with \(a>0\), \(\operatorname{abl}(C)=[0,a]\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Extreme nonnegative valid inequalities of one member correspond to generator geometry of its antiblocker.
The restriction \(y\geq0\) makes polarity compatible with coordinatewise downward closure.
boundary_notes: The involution is asserted only for closed convex lower-comprehensive sets in \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\); arbitrary nonnegative sets must first be closed and convexified appropriately.
No inspected source hint supported the exact antiblocker terminology and involution.

notation.meaning: Antiblocker or nonnegative polar of C.

children.title: Blocking Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Upward-closed polyhedral structures in nonnegative models.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession and vertex representation of nonempty upward-comprehensive polyhedra in the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^d\) be a nonempty polyhedron satisfying \(B+\mathbb{R}_+^d=B\). Then \[\operatorname{rec}B=\mathbb{R}_+^d.\] Consequently \(B\) is pointed, has a nonempty finite vertex set \(V(B)\), and \[B=\operatorname{conv}V(B)+\mathbb{R}_+^d.\] Conversely, every set \(\operatorname{conv}V+\mathbb{R}_+^d\) with nonempty finite \(V\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^d\) is a blocking polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty blocking polyhedron is the nonnegative dominant of the convex hull of finitely many vertices, and its recession cone is the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}B=\mathbb{R}_+^d\) and \(B=\operatorname{conv}V(B)+\mathbb{R}_+^d\).

notation.meaning: Finite vertex set of the blocking polyhedron

knowledge_statements.title: Dominant Representation of Blocking Polyhedra

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is blocking exactly when \(B+\mathbb{R}_+^d=B\); its blocker is \(b(B)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^d:\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\ \forall x\in B\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative, upward-closed polyhedra and their normalized blocker operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty polyhedron \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^d\) is blocking when it is upward closed in the coordinate order, equivalently, \[B+\mathbb{R}_+^d=B.\] Its blocker is the nonnegative polyhedron \[b(B)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^d:\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\ \text{for every }x\in B\}.\] Thus points of \(b(B)\) certify a unit lower bound against every point of \(B\). Under the standard nonempty blocking hypotheses for which the blocker is proper, blocker duality is involutive: \(b(b(B))=B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blocking polyhedron is a nonnegative polyhedron closed upward coordinatewise; its blocker consists of nonnegative vectors pairing to at least one with every point.
knowledge_statements.title: Blocking Polyhedra

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, but no source is supplied, and the final involutivity claim refers to unspecified 'standard nonempty blocking hypotheses.' A source and explicit hypotheses are needed before the mathematical version can be validated.

children.title: Anti-Blocking Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Downward-closed polyhedral structures in nonnegative models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative Inequality Representation of Anti-Blocking Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inequality characterization of lower-comprehensive polyhedra in the nonnegative orthant, including unbounded instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. Then \(P\) is lower-comprehensive if and only if there exist \(m\geq0\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) such that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:Ax\leq b\}.\] Rows may be absent in unbounded coordinate directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anti-blocking polyhedra are exactly nonnegative polyhedra describable by upper inequalities with nonnegative coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is lower-comprehensive}\iff\exists A\geq0,\ b\geq0:\ P=\{x\geq0:Ax\leq b\}.

notation.meaning: Every entry of the inequality matrix is nonnegative

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Inequality Representation of Anti-Blocking Polyhedra

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is anti-blocking exactly when it is lower-comprehensive in the coordinatewise order.

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise partial order on the nonnegative orthant.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the downward-closed convention for anti-blocking polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is anti-blocking if
\[
x\in P,\quad y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n,\quad 0\leq y\leq x
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y\in P.
\]
Thus membership is preserved by decreasing any coordinates without making them negative. In particular, every nonempty anti-blocking polyhedron contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An anti-blocking polyhedron lies in the nonnegative orthant and contains every nonnegative vector dominated coordinatewise by one of its points.
knowledge_statements.title: Anti-Blocking Polyhedra

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The downward-closed definition and its consequence that 0 belongs to every nonempty anti-blocking polyhedron are mathematically coherent and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonnegative-Orthant Polarity
children.top_down_role: Order-compatible polarity linking blocking-type classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp arbitrary-set extension of anti-blocker bipolarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty \(S\subseteq\mathbb R_+^n\), define \(\operatorname{down}(S):=\{z\in\mathbb R_+^n:\exists x\in S,\ 0\le z\le x\}\). Then
\[
\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(S))=\operatorname{cl}\!\bigl(\operatorname{down}(\operatorname{conv}S)\bigr).
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{abl}^2(S)=S\) exactly when \(S\) is closed, convex, and lower-comprehensive. For example, \(S=\{(1,1)\}\) has \(\operatorname{abl}^2(S)=[0,1]^2\ne S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double nonnegative polarity returns the closed convex lower-comprehensive hull; without those fixed-point properties it can enlarge the set strictly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{abl}^2(S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{down}(\operatorname{conv}S))\), with equality to \(S\) exactly for closed convex lower-comprehensive \(S\).

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise lower closure of S in the nonnegative orthant.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Bipolar Closure

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and lower-comprehensive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{abl}(C)\) has the same structural properties and \(\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(C))=C\).

notation.meaning: Anti-blocker, or nonnegative-orthant polar, of a set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States anti-blocker polarity for closed convex lower-comprehensive sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the nonnegative-orthant polar of \(C\) by
\[
\operatorname{abl}(C):=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\text{ for every }x\in C\}.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{abl}(C)\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and lower-comprehensive, and the bipolar identity is
\[
\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(C))=C.
\]
Consequently this polarity reverses inclusion: if \(C_1\subseteq C_2\), then \(\operatorname{abl}(C_2)\subseteq\operatorname{abl}(C_1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The anti-blocker consists of nonnegative vectors pairing at most one with the set; applying this polarity twice recovers any closed convex lower-comprehensive set.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative-Orthant Polarity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated anti-blocker polarity is mathematically plausible under the given closedness, convexity, nonemptiness, and lower-comprehensiveness assumptions, but the bipolar identity is a nontrivial specialized claim and has no cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Function and Exposed Face of a Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex polyhedron. Extended-real values are allowed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support geometry for bounded or unbounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support function of \(P\) is
\[
\sigma_P(u):=\sup_{x\in P}\langle u,x\rangle\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\},\qquad u\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
For every \(u\) for which the supremum is finite and attained, the objective-selected exposed face is
\[
F_P(u):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle u,x\rangle
      =\{x\in P:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_P(u)\}.
\]
For a nonempty polyhedron, every finite support value is attained. Hence \(F_P(u)\neq\varnothing\) exactly when \(u\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P\). The support function is closed, convex, positively homogeneous, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a nonempty polyhedron assigns to each objective vector the supremum of the corresponding linear objective. Whenever this value is finite, it is attained and the maximizers form an exposed face. This couples a polyhedral convex function in objective space with the facial geometry of the original set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sigma_P(u)=\sup_{x\in P}\langle u,x\rangle,\qquad F_P(u)=\{x\in P:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_P(u)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[P=\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_P(u)\ \forall u\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\]
For \(x\in P\), \[x\in F_P(u)\Longleftrightarrow u\in N_P(x),\] where \(N_P(x)=\{u:\langle u,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in P\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(P\) is bounded, then \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=\mathbb{R}^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Two closed convex polyhedra with the same support function are equal.
The domains on which a fixed face is optimal are polyhedral cones in objective space.
boundary_notes: For an arbitrary closed convex set, a finite support value need not be attained; polyhedrality supplies attainment here.
The empty-set support function is convention-dependent and is excluded.

notation.meaning: Exposed face selected by objective u.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Lipschitz Bound for Polytope Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness consequence distinguishing polytope support from the extended-valued unbounded regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polytope and set \(R_P:=\max_{x\in P}\|x\|\). Then for all \(c,d\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
|\sigma_P(c)-\sigma_P(d)|\le R_P\|c-d\|.
\]
Moreover, \(R_P\) is the least global Lipschitz constant of \(\sigma_P\) for the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope's support function is globally Lipschitz, with optimal constant equal to the greatest Euclidean norm of a point in the polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Lip}(\sigma_P)=\max_{x\in P}\|x\|\).

notation.meaning: Maximum Euclidean norm attained on P.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Maximum Support Function of a Polytope
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polytope.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded finite-dimensional polyhedral regime; the support function is real-valued on all objective vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support function of the polytope \(P\) is the finite polyhedral sublinear function
\[
\sigma_P(u):=\max_{x\in P}\langle u,x\rangle
             =\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\langle u,v_i\rangle,
\qquad u\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Its selected face is
\[
F_P(u)=\operatorname{conv}\{v_i:\langle u,v_i\rangle=\sigma_P(u)\}.
\]
Thus \(\sigma_P\) is finite, convex, continuous, positively homogeneous, and piecewise linear. A nonminimal generating list is permitted: all listed points attaining the maximum generate the selected face, while nonvertices among them cause only redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a polytope is the maximum of the finitely many linear functions obtained from any finite vertex-generating list. It is finite everywhere and piecewise linear. The points in the list that attain the maximum generate the exposed face selected by the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sigma_P(u)=\max_i\langle u,v_i\rangle<+\infty,\qquad F_P(u)=\operatorname{conv}\{v_i:\langle u,v_i\rangle=\sigma_P(u)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}\sigma_P=\{(u,t):t\geq\langle u,v_i\rangle,5 i\leq m\}.\]
\[P=\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_P(u)\ \forall u\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For a singleton \(P=\{v\}\), \(\sigma_P(u)=\langle u,v\rangle\).
For a segment \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{a,b\}\), \(\sigma_P(u)=\max\{\langle u,a\rangle,\langle u,b\rangle\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The domains of linearity of \(\sigma_P\) are unions of normal cones of faces.
The subdifferential satisfies \(\partial\sigma_P(u)=F_P(u)\).
boundary_notes: The formula remains valid for a redundant finite generating set, but the displayed points need not all be vertices.
For unbounded polyhedra the support function may equal \(+\infty\), so a recession-domain restriction is necessary.

notation.meaning: Points in a finite convex-hull representation of P.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support function \(\sigma_P(c)=\sup_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle\) is finite exactly for objectives nonpositive on every recession direction:

\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P
 =\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle c,r\rangle\leq0\text{ for all }r\in R\}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}+\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\}
\]
be a nonempty polyhedron. Then
\[
\sigma_P(c)=
\begin{cases}
\max_{1\le i\le m}\langle c,v_i\rangle,&\langle c,r_j\rangle\le0\quad(j=1,\ldots,q),\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.

The formula also covers lineality when both directions of every line are included among the recession generators.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P=Q+K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(Q=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) is a nonempty polytope and \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\}=\operatorname{rec}P\) is a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded polyhedra represented by points and recession directions; extended-real support functions are used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support function of \(P\) is
\[
\sigma_P(u)=
\begin{cases}
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\langle u,v_i\rangle,&\langle u,r_j\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }j,\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently its effective domain is the polar of the recession cone:
\[
\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=(\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ
=\{u:\langle u,r_j\rangle\leq0,5 j\leq q\}.
\]
For each \(u\) in this domain the finite maximum is attained, and the maximizing set \(F_P(u)=\{x\in P:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_P(u)\}\) is a nonempty face, possibly unbounded when \(u\) annihilates a recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron written as a polytope plus its recession cone, the support value is finite precisely on objectives that are nonpositive on every recession direction. On that domain it is the maximum over the bounded point generators. A selected face can still be unbounded when the objective is zero along some recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=(\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ,\qquad \sigma_P(u)=\max_i\langle u,v_i\rangle\ \text{on this domain}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\sigma_P=\sigma_Q+\delta_{K^\circ},\] where \(\delta_{K^\circ}\) is zero on \(K^\circ\) and \(+\infty\) outside it.
For \(u\in K^\circ\), \[\operatorname{rec}F_P(u)=K\cap u^\perp.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(K=\{0\}\), then \(P\) is a polytope and the domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(P=K\) is a cone, then \(\sigma_K(u)=0\) on \(K^\circ\) and \(+\infty\) outside.

Objectives in the relative interior of \((\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ\) are strictly negative on every nonlineality recession direction and therefore select bounded faces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face Selected by a Linear Objective
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(u\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization convention for finite linear objectives on polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The face selected by the objective \(u\) is
\[
F_P(u):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle u,x\rangle
       =P\cap\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_P(u)\}.
\]
For a nonempty face \(F\unlhd P\), its closed normal region is
\[
N_P(F):=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:F\subseteq F_P(u)\}
       =\{u:\langle u,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in P,\ \forall x\in F\}.
\]
The objectives selecting exactly \(F\) form \(\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\). Thus objectives are grouped by their common optimal face, and incidence is reversed: \(F\subseteq G\) implies \(N_P(G)\subseteq N_P(F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite objective selects the face on which its maximum is attained. The normal region of a face consists of all objectives for which that face is contained in the optimizer set. Its relative interior consists of the objectives selecting exactly that face. Larger primal faces therefore have smaller normal regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_P(u)=\{x\in P:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_P(u)\},\qquad F_P(u)=F\Longleftrightarrow u\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For any \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), \[N_P(F)=N_P(x)=\{u:\langle u,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in P\}.\]
\[u\in N_P(F)\Longleftrightarrow F\subseteq F_P(u).\]
special_cases_latex: \(F_P(0)=P\) and \(N_P(P)=(\operatorname{lin}(P-P))^\perp\).
If \(v\) is a vertex, \(N_P(v)\) is full-dimensional relative to the objective space modulo lineality exactly when \(v\) is a zero-dimensional face.
immediate_consequences_latex: The support function is linear on every normal cone \(N_P(F)\), with value \(\langle u,x\rangle\) for any \(x\in F\).
Optimal-face changes occur when the objective crosses a boundary between normal regions.
boundary_notes: For unbounded \(P\), only objectives in \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P\) have nonempty selected faces.
Using minimization instead of maximization reverses the sign of the normal regions.

notation.meaning: F is a face of P.
Normal cone or closed objective region attached to F.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An objective \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\) supports the face \(F\) when every point of \(F\) maximizes \(\langle c,\cdot\rangle\) over \(P\). The set of all such objectives is
\[
N_P(F):=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:F\subseteq M_P(c)\}
=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle c,y-x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }y\in P\text{ and every }x\in F\}.
\]
Equivalently, for any fixed \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\),
\[
N_P(F)=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle c,y-x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }y\in P\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting objective for a face is a linear objective maximized at every point of that face. These objectives form the face normal cone, which can be computed at any relative-interior point of the face.
knowledge_statements.title: Supporting Objectives

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}
\]
is nonempty, with row normals \(a_i^\top\), and let \(F\) be a nonempty face. Define
\[
I(F):=\{i:a_i^\top x=b_i\text{ for every }x\in F\}.
\]
Then
\[
N_P(F)=\operatorname{cone}\{a_i:i\in I(F)\}.
\]
Consequently, \(c\) supports \(F\) if and only if there is \(\lambda\ge0\), supported on \(I(F)\), such that \(c=A^\top\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objectives supporting a face are precisely nonnegative combinations of inequalities active throughout that face, yielding a finite multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_P(F)=\operatorname{cone}\{a_i:i\in I(F)\}\), equivalently \(c=A^\top\lambda\) for some \(\lambda\ge0\) supported on \(I(F)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximizer set of a finite supporting objective is
\[
F_c:=\operatorname{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle
 =\{x\in P:\langle c,x\rangle=\sigma_P(c)\}.

It is a nonempty face of \(P\). Conversely, because \(P\) is polyhedral, every nonempty face \(F\) is exposed: there exists \(c\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P\) such that \(F=F_c\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the optimal-face map \(F_c=\operatorname{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle\), one has
\[
\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:F_c=F\}=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).
\]
Consequently two finite objectives \(c\) and \(d\) select the same face exactly when they lie in the relative interior of the same normal cone. Passing to the boundary of \(N_P(F)\) can enlarge the selected face.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. The relative interiors of its face normal cones form a disjoint partition of the finite-objective domain:
\[
\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=\bigsqcup_{\varnothing\ne F\unlhd P}\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).
\]
Moreover,
\[
F\subseteq G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N_P(G)\subseteq N_P(F),
\qquad \dim F+\dim N_P(F)=n.
\]
Thus objective-equivalence regions are the relatively open cones of the normal fan, with closure order opposite to face inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite objective space is partitioned by relative interiors of face normal cones; their closure order reverses face inclusion and their dimensions complement face dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P\) is the disjoint union of \(\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\), ordered oppositely to the nonempty faces of \(P\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent and Normal Cones as Polar Cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set and let \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex tangent and normal cones under the nonpositive polar convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The tangent cone and normal cone of \(C\) at \(x\) are
\[
T_C(x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-x)
=\operatorname{cl}\{\alpha(y-x):\alpha\geq0,\ y\in C\},
\]
\[
N_C(x):=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle s,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}.
\]
They form a polar pair:
\[
N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,
\qquad T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.
\]
Both are closed convex cones. For a polyhedron they are polyhedral, and the closure in the tangent-cone formula may be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a closed convex set, the tangent cone is the closure of all nonnegative multiples of feasible displacements, while the normal cone consists of vectors making a nonpositive inner product with every feasible displacement. Each cone is the polar of the other. In the polyhedral case both are polyhedral and the generated tangent cone is already closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,\qquad T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in T_C(x)\Longleftrightarrow\langle s,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall s\in N_C(x).\]
\[s\in N_C(x)\Longleftrightarrow x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(T_C(x)=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\).
If \(C=K\) is a closed convex cone and \(x=0\), then \(T_K(0)=K\) and \(N_K(0)=K^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For a polyhedron \(C=\{z:Az\leq b\}\) with active row set \(I(x)\), \[T_C(x)=\{d:A_{I(x)}d\leq0\},\qquad N_C(x)=\{A_{I(x)}^\top\lambda:\lambda\geq0\}.\]
Normal directions encode precisely the linear objectives maximized at the base point.
boundary_notes: For nonconvex sets, several inequivalent tangent and normal constructions exist; this record uses the convex contingent tangent and its polar normal.
Sign conventions vary: a nonnegative dual cone introduces a minus sign.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let q(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Qx+c^\top x, where Q=Q^\top, and let P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge b\}. For \bar x\in P, \mathcal C(\bar x;q;P):=\mathcal T(\bar x;P)\cap\nabla q(\bar x)^\perp. If \bar x is stationary and \Lambda(\bar x):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m:\nabla q(\bar x)-A^\top\lambda=0,\ 0\le\lambda\perp A\bar x-b\ge0\}, then \mathcal C(\bar x;q;P)=\{v\in\mathcal T(\bar x;P):\exists\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar x)\text{ such that }A_{i\bullet}v=0\text{ for every }i\in\operatorname{supp}(\lambda)\}.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, and for every nonempty face \(F\unlhd P\) let \(N_P(F)=\{u:F\subseteq F_P(u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-space conical complex attached to a possibly unbounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The normal-fan complex of \(P\) is the finite collection
\[
\mathcal{N}(P):=\{N_P(F):\varnothing\neq F\unlhd P\}.
\]
Its cones satisfy the conical-complex compatibility conditions: every face of a cone in \(\mathcal{N}(P)\) is another cone in the collection, and the intersection of two cones is a face of each. Its support is
\[
|\mathcal{N}(P)|:=\bigcup_{F\unlhd P,\,F\neq\varnothing}N_P(F)
=\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=(\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ.
\]
The relatively open cones \(\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\) partition this support according to the exact optimal face: \(u\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\) exactly when \(F_P(u)=F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal-fan complex of a polyhedron is the finite family of normal cones attached to all nonempty faces. These cones meet face-to-face and include all their faces. Their union is the domain of finite support objectives, and the relative interiors partition that domain according to which primal face is exactly optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal{N}(P)=\{N_P(F):\varnothing\neq F\unlhd P\},\qquad |\mathcal{N}(P)|=(\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=\bigsqcup_{\varnothing\neq F\unlhd P}\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).\]
The cones of \(\mathcal{N}(P)\) are the closures of the objective regions on which the optimizer face of \(P\) is constant.
special_cases_latex: If \(P\) is a polytope, \(|\mathcal{N}(P)|=\mathbb{R}^n\), so the fan is complete.
If \(P\) has lineality space \(L\), every normal cone lies in \(L^\perp\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Face inclusion is reversed by the normal-cone assignment.
The support function \(\sigma_P\) is linear on each cone of \(\mathcal{N}(P)\).
boundary_notes: For unbounded polyhedra the normal fan is generally not complete in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

Every face of a cone in \(\mathcal{N}(P)\) is another cone in the collection, and the intersection of any two cones is a common face of both. Since every objective attains its maximum on the compact set \(P\),

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete Normal Fan of a Polytope
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polytope. For each nonempty face \(F\), define \(N_P(F)=\{u:F\subseteq F_P(u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded polyhedral regime; lower-dimensional polytopes are allowed with their lineality in objective space made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The normal fan of \(P\) is
\[
\mathcal{N}(P)=\{N_P(F):\varnothing\neq F\unlhd P\}.
\]
Because \(P\) is bounded, every linear objective has a maximizer, and hence
\[
\bigcup_{F\unlhd P,\,F\neq\varnothing}N_P(F)=\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal{N}(P)\) is a complete polyhedral fan. Its maximal cones are the normal cones of vertices; more generally, if \(P\) is full-dimensional then \(\dim N_P(F)=n-\dim F\). The relative interior of \(N_P(F)\) consists exactly of the objectives selecting \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal fan of a polytope contains the normal cone of every nonempty face. Boundedness ensures that these cones cover all objective space, so the fan is complete. Vertex normal cones are maximal, and the dimension of a normal cone complements the dimension of its primal face for a full-dimensional polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|\mathcal{N}(P)|=\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad u\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\Longleftrightarrow F_P(u)=F.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The domains of linearity of \(\sigma_P(u)=\max_{v\in\operatorname{vert}P}\langle u,v\rangle\) form the normal fan.
For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), there is a unique face \(F\) such that \(u\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}(P-P)\). For every nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\), \[\operatorname{lin}N_P(F)=L^\perp.\] Thus all cones of the normal fan are pointed exactly when \(P\) is full-dimensional. If \(P\) is lower-dimensional, their images in \(\mathbb R^n/L^\perp\) form a pointed fan; in the ambient space the collection is a fan only under conventions allowing common lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face normal cone has the orthogonal complement of the polyhedron's direction space as its lineality. Lower-dimensional polyhedra therefore require a fan convention allowing lineality, or passage to a quotient.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a nonempty face of \(P\), and \(L=\operatorname{span}(P-P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}N_P(F)=L^\perp\); the ambient normal cones are pointed iff \(L=\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\mathcal{N}(P):=\{N_P(F):F\text{ is a nonempty face of }P\}.
\]
These normal cones meet face-to-face and form a polyhedral fan. Its support is exactly the effective objective domain:
\[
|\mathcal{N}(P)|:=\bigcup_{F\neq\varnothing}N_P(F)
 =\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=R^\circ.
\]
Consequently the fan is complete precisely when \(R^\circ=\mathbb{R}^n\), equivalently when \(R=\{0\}\); otherwise objectives outside its support are unbounded above on \(P\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restricted Normal Fan of an Unbounded Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty unbounded polyhedron with recession cone \(K=\operatorname{rec}P\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded finite-dimensional polyhedra; the fan is supported only on bounded-above objective directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The normal fan of \(P\) is the conical complex
\[
\mathcal{N}(P):=\{N_P(F):\varnothing\neq F\unlhd P\},
\qquad N_P(F)=\{u:F\subseteq F_P(u)\}.
\]
Its support is the polar recession cone
\[
|\mathcal{N}(P)|=K^\circ=\{u:\langle u,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in K\}.
\]
It is therefore generally incomplete in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(u\in K^\circ\), the selected face is nonempty and
\[
\operatorname{rec}F_P(u)=K\cap u^\perp.
\]
Hence objectives in the relative interior of \(K^\circ\) select bounded faces when \(K\) is pointed, whereas boundary objectives may select unbounded faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal fan of an unbounded polyhedron consists of its face normal cones, but these cones cover only objectives that are nonpositive on every recession direction. This is the polar of the recession cone. Boundary objectives can be constant along recession directions and therefore select unbounded faces; interior objectives select bounded faces when the recession cone is pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|\mathcal{N}(P)|=(\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ,\qquad \operatorname{rec}F_P(u)=\operatorname{rec}P\cap u^\perp.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\notin|\mathcal{N}(P)|\Longleftrightarrow\sigma_P(u)=+\infty.\]
\[u\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\Longleftrightarrow F_P(u)=F.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(P=Q+K\) with \(Q\) a polytope, then every finite support value is determined by \(Q\), while \(K^\circ\) determines the fan support.
If \(P\) contains a lineality space \(L\), then \(|\mathcal{N}(P)|\subseteq L^\perp\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Completeness occurs only after restricting objective space to \((\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ\), or globally when \(P\) is bounded.
The recession geometry determines which parametric objective regions exist.
boundary_notes: The assertion that relative-interior objectives select bounded faces needs pointedness of the recession cone.
The source inspected for unbounded support functions does not explicitly formulate the resulting collection as an incomplete fan.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional maximization convention for normal cones of a polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty face \(F\) define \[N_P(F)=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle c,x\rangle\geq\langle c,y\rangle\ \text{for all }x\in F,y\in P\}.\] Then the assignment \(F\mapsto N_P(F)\) reverses incidence: \(F\subseteq G\) if and only if \(N_P(G)\subseteq N_P(F)\). Moreover, an objective vector exposes exactly \(F\) precisely when it lies in the relative interior of its normal cone: \[\operatorname{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle=F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).\]

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. For every nonempty face \(F\unlhd P\), choose any \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-to-cone correspondence for polyhedra under maximization-oriented normal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The normal cone attached to \(F\) is
\[
N_P(F):=N_P(x)=\{u:\langle u,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }y\in P\},
\qquad x\in\operatorname{ri}F.
\]
This definition is independent of the chosen relative-interior point. It satisfies
\[
u\in N_P(F)\Longleftrightarrow F\subseteq F_P(u),
\qquad u\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\Longleftrightarrow F=F_P(u).
\]
The correspondence reverses incidence:
\[
F\subseteq G\Longleftrightarrow N_P(G)\ \text{is a face of }N_P(F).
\]
For full-dimensional \(P\), \(\dim F+\dim N_P(F)=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cone of a face is the point normal cone at any relative-interior point of that face. It consists of objectives for which the face is contained in the optimizer set, while its relative interior consists of objectives selecting exactly that face. Face containment is reversed as face containment among the corresponding normal cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F\subseteq G\Longleftrightarrow N_P(G)\unlhd N_P(F),\qquad F_P(u)=F\Longleftrightarrow u\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[N_P(F)=\bigcap_{x\in F}N_P(x)=N_P(x_F)\quad(x_F\in\operatorname{ri}F).\]
The map \(F\mapsto N_P(F)\) is an anti-isomorphism from the nonempty face poset of \(P\) to the cone poset of its normal fan.
special_cases_latex: Vertices correspond to maximal normal cones.
Facets of a full-dimensional polyhedron correspond to one-dimensional normal cones generated by outward facet normals.

The face lattice can be recovered from the normal fan together with reversed order.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Refinement Normal Fan of a Minkowski Sum
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P,Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty polytopes, and let \(P+Q=\{p+q:p\in P,q\in Q\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded polyhedral Minkowski sums; the normal fans are complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every objective \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the selected face of the Minkowski sum is
\[
F_{P+Q}(u)=F_P(u)+F_Q(u),
\]
and its normal cone is
\[
N_{P+Q}(F_P(u)+F_Q(u))=N_P(F_P(u))\cap N_Q(F_Q(u)).
\]
Consequently the normal fan of \(P+Q\) is the common refinement
\[
\mathcal{N}(P+Q)=\mathcal{N}(P)\wedge\mathcal{N}(Q),
\]
whose cones are the nonempty intersections \(C\cap D\) with \(C\in\mathcal{N}(P)\) and \(D\in\mathcal{N}(Q)\), together with all their faces. Thus \(\mathcal{N}(P+Q)\) refines each summand fan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For polytopes P and Q, an objective selects on their Minkowski sum the sum of the faces it selects on the two summands. The corresponding normal cone is the intersection of the two normal cones. Therefore the normal fan of the sum is precisely the common refinement of the summand fans.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_{P+Q}(u)=F_P(u)+F_Q(u),\qquad \mathcal{N}(P+Q)=\mathcal{N}(P)\wedge\mathcal{N}(Q).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\sigma_{P+Q}=\sigma_P+\sigma_Q.\]
Two objectives lie in the same relatively open cone of \(\mathcal{N}(P+Q)\) exactly when they select the same face in both \(P\) and \(Q\).
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=\{q\}\), translation does not change the normal fan: \(\mathcal{N}(P+q)=\mathcal{N}(P)\).
For \(Q=\lambda P\) with \(\lambda>0\), \(\mathcal{N}(P+Q)=\mathcal{N}(P)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every cone of \(\mathcal{N}(P+Q)\) is contained in a cone of each summand fan.
Repeated Minkowski addition produces the common refinement of all participating normal fans.
boundary_notes: For unbounded polyhedra the same formulas require restriction to the common finite-support domain.
The inspected support-function source gives additivity but not an explicit locator for the normal-fan common-refinement statement.

notation.meaning: Common refinement of the two fans.

children.title: Common Fan Refinements
children.top_down_role: Shared subdivisions resolving multiple fan decompositions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support identity and the refinement-order boundary for finite fans that need not have equal support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) be finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb R^n\), and form \[\mathcal F:=\left\{\bigcap_{i=1}^m\sigma_i:\sigma_i\in\mathcal F_i\right\}\] with duplicates removed. Then \[|\mathcal F|=\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal F_i|,\qquad |\mathcal G|:=\bigcup_{\sigma\in\mathcal G}\sigma.\] Thus \(\mathcal F\) is complete exactly when every input fan is complete. Under the convention that refinement requires equal support, \(\mathcal F\) is a common refinement of all inputs only when their supports coincide; otherwise it is the common refinement of their restrictions to the common support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection construction has support equal to the intersection of the input supports; unequal supports must therefore be restricted before it is a common refinement under the equal-support convention.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) are finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal F|=\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal F_i|\), with equal input supports required for an equal-support common refinement.

notation.meaning: Support, or union of cones, of a fan.
Fan formed by all intersections of one cone from each input fan.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Convention for Common Refinements

assumptions_latex: Each \(\mathcal F_i\) is a finite polyhedral fan in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigwedge_{i=1}^m\mathcal F_i=\{\bigcap_{i=1}^m\sigma_i:\sigma_i\in\mathcal F_i\}\) is the coarsest fan refining every \(\mathcal F_i\).

notation.meaning: Common refinement of the listed fans.
A cone belonging to the i-th fan.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common refinement of finitely many polyhedral fans with common ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The common refinement of \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) is \[\bigwedge_{i=1}^m\mathcal F_i:=\left\{\bigcap_{i=1}^m\sigma_i:\sigma_i\in\mathcal F_i\right\},\] with duplicate cones removed. It is a polyhedral fan. Every cone in it is contained in a cone of each \(\mathcal F_i\); hence it refines every \(\mathcal F_i\). If another fan \(\mathcal H\) refines every \(\mathcal F_i\), then each cone of \(\mathcal H\) is contained in a cone of \(\bigwedge_{i=1}^m\mathcal F_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting one cone from each fan produces their common refinement, the coarsest fan that refines every input fan.
knowledge_statements.title: Common Fan Refinements

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support identity and completeness boundary for finite fans in one ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) be finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\mathcal F=\bigwedge_{i=1}^m\mathcal F_i\) be their intersection refinement. Then \[|\mathcal F|=\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal F_i|,\qquad |\mathcal G|:=\bigcup_{\sigma\in\mathcal G}\sigma.\] Hence \(\mathcal F\) is complete if and only if every \(\mathcal F_i\) is complete. For incomplete fans the construction refines only their common support; it does not fill directions absent from an input fan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support of a common refinement is the intersection of the input supports, so completeness is preserved exactly when all input fans are complete.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) are finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(\mathcal F\) is their common intersection refinement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-fan identity for Minkowski sums of polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the face of the Minkowski sum exposed by \(c\) satisfies \[F_{P+Q}(c)=F_P(c)+F_Q(c).\] If \(F=F_P(c)\) and \(G=F_Q(c)\), then the associated normal cone is \[N_{P+Q}(F+G)=N_P(F)\cap N_Q(G).\] Consequently the normal fan of the sum is exactly the common refinement of the summand normal fans: \[\mathcal N(P+Q)=\mathcal N(P)\wedge\mathcal N(Q).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exposed face of a Minkowski sum is the sum of exposed faces, and its normal fan is the common refinement of the summand fans.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N(P+Q)\preceq\mathcal N(P)\) and \(\mathcal N(P+Q)\preceq\mathcal N(Q)\); moreover, \(\mathcal N(P+Q)=\mathcal N(P)\iff\mathcal N(P)\preceq\mathcal N(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Refinement order among normal fans of two summands and their sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(\mathcal F\preceq\mathcal G\) when every cone of \(\mathcal F\) is contained in a cone of \(\mathcal G\). Then \[\mathcal N(P+Q)\preceq\mathcal N(P)\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal N(P+Q)\preceq\mathcal N(Q).\] Equality with a summand fan is characterized by comparability: \[\mathcal N(P+Q)=\mathcal N(P)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal N(P)\preceq\mathcal N(Q),\] and symmetrically after exchanging \(P\) and \(Q\). Thus adding a summand can subdivide, but cannot coarsen, the original normal regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Minkowski sum's normal fan refines both summand fans; it equals one summand fan exactly when that fan already refines the other.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends objective-region stratification from polytopes to the finite-support domain of an arbitrary polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=\operatorname{rec}(P)\). For every nonempty face \(F\) define \[\mathcal R_F:=\{c:\operatorname{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle=F\}.\] Then \[\mathcal R_F=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F),\qquad \overline{\mathcal R_F}=N_P(F),\] and the nonempty regions \(\mathcal R_F\) partition \(R^\circ\). If \(c\notin R^\circ\), the objective is unbounded above and belongs to no optimal-face region.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-Parameter Region of a Fixed Optimal Face
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and consider the parametric linear optimization problem \(\max_{x\in P}\langle u,x\rangle\), with parameter \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-parametric linear optimization over a fixed polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each nonempty face \(F\unlhd P\), its closed parametric normal region and exact-face region are
\[
\mathcal{R}_{\supseteq F}:=\{u:F\subseteq F_P(u)\}=N_P(F),
\]
\[
\mathcal{R}_{=F}:=\{u:F_P(u)=F\}=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).
\]
Thus the closed region permits enlargement of the optimal face on its boundary, while the relatively open region has a stable exact optimal face. The regions \(\mathcal{R}_{=F}\) are pairwise disjoint and partition \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=(\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ\). Their closures are the cones of the normal-fan complex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an objective-parametric linear program, the closed normal region of a face contains all objective vectors for which that face remains optimal, possibly as part of a larger optimizer face. Its relative interior contains exactly the objectives whose full optimizer set equals that face. These exact-face regions partition the domain of finite objectives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal{R}_{=F}=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F),\qquad \operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=\bigsqcup_{F\neq\varnothing}\mathcal{R}_{=F}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x_F\in\operatorname{ri}F\), \[\mathcal{R}_{\supseteq F}=\{u:\langle u,y-x_F\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in P\}.\]
If \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\), a normal region is generated by the normals of constraints active on the corresponding face.
special_cases_latex: For a polytope, the exact-face regions partition all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
A generic objective belongs to the relative interior of a maximal normal cone and selects a vertex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Crossing a common boundary between regions can enlarge or change the optimal face.
Within one exact-face region, the support value is given by the same linear form \(u\mapsto\langle u,x_F\rangle\).
boundary_notes: This record parametrizes the objective only; right-hand-side or matrix perturbations produce different critical-region constructions.
No supplied source explicitly names these sets as parametric normal regions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Polyhedral Complexes and Their Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite polyhedral complexes; conical specialization is owned by the conical-complex sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite collection \(\mathcal C\) of polyhedra in \(\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedral complex when every face of every \(C\in\mathcal C\) belongs to \(\mathcal C\), and for all \(C,D\in\mathcal C\), \(C\cap D\) is empty or a face of both. Its support is \[|\mathcal C|:=\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal C}C.\] Members are cells, and inclusion-maximal members are maximal cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite polyhedral complex is face-closed and its cells meet, if at all, in a common face; its support is their union.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a finite collection of polyhedra in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a polyhedral complex exactly when it is face-closed and every nonempty pairwise intersection is a face of both cells.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Polyhedral Complexes and Their Support

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Partition of a Polyhedral Complex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic stratification property of a finite polyhedral complex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite polyhedral complex \(\mathcal C\), the relative interiors of its nonempty cells are pairwise disjoint and satisfy \[|\mathcal C|=\bigsqcup_{C\in\mathcal C,\,C\ne\varnothing}\operatorname{ri}C.\] Equivalently, every point of the support lies in the relative interior of a unique cell, namely the inclusion-minimal cell containing it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interiors of the cells form a disjoint partition of the support, so every support point has a unique carrier cell.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a finite polyhedral complex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in|\mathcal C|\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\) for exactly one cell \(C\in\mathcal C\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper convex function, and define \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):t\geq f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper extended-real convex functions; polyhedrality includes domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is polyhedral convex when its epigraph is a nonempty polyhedral convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). Equivalently, there exist vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\), scalars \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k\), and a nonempty polyhedron
\[
D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:B x\leq d\}
\]
such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}+\delta_D(x),
\]
where \(\delta_D(x)=0\) for \(x\in D\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Hence \(f\) is closed and is piecewise affine on its polyhedral effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is polyhedral when its epigraph is a polyhedron. Equivalently, on a polyhedral domain it is the maximum of finitely many affine functions, and it is positive infinity outside that domain. Such a function is closed and piecewise affine on its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\ \text{is polyhedral}\Longleftrightarrow f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq k}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_D(x)\ \text{for a polyhedron }D.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):Bx\leq d,\ t\geq\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i,5 i\leq k\}.\]
A proper convex function is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated in the epigraphical point-and-direction sense.
special_cases_latex: If \(D=\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(f\) is a finite maximum of affine functions and is finite everywhere.
If \(k=1\) with affine term zero, \(f=\delta_D\) is the indicator of a nonempty polyhedron.
The support function of a nonempty polyhedron is a polyhedral convex function.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Fenchel conjugate of a polyhedral convex function is polyhedral.
Every sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\leq\beta\}\) is polyhedral.
Finite maxima of polyhedral convex functions and finite intersections of their epigraphical constraints remain polyhedral.
boundary_notes: A merely piecewise-affine function need not be convex; the maximum representation enforces convexity.
Allowing the improper constant functions requires separate conventions and is excluded by properness.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, epigraph polyhedrality requires a different finite-codimensional formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Epigraphical and Max-Affine Representations of a Polyhedral Convex Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper convex function. A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, extended-real-valued convex functions; properness excludes the identically \(+\infty\) function and all values \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is polyhedral convex precisely when \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):f(x)\le t\}\) is a polyhedron in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\). Equivalently, there exist finite families \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb R\), \(c_j\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d_j\in\mathbb R\) such that \[C:=\{x:\langle c_j,x\rangle\le d_j\ \text{for every }j\}\ne\varnothing\] and \[f(x)=\max_i\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}+\delta_C(x).\] Thus \(\operatorname{dom}f=C\), and its epigraph has the inequality representation \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):\langle c_j,x\rangle\le d_j\ \forall j,\ t\ge\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\ \forall i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space is polyhedral when its epigraph is a polyhedron. This is equivalent to representing it on a nonempty polyhedral domain as the maximum of finitely many affine functions and assigning value plus infinity outside that domain. The domain inequalities give the vertical half-spaces of the epigraph, while the affine pieces give its nonvertical lower supporting half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is polyhedral convex}\iff \operatorname{epi}f\text{ is polyhedral}\iff f=\max_i(\langle a_i,\cdot\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C\text{ for a polyhedron }C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A convex function is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated: its epigraph is the convex hull of finitely many points and recession directions, including the upward direction \((0,1)\).
For proper \(f\), the finite max-affine representation implies that \(f\) is closed and that every finite value is attained by the lower boundary of its epigraph.
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb R^n\), then \(f(x)=\max_i\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}\) is finite everywhere.
If there is a single affine piece, then \(f\) is an affine function restricted to the polyhedron \(C\).
Taking every affine piece equal to zero yields the indicator \(\delta_C\) of a polyhedron.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\le r\}\) is a polyhedron.
The effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is a polyhedron, and a proper polyhedral convex function is lower semicontinuous.
boundary_notes: An arbitrary piecewise-affine function need not be convex and therefore need not admit a maximum-of-affine-pieces representation.
This definition is finite-dimensional; infinite-dimensional notions of polyhedrality require separate conventions.

notation.meaning: The convex indicator, equal to \(0\) on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(f\) is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated. If such an \(f\) is proper, then \(f\) is closed. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite representations of polyhedral and finitely generated convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical and finite affine-piece representation of polyhedral convex functions, together with the distinct point-direction definition of finitely generated convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(f\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is polyhedral. Equivalently, for suitable finite families \((b_i,\beta_i)\), \[f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\{\langle x,b_i\rangle-\beta_i\}+\delta_C(x),\qquad C=\{x:\langle x,b_i\rangle\leq\beta_i,\ i=k+1,\ldots,m\}.\] Separately, \(f\) is finitely generated if there exist \((a_i,\alpha_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(0\leq k\leq m\), such that \[f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\alpha_i:\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i=x,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\},\] with the normalization omitted when \(k=0\). The associated epigraph is generated by the points \((a_i,\alpha_i)\) for \(i\leq k\), the directions \((a_i,\alpha_i)\) for \(i>k\), and the upward direction \((0,1)\). Whenever the defining infimum is finite, it is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral convex function is one whose epigraph is polyhedral; equivalently, it is a finite maximum of affine functions on a polyhedral domain and is positive infinity outside that domain. A finitely generated convex function is defined separately through a finite point-direction formula for its epigraph. In that formula, every finite infimum is attained.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a convex function on }\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}f\text{ is polyhedral exactly when }f\text{ has the stated finite affine-piece/domain representation; the stated finite-generator construction yields its epigraph and attains each finite defining infimum.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation, regularity, and domain properties of extended-real-valued polyhedral functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbf E\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is polyhedral, then \(f\) is closed and convex and can be written as \[f=\max_{i\in I}g_i+\delta_P,\] where \(I\) is finite and possibly empty, each \(g_i\) is affine, and \(P\subseteq\mathbf E\) is polyhedral and possibly empty. Moreover, \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is polyhedral, and if \(f\) is proper, then \(\operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{dom}\partial f\).
