knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Subdifferential of a Polyhedral Convex Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex and write \(f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C(x)\) with \(C\) polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex subdifferentials at every point of the effective domain, including relative-interior and boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f=C\), the subdifferential polyhedron is \[\partial f(x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle v,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\] If \(I_f(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i=f(x)\}\), then \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}+N_C(x).\] This set is nonempty, closed, convex, and polyhedral. For \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\), define \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential polyhedron at a domain point is the set of all vectors satisfying the global subgradient inequality. For a max-affine polyhedral function on a polyhedral domain, it equals the convex hull of active affine slopes plus the domain normal cone, and is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}+N_C(x)\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\).
\(f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)\) for every direction \(d\).
special_cases_latex: When \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), the normal term vanishes and \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\).
For \(f=\delta_C\), one has \(\partial f(x)=N_C(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at an interior point precisely when all active slopes coincide.
The recession cone of \(\partial f(x)\) is \(N_C(x)\) up to the lineality induced by the affine hull.
boundary_notes: The displayed generator formula assumes a max-affine-plus-indicator representation.
Subdifferentials of nonpolyhedral convex functions need not be polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C(x)\) be proper polyhedral convex, and let \(L:=\operatorname{lin}(C-C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Points in the relative interior of a possibly lower-dimensional polyhedral effective domain; the full-dimensional case is obtained by setting \(L=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), the interior subdifferential is \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}+L^\perp.\] Its intrinsic subgradient polytope in the affine hull of \(C\) is the projection \[\partial_C f(x):=P_L\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{P_La_i:i\in I_f(x)\}.\] If \(C\) is full-dimensional, then \(L^\perp=\{0\}\), so \(\partial f(x)\) itself is the compact polytope generated by the active affine slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a relative-interior point of the polyhedral domain, no proper boundary normal is present. The ambient subdifferential is the convex hull of the active slopes plus the orthogonal complement of the domain’s affine hull. Projecting onto the domain’s direction space gives a compact subgradient polytope.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper polyhedral convex with effective domain \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}+L^\perp\), and \(\partial_Cf(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{P_La_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(N_C(x)=L^\perp\) for \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\).
When \(C\) is full-dimensional, \(v\in\partial f(x)\iff v\in\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\).
special_cases_latex: If exactly one projected active slope occurs, then \(\partial_Cf(x)\) is a singleton.
If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The intrinsic subdifferential is bounded at every relative-interior point.
Multiplicity of intrinsic subgradients is controlled entirely by the active affine slopes.
boundary_notes: Relative interior, not ambient interior, is required when \(C\) is lower-dimensional.
At boundary points, additional nonzero domain normals generally make the subdifferential unbounded.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{x:Bx\le d\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron and \(f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C(x)\). Let \(x\in C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-boundary points of finite-dimensional polyhedral domains; redundant inequalities are allowed, although the resulting normal cone is intrinsic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The boundary subdifferential at \(x\) is the polyhedron \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}+N_C(x),\] where \[N_C(x)=\operatorname{cone}\{B_j^T:j\in J_C(x)\}+\operatorname{lin}(C-C)^\perp.\] The first summand records active affine pieces, and the second records outward domain normals. Its recession cone satisfies \[\operatorname{rec}\partial f(x)=N_C(x).\] Hence boundary subdifferentials may be unbounded even when the active-slope convex hull is a compact polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a boundary point, the subdifferential is the convex hull of active affine slopes enlarged by the domain normal cone. Active constraint normals generate the added directions, and this normal cone is the recession cone of the resulting subdifferential polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper polyhedral convex in the displayed representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}+\operatorname{cone}\{B_j^T:j\in J_C(x)\}+\operatorname{lin}(C-C)^\perp\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\iff v=p+n\) for some \(p\in\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\) and \(n\in N_C(x)\).
\(N_C(x)=\partial\delta_C(x)\), so the formula is the exact polyhedral sum rule for the max-affine part and the domain indicator.
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), the boundary subdifferential is exactly \(N_C(x)\).
At a vertex of a full-dimensional pointed polyhedron, \(N_C(x)\) is a full-dimensional polyhedral cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: Boundary nondifferentiability may arise from domain normals even when only one affine piece is active.
Every boundary subdifferential remains nonempty and polyhedral.
boundary_notes: The active constraint generators depend on the inequality representation, but their generated normal cone does not.
The formula concerns the convex subdifferential, not nonconvex limiting subdifferentials.

children.title: Subgradient-Multiplicity Strata
children.top_down_role: Cells distinguished by uniqueness or multiplicity of subgradients.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex. For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the set \(\partial f(x)\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity is measured by affine dimension of the subdifferential; singleton values constitute the zero-dimensional stratum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the subgradient multiplicity index by \[\mu_f(x):=\dim\operatorname{aff}\partial f(x),\qquad x\in\operatorname{dom}f.\] For each \(r\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), the multiplicity stratum is \[\mathcal S_r(f):=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:\mu_f(x)=r\}.\] In a fixed active-region decomposition, \(\partial f(x)\) has constant polyhedral generator structure on the relative interior of every cell; refining those cells by the dimension of the resulting subdifferential yields a finite polyhedral stratification. The uniqueness stratum is \(\mathcal S_0(f)=\{x:\partial f(x)\text{ is a singleton}\}\); the union \(\bigcup_{r\ge1}\mathcal S_r(f)\) is the multiple-subgradient locus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient-multiplicity index at a point is the affine dimension of its subdifferential polyhedron. Points with a common index form multiplicity strata. Dimension zero means a unique subgradient, while positive dimension means multiple subgradients. For a polyhedral convex function these sets admit a finite refinement by polyhedral active regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}f=\bigsqcup_{r=0}^n\mathcal S_r(f)\), with \(\mathcal S_0(f)=\{x:|\partial f(x)|=1\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\mathcal S_0(f)\iff\partial f(x)=\{v\}\) for some \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
For an interior max-affine point, \(\mu_f(x)=\dim\operatorname{aff}\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\).
special_cases_latex: At an interior point with one nonredundant active slope, \(x\in\mathcal S_0(f)\).
At a full-dimensional domain boundary, nontrivial normal-cone directions force \(\mu_f(x)\ge1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The multiple-subgradient locus is controlled by finitely many active-piece and active-face patterns.
On the interior of the effective domain, \(\mathcal S_0(f)\) is the differentiability locus.
boundary_notes: Cardinality is not used because every nonsingleton convex subdifferential is typically infinite.
For lower-dimensional domains, ambient singleton uniqueness differs from uniqueness of the intrinsic projected subgradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedral directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) is \[f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}.\] It is the positively homogeneous polyhedral convex function \[f'(x;d)=\begin{cases}\max_{i\in I_f(x)}\langle a_i,d\rangle,&d\in T_C(x),\\+\infty,&d\notin T_C(x),\end{cases}\] and equivalently \[f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)=\sup_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,d\rangle.\] Thus it is a local piecewise-linear first-order model on the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the one-sided rate along a direction. For a polyhedral convex function, it is finite exactly on the tangent cone of the domain and there equals the maximum of the active affine slopes applied to the direction. equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\delta_{T_C(x)}(d)+\max_{i\in I_f(x)}\langle a_i,d\rangle\).

If one affine piece is active and \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(f'(x;d)=\langle a_i,d\rangle\).

The derivative model is piecewise linear on a finite polyhedral conic subdivision.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph Geometry of a Polyhedral Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional primal-dual geometry of the convex subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subdifferential graph geometry of \(f\) is the subset \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f:=\{(x,v)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n:v\in\partial f(x)\}.\] Equivalently, \[(x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle.\] For polyhedral convex \(f\), this graph is a finite union of polyhedra. A finite active-region decomposition of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) gives graph pieces on which the active affine indices, active domain face, and polyhedral description of \(\partial f(x)\) are fixed. The first coordinate is primal and the second is dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential graph is the set of all primal points paired with their subgradients. The same pairs are exactly the equality cases of the Fenchel inequality. For a polyhedral convex function, this graph is a finite union of polyhedra indexed by finitely many active primal and dual patterns.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\{(x,v):f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle\}\) is piecewise polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\iff(v,x)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*\).
\(\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\{(x,v):x\in\partial f^*(v)\}\) after exchanging coordinates.
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), the graph is \(\operatorname{gph}N_C\).
For affine \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+\alpha\), the graph is \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{a\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal projection is \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{dom}f\) in the polyhedral regime.
The dual projection is \(\operatorname{rge}\partial f=\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*\).
boundary_notes: The graph is generally nonconvex even though every value \(\partial f(x)\) is convex.
Piecewise polyhedral does not mean that the whole graph is one polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Polyhedral Decomposition of a Subdifferential Graph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition applies to subdifferential mappings whose graphs admit a finite polyhedral covering; polyhedral convex functions form an important special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subdifferential graph of \(f\) is piecewise polyhedral if there exist an integer \(N<\infty\) and polyhedra \(G_1,\ldots,G_N\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\bigcup_{k=1}^N G_k.\] The sets \(G_k\) are graph pieces and need not be disjoint or convex as a union. A representation may be refined so that each piece corresponds to a fixed primal active region and a fixed face of its subdifferential value. For proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\), this property is equivalent to \(f\) being piecewise linear-quadratic; hence every proper polyhedral convex function has a piecewise-polyhedral subdifferential graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subdifferential graph is piecewise polyhedral when it is the union of finitely many polyhedra in the product of primal and dual spaces. The pieces may overlap, and the whole graph need not be convex. For proper closed convex functions this is equivalent to piecewise linear-quadratic structure of the function.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\partial f\) is the convex subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\bigcup_{k=1}^NG_k\) for finitely many polyhedra \(G_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\partial f\) is a piecewise-polyhedral mapping.
For proper lsc convex \(f\), \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) is piecewise polyhedral if and only if \(f\) is piecewise linear-quadratic.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is polyhedral convex, it is piecewise linear-quadratic with zero quadratic terms.
If \(f=\delta_C\) for a polyhedron \(C\), then \(N_C\) has a piecewise-polyhedral graph.
immediate_consequences_latex: The inverse mapping \((\partial f)^{-1}\) is piecewise polyhedral.
Every graph point lies in at least one finite-dimensional polyhedral graph piece.
boundary_notes: A finite union of polyhedra is not necessarily a polyhedron.
The decomposition is not unique and can be refined without changing the mapping.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Strata of a Polyhedral Subgradient Graph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\) be proper polyhedral convex. Choose a finite relatively open polyhedral partition \(\mathscr R\) of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) such that \(Q_R:=\partial f(x)\) is constant for \(x\in R\), after refining by active graph patterns.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional graph stratification; strata are indexed by a primal activity cell and a relative-interior face of its dual subdifferential polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R\in\mathscr R\) and a nonempty face \(H\) of \(Q_R\), define the primal-dual graph stratum \[\Gamma_{R,H}:=R\times\operatorname{ri}H\subseteq\operatorname{gph}\partial f.\] Equivalently, every \((x,v)\in\Gamma_{R,H}\) satisfies \[v\in\partial f(x),\qquad x\in\partial f^*(v),\qquad f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle.\] The collection of all nonempty \(\Gamma_{R,H}\), with a common polyhedral refinement when necessary, partitions the subdifferential graph into finitely many relatively open polyhedral primal-dual cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual graph stratum pairs a relatively open primal activity cell with the relative interior of a face of its constant subdifferential polyhedron. Every pair in the stratum satisfies both reciprocal subgradient relations and Fenchel equality. A finite refinement yields a partition of the whole subdifferential graph.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathscr R\) is a finite active-pattern refinement on which the subdifferential value is constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma_{R,H}=R\times\operatorname{ri}H\) is a relatively open polyhedral subset of \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\), and finitely many such strata cover the graph.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((x,v)\in\Gamma_{R,H}\Rightarrow (v,x)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*\).
Each stratum lies in the Fenchel-equality set \(\{(x,v):f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle\}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), strata couple relative interiors of faces of \(C\) with relative interiors of faces of their normal cones.
If \(f\) is affine, there is one stratum \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{a\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Exchanging primal and dual coordinates sends the stratification to one for \(f^*\).
Primal and dual activity remain constant within each stratum.
boundary_notes: A preliminary refinement may be needed because a coarse primal active cell need not make every dual face label constant.
The strata are relatively open; their closures may overlap along lower-dimensional strata.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed proper finite-dimensional convex functions; polyhedrality is imposed for the finite graph-piece specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse subdifferential geometry of \(f\) is the inverse multifunction \[(\partial f)^{-1}(v):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:v\in\partial f(x)\}.\] Conjugacy identifies it exactly with the subdifferential of the conjugate: \[(\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*.\] Equivalently, for every \(x,v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[v\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\partial f^*(v)\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*=\{(v,x):(x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\}\). If \(f\) is polyhedral convex, then \(f^*\) is polyhedral convex and both graphs are finite unions of polyhedra exchanged by the coordinate-swap map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse of the subdifferential sends a dual vector to all primal points having it as a subgradient. For a proper closed convex function this inverse is exactly the subdifferential of the convex conjugate. Their graphs are obtained from one another by swapping primal and dual coordinates; polyhedral graph structure is preserved.

For the final specialization, \(f\) is additionally polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\) and \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*=\{(v,x):(x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\partial f^*(v)\).
\(v\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), \((N_C)^{-1}=\partial\sigma_C\).
If \(f\) is differentiable and strictly convex with an invertible gradient, then \(\nabla f^*=(\nabla f)^{-1}\).

Piecewise-polyhedrality is preserved by inversion.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\operatorname{gph}S:=\{(x,y):y\in S(x)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedral set-valued mapping family consists of two nested graph classes. The convex-polyhedral class is \[\mathcal P_{n,m}:=\{S:\operatorname{gph}S\text{ is a polyhedron in }\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\},\] and the piecewise-polyhedral class is \[\mathcal{PP}_{n,m}:=\left\{S:\operatorname{gph}S=\bigcup_{k=1}^NG_k,\ N<\infty,\ G_k\text{ polyhedral}\right\}.\] Thus \(\mathcal P_{n,m}\subseteq\mathcal{PP}_{n,m}\). Membership is a property of the complete graph, not merely of individual values. Coordinate exchange preserves both classes, so \(S\) and \(S^{-1}\) belong to corresponding classes simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-polyhedral multifunction has one polyhedral complete graph. A piecewise-polyhedral multifunction has a graph that is a finite union of polyhedra. The first class is contained in the second, and both are preserved by taking the inverse mapping.
assumptions_latex: All graph pieces are finite-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal P_{n,m}\) iff \(\operatorname{gph}S\) is polyhedral, while \(S\in\mathcal{PP}_{n,m}\) iff its graph is a finite union of polyhedra.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(S\in\mathcal{PP}_{n,m}\iff\exists G_1,\ldots,G_N:\ y\in S(x)\iff(x,y)\in\bigcup_{k=1}^NG_k\).
\(S\in\mathcal P_{n,m}\iff S^{-1}\in\mathcal P_{m,n}\), and likewise for \(\mathcal{PP}\).
special_cases_latex: Polyhedral convex processes are positively homogeneous members of \(\mathcal P_{n,m}\).
Subdifferentials of convex piecewise linear-quadratic functions belong to \(\mathcal{PP}_{n,n}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Domains and ranges are finite unions of polyhedra, and are polyhedra in the convex-graph subclass.
Every value is a finite union of polyhedra; in the convex-graph subclass every nonempty value is a polyhedron.
boundary_notes: Having polyhedral values for every input does not by itself imply a polyhedral graph.
A finite union of polyhedra may be nonconvex and disconnected.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\). A polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) is an intersection of finitely many closed affine half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional set-valued mappings whose entire graph, rather than merely each value, is one convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(S\) has a convex polyhedral graph if \[\operatorname{gph}S:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m:y\in S(x)\}\] is a polyhedron. Equivalently, there exist a finite number of rows and matrices \(A\), \(B\), and a vector \(c\) such that \[y\in S(x)\iff Ax+By\le c.\] Consequently, \[S(x)=\{y:By\le c-Ax\},\quad \operatorname{dom}S=\{x:\exists y,\ Ax+By\le c\},\] and the inverse graph is obtained by exchanging \(x\) and \(y\). Empty values are permitted outside the projected domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping has a convex polyhedral graph when all input-output pairs satisfying the mapping form one polyhedron. Equivalently, membership can be expressed by finitely many joint linear inequalities in the input and output. Every value is then a polyhedron, and the domain is the polyhedral projection of the graph.
assumptions_latex: The complete graph is required to be one convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}S=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le c\}\) for some finite linear-inequality system.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(S(x)=\{y:By\le c-Ax\}\) for every \(x\).
\(\operatorname{gph}S^{-1}=\{(y,x):Ax+By\le c\}\) is also a polyhedron.
special_cases_latex: If the graph is a polyhedral cone, \(S\) is a polyhedral convex process.
A single-valued affine mapping on a polyhedral domain has a convex polyhedral graph.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty value \(S(x)\) is closed and convex polyhedral.
Both \(\operatorname{dom}S\) and \(\operatorname{rge}S\) are polyhedra because linear images of polyhedra are polyhedral.
boundary_notes: Polyhedral values at each point are insufficient without a joint finite graph representation.
A piecewise-polyhedral graph need not be a convex polyhedral graph.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), and let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be a set-valued mapping with graph \(\operatorname{gph}F:=\{(x,y):y\in F(x)\}\). A set is polyhedral when it is the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex polyhedral multifunctions and graph operations representable by finite linear systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is polyhedral when \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is a polyhedral convex set. Polyhedral multifunction calculus is the collection of graph operations obtained from finite Cartesian products, intersections, inverse images under linear maps, inverses, and compositions: \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\) and \(\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)=\{(x,z):\exists y,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F,\ (y,z)\in\operatorname{gph}G\}\). An operation belongs to this calculus when its output graph is obtained from finitely many polyhedral graphs by affine slicing, finite intersection, coordinate permutation, Cartesian product, and linear projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping is polyhedral exactly when its graph is a convex polyhedron. Its calculus consists of operations whose output graphs are constructed from finitely many such graphs using affine slices, finite intersections, products, coordinate permutations, and projections. This includes inversion and composition, with the intermediate value in a composition eliminated by projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is polyhedral}\iff\operatorname{gph}F\text{ is polyhedral}\), and every graph produced by the specified finite affine-intersection-product-projection operations is polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exist matrices \(A,B\) and a vector \(c\) such that \(\operatorname{gph}F=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le c\}\).
Equivalently, \(F(x)=\{y:By\le c-Ax\}\) after choosing a finite inequality representation of its graph.
special_cases_latex: For a polyhedral set \(P\subseteq X\), the constant mapping \(F(x)=P\) has graph \(X\times P\).

immediate_consequences_latex: Domains and ranges of polyhedral multifunctions are polyhedral because they are coordinate projections of the graph.
Fibers \(F(x)\) are polyhedral for every \(x\), including the empty fiber.
boundary_notes: This definition concerns convex polyhedral graphs; finite unions of polyhedra are piecewise-polyhedral rather than necessarily polyhedral.
Infinite-dimensional projections need not preserve the same finite linear representation.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P(b):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), let \(P(b)\) be nonempty at a reference parameter \(\bar b\), and write \((u)_+\) componentwise. Distances are taken with fixed norms on the relevant finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite linear inequality systems viewed simultaneously through infeasibility certificates, residual error bounds, and perturbation stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral certificate-stability system is a finite linear representation \(Ax\le b\), together with: (i) a dual certificate cone \(K:=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^m:A^{\mathsf T}y=0\}\), where \(y\in K\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) certify infeasibility; and (ii) a stability modulus \(\kappa\ge0\) for which \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P(b))\le\kappa\|(Ax-b)_+\|\) whenever \(P(b)\ne\varnothing\). A parameterized family has the certificate-stability property on \(B\) when the same certificate rule is valid for every \(b\in B\) and one finite \(\kappa\) applies throughout the stated region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral certificate-stability system packages a finite inequality system with two consequences of its linear representation. Nonnegative left-null multipliers having negative pairing with the right-hand side certify infeasibility. When the system is feasible, a finite constant bounds distance to its feasible set by the positive-part residual. Uniform certificate-stability on a parameter region requires the same rules and one finite residual-to-distance modulus throughout that region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining data satisfy \(K=\{y\ge0:A^{\mathsf T}y=0\}\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\Rightarrow P(b)=\varnothing\), and \(P(b)\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(x,P(b))\le\kappa\|(Ax-b)_+\|\) for all \(x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The error-bound component is metric subregularity of the residual mapping \(x\mapsto Ax-b+\mathbb R_-^m\).
The certificate component states that infeasibility is separated from the cone \(\{Ax+s:x\in\mathbb R^n,\ s\in\mathbb R_-^m\}\) by a nonnegative multiplier.
special_cases_latex: Equality constraints can be represented by paired inequalities, producing unrestricted multipliers as differences of nonnegative multipliers.
For a fixed matrix \(A\), a Hoffman constant can serve as \(\kappa\) for every feasible right-hand side under fixed norms.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero certificate is finitely checkable through linear equalities, inequalities, and one strict scalar inequality.
Small residual implies proximity to feasibility whenever the stability component applies.
boundary_notes: The title is an umbrella term rather than a universally standardized named object.
The displayed definition does not assert a uniform modulus when the coefficient matrix also varies.

children.title: Polyhedral Theorems of the Alternative
children.top_down_role: Named certificate families for finite linear systems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a finite linear feasibility system be represented by a matrix-vector pair, and let its proposed certificate consist of finitely many multiplier equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear, affine, conic, strict, or mixed-strict feasibility systems admitting finite dual certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral theorem of the alternative is a pair of finite systems \(\mathcal P\) and \(\mathcal D\), called the primal feasibility system and dual certificate system, such that for every admissible data instance exactly one system is solvable: \[(\exists x\;\mathcal P(x))\ \mathbin{\dot\vee}\ (\exists y\;\mathcal D(y)).\] The certificate conditions must imply that every primal constraint combination selected by \(y\) yields an impossible scalar relation, so simultaneous solvability is excluded; exhaustiveness requires a certificate whenever the primal polyhedron is empty. Farkas, Gordan–Stiemke, and Motzkin alternatives are members distinguished by whether the primal constraints are affine, homogeneous, strict, or nonstrict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral theorem of the alternative pairs a finite primal feasibility system with a finite multiplier certificate system. For every data instance, exactly one has a solution. The certificate combines the primal constraints into an impossible scalar relation, and every infeasible primal instance must possess such a certificate. Different named alternatives correspond to affine, homogeneous, strict, and mixed-strict systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every admissible instance, \((\exists x\;\mathcal P(x))\mathbin{\dot\vee}(\exists y\;\mathcal D(y))\), where \(\dot\vee\) denotes exclusive disjunction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Primal feasibility is equivalent to nonexistence of a dual certificate: \(\exists x\,\mathcal P(x)\iff\neg\exists y\,\mathcal D(y)\).
Primal infeasibility is equivalent to dual-certifier feasibility: \(\neg\exists x\,\mathcal P(x)\iff\exists y\,\mathcal D(y)\).
special_cases_latex: Farkas alternatives cover affine equality or inequality systems.
Gordan–Stiemke alternatives cover homogeneous systems, while Motzkin transposition covers mixed strict and nonstrict inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Infeasibility has a finite-dimensional multiplier witness.
Alternative systems provide separation certificates for disjoint polyhedral sets and cones.
boundary_notes: Exact certificate signs and normalizations depend on the chosen primal convention.
This schema does not itself specify a computational complexity bound or a numerical tolerance for approximate certificates.
review_flags: No inspected source locator supports the exact umbrella schema and named-family scope.
Each named alternative requires sign conventions to be checked against an authoritative statement.

Conversely, every \(\widehat y\) satisfying the normalized system is a Farkas infeasibility certificate for \(Ax=b,\ x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every strict equality-form Farkas certificate can be positively scaled so that its pairing with the target equals minus one.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form Farkas alternative for nonnegative feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[\text{(i) }Ax=b,\quad x\ge0;\qquad \text{(ii) }A^\top y\ge0,\quad b^\top y<0.\] A vector \(y\) satisfying (ii) is a directly checkable infeasibility certificate for (i), because every feasible \(x\) would imply \(b^\top y=x^\top A^\top y\ge0\), contradicting \(b^\top y<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative solution of Ax=b exists exactly when no vector separates b from the cone generated by the columns of A.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex sets, with linear inequalities represented by closed halfspaces. For \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), set \(C_I:=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite convex feasibility, emphasizing small and inclusion-minimal infeasible subfamilies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite infeasibility structure of \(\{C_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is the collection \[\mathcal I:=\{I\subseteq[m]:C_I=\varnothing\},\qquad \mathcal M:=\{I\in\mathcal I:C_J\ne\varnothing\ \text{for every}\ J\subsetneq I\}.\] Members of \(\mathcal I\) are infeasible subsystems and members of \(\mathcal M\) are minimal infeasible subsystems. In \(\mathbb R^n\), the family has a dimension-sensitive witness when every infeasible full system contains some \(I\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|\le n+1\). For linear inequalities, multiplier certificates provide a second finite structure through inclusion-minimal supports of nonnegative infeasibility multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite infeasibility structure records every index set whose associated constraints have empty intersection and, within it, every inclusion-minimal infeasible index set. A dimension-sensitive witness is an infeasible subfamily containing at most the ambient dimension plus one constraints. For linear inequalities, the supports of nonnegative alternative-theorem certificates give an algebraic representation of the same localized-witness idea.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I=\{I:C_I=\varnothing\}\) and \(\mathcal M=\{I\in\mathcal I:\forall J\subsetneq I,\ C_J\ne\varnothing\}\), with a Helly-size witness satisfying \(|I|\le n+1\) whenever the finite convex family is infeasible.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(I\in\mathcal M\) iff \(C_I=\varnothing\) and \(C_{I\setminus\{i\}}\ne\varnothing\) for every \(i\in I\).
For a linear system \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), a certificate support is \(\operatorname{supp}y:=\{i:y_i>0\}\) for a nonnegative Farkas multiplier \(y\).
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), every infeasible finite convex family has an infeasible subfamily of at most two members.
For halfspace systems in \(\mathbb R^n\), minimal infeasible subsystems need not all have size \(n+1\), but at least one small witness exists.

Finite infeasibility can be localized to a bounded-size subsystem in fixed dimension.
boundary_notes: Minimal means inclusion-minimal, not minimum cardinality.
The bound \(n+1\) concerns finite convex families in \(\mathbb R^n\), not arbitrary nonconvex constraints.

children.top_down_role: Residual, distance, and growth relationships specific to polyhedral systems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\ne\varnothing\). Fix norms and define \(r(x):=\bigl((Ax-b)_+,Cx-d\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global finite-dimensional error bounds for a fixed feasible linear equality-inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral error bound for \(P\) is an inequality \[\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H\,\|r(x)\|\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n,\] where \(H<\infty\) depends on the coefficient matrices and chosen norms but not on \(x\). The least admissible constant is the error-bound modulus \[H_*:=\sup_{x\notin P}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,P)}{\|r(x)\|}.\] A local polyhedral error bound replaces all \(x\) by points in a specified neighborhood. For a fixed finite linear system, the canonical Hoffman property is the existence of a finite global modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral error bound controls the distance from any point to a nonempty polyhedral feasible set by a norm of its violated inequalities and equality residuals. A global bound uses one finite constant for every point. The smallest such constant is the supremum of the distance-to-residual ratio outside the feasible set. A local bound restricts the points to a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_*:=\sup_{x\notin P}\operatorname{dist}(x,P)/\|r(x)\|<\infty\), and every \(H\ge H_*\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H\|r(x)\|\) for all \(x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The solution mapping \(S(u,v):=\{x:Ax\le b+u,\ Cx=d+v\}\) has a Lipschitz-type inverse estimate at the unperturbed right-hand side.
The residual mapping \(R(x):=(Ax-b,Cx-d)+(\mathbb R_-^m\times\{0\})\) is globally metrically subregular at \(0\).
special_cases_latex: For inequalities only, \(r(x)=(Ax-b)_+\).
For equalities only, the estimate reduces to distance from \(x\) to \(\{z:Cz=d\}\) controlled by \(\|Cx-d\|\), provided the affine set is nonempty.
immediate_consequences_latex: A sequence with residual converging to zero has distance to \(P\) converging to zero.
Residual tolerances translate directly into geometric feasibility tolerances through \(H\).
boundary_notes: The feasible-set nonemptiness assumption is essential because distance to the empty set is not finite.
The modulus depends on norms and representation; adding or rescaling constraints changes the residual and may change the constant.
review_flags: No inspected locator supports the exact equality-inequality Hoffman formulation.
The claimed global scope and dependence of the modulus require authoritative evidence.

knowledge_statements.source_title: Weak Sharp Minima for Polyhedral Problems
knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), let \(f^*:=\inf_{xi X}f(x)\), and let \(S:=\operatorname{argmin}_{xi X}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional optimization; the polyhedral regime takes both the feasible set and the objective epigraph to be polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution set \(S\) is a set of weak sharp minima of order one with modulus \(\alpha>0\) when \[f(x)-f^*\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\qquad\text{for every }xi X.\] The weak-sharpness modulus is \[\alpha_*:=\inf_{xi X\setminus S}\frac{f(x)-f^*}{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}.\] Thus global weak sharpness is equivalent to \(\alpha_*>0\). A local version requires the inequality only for \(x\) in a neighborhood of \(S\). For a polyhedral problem, this definition applies when \(X\) is polyhedral and \(f\) is a proper polyhedral convex function on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty solution set is weakly sharp when objective suboptimality grows at least linearly with distance from that set. The largest possible growth coefficient is the infimum of the objective-gap to distance ratio over nonsolutions. Positive modulus gives global weak sharpness; restricting the inequality to a neighborhood gives local weak sharpness. In a polyhedral problem, the feasible set and objective epigraph have finite polyhedral representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is globally weakly sharp}\iff\alpha_*:=\inf_{xi X\setminus S}(f(x)-f^*)/\operatorname{dist}(x,S)>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For any \(0<\alpha\le\alpha_*\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\alpha^{-1}(f(x)-f^*)\) for all \(xi X\).
The objective gap is a global error-bound residual for the solution set.
special_cases_latex: For a linear program, \(f(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x\) on a polyhedral feasible set.
For unconstrained polyhedral convex minimization, take \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and polyhedral \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An objective-gap tolerance \(f(x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) implies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\varepsilon/\alpha\).
Every point outside \(S\) has strictly positive objective gap when a positive global modulus exists.
boundary_notes: Weak sharpness does not require the minimizer to be unique.
This order-one definition differs from quadratic growth, which uses \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\).
review_flags: No inspected source locator supports this exact weak-sharpness definition and polyhedral specialization.
The assertion that a given polyhedral problem has positive modulus is not made without evidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak sharp minimum set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Minimum Condition for Polyhedral Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear objective growth away from the nonempty minimizer set of a polyhedral function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be polyhedral, let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\), and write \(f^*=\min f\). Then there exists \(\beta>0\) such that \[f^*+\beta\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq f(x)\qquad\forall x\notin X^*,\] where \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)=\min_{x^*\in X^*}\|x-x^*\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral function with a nonempty minimizer set grows at least linearly with distance from that set at every nonoptimal point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical region of a parametric polyhedral problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(pi\mathcal P
i\mathbb R^k\) parameterize a finite-dimensional linear or polyhedral optimization problem. Let \(S(p) be its solution set and \(I(p,x) the active-constraint index set at a feasible pair \((p,x).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polyhedral parameter partitions on which an active face and associated solution formula remain invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A critical region is a maximal connected polyhedron \(R
i\mathcal P\) for which there exist a fixed active index set \(I\), a fixed optimal face type, and matrices \(K\), \(k\) such that, for every \(pi\operatorname{ri}R\), the designated solution selection satisfies \(x(p)=Kp+k\), remains feasible and optimal, and has active set \(I(p,x(p))=I\). Critical-region stability at \(\bar pi\operatorname{ri}R\) means that some neighborhood of \(\bar p\) relative to \(\mathcal P\) lies in \(R\), so the active structure and affine solution formula persist there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical region is a maximal connected polyhedral parameter cell on whose relative interior a chosen optimizer is affine and has one fixed active-constraint pattern and optimal face type. A reference parameter is critically stable when it lies in the relative interior of such a cell, ensuring that sufficiently small admissible perturbations preserve the same structural regime and affine formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(pi\operatorname{ri}R\), \(x(p)=Kp+k\), \(x(p) is feasible and optimal, and \(I(p,x(p))=I\); if \(\bar pi\operatorname{ri}R\), these properties persist on a relative neighborhood of \(\bar p\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A critical region can be described by the parameter inequalities obtained after substituting \(x(p)=Kp+k\) into primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and the fixed active-set conditions.
Critical-region stability is local constancy of the active regime together with affine dependence of the selected solution.
special_cases_latex: For a nondegenerate multiparametric linear program with a fixed optimal basis, the basic solution is affine in the parameter on its basis-feasibility region.
For a strictly convex multiparametric quadratic program with affine parameter dependence, the optimizer is unique and piecewise affine under standard regularity conditions.
immediate_consequences_latex: The selected solution is Lipschitz on each critical region with modulus bounded by the operator norm of \(K\).
Structural changes can occur only when the parameter crosses a region boundary or encounters degeneracy.
boundary_notes: At a region boundary, several active regimes may be valid and the active set need not be locally constant.
Without uniqueness or a prescribed selection, the entire solution set need not equal one affine graph on a region.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x\tfrac12x^2-px\) subject to \(x\ge0\). Its unique solution is \(x(p)=\max\{p,0\}\). At \(p=0\), the constraint is active with zero multiplier; it is active for \(p<0\) and inactive for \(p>0\). The reference active set therefore persists on no neighborhood of zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a zero active multiplier, arbitrarily small perturbations can make the constraint enter or leave the active set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I(p)\text{ is not locally constant at }p=0.

A polyhedron \(P
i\mathbb R^n\) may be represented externally as \(P=\{x:Axi b\}\) or internally as \(P=\operatorname{conv}V+\operatorname{cone}R+L\), where \(V,R\) are finite and \(L\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact polyhedral representations, structure-preserving operations, and representation-sensitive computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedral operations-computation interface is the specification of a polyhedral object by a finite representation together with operations whose outputs admit finite polyhedral representations. Its primitive operations include affine images and preimages, finite intersections, Cartesian products, Minkowski sums, polarity under the required origin conventions, face extraction, and coordinate projection. An operation is representation preserving when an output \(H\)- or \(V\)-description can be obtained from the input descriptions by finitely many linear-algebraic, linear-inequality, redundancy-removal, and projection or elimination steps. Representation conversion is the task of passing between \(H\)- and \(V\)-descriptions of the same polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The operations-computation interface connects finite descriptions of polyhedra with operations that preserve polyhedral structure. A polyhedron may be given by inequalities or by finitely many points, rays, and a lineality space. Intersections, affine transformations, products, sums, polarity under suitable conventions, faces, and projections remain within the polyhedral class. Computation depends on the input and requested output representations, and conversion between inequality and generator descriptions is itself a central operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every object produced by the stated finite affine, intersection, product, Minkowski-sum, face, polarity, and projection operations is polyhedral and admits a finite \(H\)- or \(V\)-representation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: An \(H\)-description specifies finitely many affine halfspaces whose intersection is \(P\).
A \(V\)-description specifies finite sets \(V,R\) and a subspace \(L\) with \(P=\operatorname{conv}V+\operatorname{cone}R+L\).
special_cases_latex: Intersection is immediate in \(H\)-representation by concatenating inequalities.
Minkowski addition is immediate in \(V\)-representation by combining generators, while projection is immediate as a linear image of generators.
immediate_consequences_latex: The most convenient representation depends on the requested operation.
Finite representability is preserved even when the output description may be much larger than the input description.
boundary_notes: Closure under an operation does not imply polynomial output size or polynomial running time.
Polarity formulas require attention to whether the set contains the origin, is full-dimensional, or has lineality.
Numerical floating-point implementations require tolerances not included in this exact-arithmetic definition.

children.title: Polyhedral Set Calculus

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in finite-dimensional real spaces. A polyhedron is a set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), with finitely many weak linear inequalities; the empty set is allowed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry concerns exact set operations on finite-dimensional polyhedra, not numerical approximation or infinite-dimensional generalized polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedral set calculus consists of the operations \(P_1\cap\cdots\cap P_k\), \(P_1\times\cdots\times P_k\), affine inverse image \(T^{-1}(Q)=\{x: Mx+c\in Q\}\), affine image \(T(P)=\{Mx+c:x\in P\}\), and Minkowski sum \(P+Q=\{p+q:p\in P,q\in Q\}\). For every finite family of polyhedra and every affine map \(T(x)=Mx+c\), each resulting set is again a polyhedron. A direct constraint description exists for intersections, products, and inverse images; images and sums may instead be obtained as projections of higher-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral set calculus is the collection of finite intersection, Cartesian product, affine inverse-image, affine-image, and Minkowski-sum operations on finite-dimensional polyhedra. Every listed operation returns a polyhedron. Intersections, products, and inverse images have immediate finite inequality descriptions, while images and sums can be represented as projections of polyhedra in product spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_i,Q\text{ polyhedral and }T\text{ affine}\Longrightarrow \bigcap_iP_i,\ \prod_iP_i,\ T^{-1}(Q),\ T(P_1),\ P_1+P_2\text{ are polyhedral}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P+Q=L(P\times Q)\), where \(L(p,q)=p+q\).
\(T(P)=\{y:\exists x,\ Ax\le b,\ y=Mx+c\}\) when \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\).
special_cases_latex: Affine subspaces, polyhedral cones, and polytopes are closed under the applicable listed operations.
Coordinate projection is the affine-image case in which \(M\) selects coordinates.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every set produced by this calculus admits both a finite half-space description and a finite point-ray-lineality description.
Minkowski sums of polyhedra are closed, unlike sums of arbitrary closed convex sets.
boundary_notes: Set union and ordinary set difference do not generally preserve convexity and are not included.
An affine image can have a much larger irredundant inequality description than its input.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_ix\le b_i\}\), \(Q=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:Cy\le d\}\), and \(T(x)=Mx+c\). Inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The calculus is restricted to constructions whose output inequalities follow directly from input inequalities, without existential variable elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Constraint-side set calculus assigns finite inequality descriptions to intersections, Cartesian products, and affine inverse images. Explicitly, \(\bigcap_{i=1}^kP_i=\{x:[A_1^\top\ \cdots\ A_k^\top]^\top x\le[b_1^\top\ \cdots\ b_k^\top]^\top\}\); \(P_1\times P_2=\{(x,z):A_1x\le b_1,\ A_2z\le b_2\}\); and \(T^{-1}(Q)=\{x:CMx\le d-Cc\}\). Equalities may be retained or replaced by two opposite inequalities. These formulas define polyhedra even when the resulting system is infeasible or contains redundant constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint-side polyhedral calculus forms intersections by stacking inequalities, Cartesian products by placing systems on separate variable blocks, and affine inverse images by substituting the affine map into the target inequalities. The formulas remain valid for infeasible and redundant systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_iP_i,\ P_1\times P_2,\text{ and }T^{-1}(Q)\) have the displayed finite constraint descriptions and are polyhedra.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Q=\{y:Cy\le d,\ Ey=f\}\), then \(T^{-1}(Q)=\{x:CMx\le d-Cc,\ EMx=f-Ec\}\).
special_cases_latex: For a linear map \(T(x)=Mx\), the pullback is \(\{x:CMx\le d\}\).
Intersecting with an affine subspace amounts to appending linear equations.
immediate_consequences_latex: The number of displayed constraints is additive under finite intersection and Cartesian product.
No projection or conversion procedure is needed for these operations.
boundary_notes: Affine images generally do not have a direct constraint description by substitution and belong to projection-elimination calculus.
The displayed systems need not be irredundant.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Cartesian product admits the block inequality representation
\[
P_1\times P_2=\left\{(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R^{n_1+n_2}:\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0\\0&A_2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{pmatrix}\le\begin{pmatrix}b_1\\b_2\end{pmatrix}\right\}.
\]
Consequently, Cartesian products preserve polyhedrality; the representation uses the combined constraints without introducing auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Cartesian product of two polyhedra is described by stacking their inequalities in block-diagonal form, and is therefore a polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\cap L=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\) is a polyhedron, possibly empty.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Affine Sets and Convex Sets p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine section has the explicit representation
\[
P\cap L=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}.
\]
Equivalently, replacing the equality by two inequalities gives
\[
P\cap L=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Cx\le d,\ -Cx\le-d\}.
\]
Thus an affine section of a polyhedron is a polyhedron. No consistency assumption is required, so the resulting polyhedron may be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting a polyhedron with an affine set amounts to adjoining affine equality constraints, producing another, possibly empty, polyhedron.

children.title: Affine Transformation Pair
children.top_down_role: Transformation of polyhedra under affine mappings.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be \(T(x)=Mx+c\), and let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine maps are allowed to be singular, injective, surjective, or constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine transformation pair consists of the image \(T(P)=\{Mx+c:x\in P\}\) and inverse image \(T^{-1}(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Mx+c\in Q\}\). If \(Q=\{y:Ay\le b\}\), then \(T^{-1}(Q)=\{x:AMx\le b-Ac\}\). If \(P=\{x:Bx\le d\}\), then \(T(P)=\{y:\exists x,\ Bx\le d,\ y=Mx+c\}\). Both members of the pair are polyhedra; the inverse image has a direct constraint description, whereas the image is naturally an existential projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine map, the transformation pair is its image operation and its inverse-image operation. Substitution gives the inverse-image inequalities directly. The image is the set of target vectors admitting a feasible preimage and is therefore a projection. Both operations preserve polyhedrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P,Q\text{ polyhedral}\Longrightarrow T(P)\text{ and }T^{-1}(Q)\text{ are polyhedral}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in T(P)\iff \exists x\in P\text{ such that }y=Mx+c\).
\(x\in T^{-1}(Q)\iff T(x)\in Q\).
special_cases_latex: Translation is obtained with \(M=I\).
Coordinate projection is obtained when \(M\) selects a subset of coordinates.
immediate_consequences_latex: Affine equivalences preserve the face dimensions and inclusion structure of a polyhedron.
A singular image may reduce affine dimension or collapse distinct generators.
boundary_notes: The notation \(T^{-1}(Q)\) denotes a set preimage and does not require an inverse mapping.
The displayed existential image need not be an irredundant formulation.

children.title: Polyhedral Additive-Erosion Calculus
children.top_down_role: Additive and erosion-type operations that retain polyhedral structure.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P,Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be polyhedra. For \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), write \(\sigma_Q(a)=\sup_{q\in Q}a^\top q\), with values in \(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is finite-dimensional exact set calculus. The explicit erosion formula uses an H-description of the minuend.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The additive-erosion pair is the Minkowski sum \(P+Q=\{p+q:p\in P,q\in Q\}\) and the geometric erosion \(P\ominus Q=\{x:x+Q\subseteq P\}=\bigcap_{q\in Q}(P-q)\). If \(P=\{x:a_i^\top x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), then \(P\ominus Q=\{x:a_i^\top x\le b_i-\sigma_Q(a_i),\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), interpreted as empty if some required support value is \(+\infty\). Thus both \(P+Q\) and \(P\ominus Q\) are polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski addition collects all sums of one point from each set. Erosion collects all translations whose copy of the second set lies in the first. For a polyhedral minuend, each erosion inequality is obtained by subtracting the support value of the eroding set in the corresponding normal direction. Both operations preserve polyhedrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P,Q\text{ polyhedral}\Longrightarrow P+Q\text{ and }P\ominus Q\text{ are polyhedral}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in P\ominus Q\iff x+q\in P\) for every \(q\in Q\).
\(P+Q=L(P\times Q)\) for \(L(p,q)=p+q\).
special_cases_latex: \(P\ominus\{q\}=P-q\).
For \(Q=\{0\}\), both operations return \(P\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(Q\) is a polytope, each \(\sigma_Q(a_i)\) is attained at a vertex.
Erosion may be empty even when both input polyhedra are nonempty.
boundary_notes: Erosion is not ordinary Minkowski subtraction and need not invert Minkowski addition.
If \(Q\) is empty, conventions for \(P\ominus Q\) must be fixed separately.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
P\ominus Q=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:z+Q\subseteq P\},\qquad \sigma_Q(u)=\sup_{q\in Q}u^{\mathsf T}q.
\]
Then
\[
P\ominus Q=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}z\le b_i-\sigma_Q(a_i),\ i=1,\ldots,r\}.
\]
If some \(\sigma_Q(a_i)=+\infty\), the difference is empty; otherwise the displayed finite inequalities show that it is a polyhedron.

children.top_down_role: Effects of recession structure or unbounded operands on additive set operations.

assumptions_latex: When discussing \(P\ominus Q\), assume it is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P+Q\) is bounded exactly when both summands are bounded, while \(P\ominus Q\) is bounded exactly when \(P\) is bounded.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of a nonempty closed convex set.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession identities are
\[
\operatorname{rec}(P+Q)=\operatorname{rec}(P)+\operatorname{rec}(Q),\qquad
\operatorname{rec}(P\ominus Q)=\operatorname{rec}(P).
\]
Therefore \(P+Q\) is bounded if and only if both \(P\) and \(Q\) are bounded. If \(P\ominus Q\ne\varnothing\), it is bounded if and only if \(P\) is bounded. Moreover, nonemptiness of \(P\ominus Q\) requires \(\operatorname{rec}(Q)\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum is bounded exactly when both polyhedra are bounded; a nonempty Pontryagin difference inherits precisely the recession directions of its minuend.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p:Ax+Bz\le b\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The entry concerns exact elimination of finitely many real variables from weak linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Projection-elimination calculus identifies the coordinate projection \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists z\in\mathbb R^p,\ Ax+Bz\le b\}\) with elimination of the quantified variables \(z\). An elimination description is any finite system \(Cx\le d\) satisfying \(\{x:Cx\le d\}=\operatorname{proj}_x(P)\). Such a system always exists because coordinate projections, and therefore arbitrary linear images, of polyhedra are polyhedra. Successive one-variable elimination is one valid realization of this calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection-elimination calculus treats projecting a polyhedron onto selected coordinates as eliminating existentially quantified variables from a finite linear-inequality system. An elimination description is any finite inequality system defining exactly the projected set. It always exists in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)=\{x:\exists z,\ Ax+Bz\le b\}=\{x:Cx\le d\}\) for some finite \(C,d\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every linear image can be written as a coordinate projection of \(\{(x,y):x\in P,\ y=Mx\}\).
special_cases_latex: Eliminating one scalar variable gives Fourier–Motzkin elimination.
If \(p=0\), no elimination occurs.

The output description may contain redundant inequalities.
boundary_notes: Projection here is a linear image, not nearest-point metric projection.

The projected set is a polyhedron, including when it is empty, all of \(\mathbb R^n\), or lower-dimensional.

assumptions_latex: A finite system is written as \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_i t\le b_i\), with one scalar variable \(t\) to eliminate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated inequalities describe exactly the projection onto the \(x\)-coordinates.

notation.meaning: Indices with positive, negative, and zero coefficients of the eliminated variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-variable elimination; iteration eliminates several variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Partition the inequalities by \(I_+=\{i:\alpha_i>0\}\), \(I_-=\{i:\alpha_i<0\}\), and \(I_0=\{i:\alpha_i=0\}\). Retain \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) for \(i\in I_0\). For every \((i,j)\in I_+\times I_-\), generate
\[
(\alpha_i a_j-\alpha_j a_i)^{\mathsf T}x\le \alpha_i b_j-\alpha_j b_i.
\]
Remove the variable \(t\), optionally discard redundant inequalities, and repeat for further variables. The final system represents the required coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fourier–Motzkin elimination pairs every upper bound with every lower bound on an eliminated variable, retaining constraints independent of that variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Fourier–Motzkin Elimination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-variable Fourier–Motzkin update and its signs are correct, and algorithm is the exact content kind for this leaf. No source or inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P=\{(x,t):a_i^\top x+\alpha_i t\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(t\in\mathbb R\) is to be eliminated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is exact elimination for weak real linear inequalities; redundancy removal is not part of the defining rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the rows into \(I_+=\{i:\alpha_i>0\}\), \(I_-=\{i:\alpha_i<0\}\), and \(I_0=\{i:\alpha_i=0\}\). Fourier–Motzkin elimination of \(t\) retains \(a_i^\top x\le b_i\) for \(i\in I_0\) and, for every \((i,k)\in I_-\times I_+\), adds the comparison of the lower bound from row \(i\) with the upper bound from row \(k\): \((b_i-a_i^\top x)/\alpha_i\le(b_k-a_k^\top x)/\alpha_k\). The resulting finite system defines exactly \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fourier–Motzkin elimination partitions inequalities according to the sign of the eliminated variable's coefficient. It retains zero-coefficient rows and combines every lower-bound row with every upper-bound row. The resulting inequalities define exactly the projection after eliminating that variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)\) equals the solution set of the retained \(I_0\) inequalities and all pairwise \(I_-\)-to-\(I_+\) bound comparisons.
equivalent_formulations_latex: After positive rescaling, every generated inequality is the sum of one row with positive \(t\)-coefficient and one row with negative \(t\)-coefficient, cancelling \(t\).
special_cases_latex: If \(I_+=\varnothing\) or \(I_-=\varnothing\), no paired inequalities are generated.
Repeated application eliminates a block of variables.
immediate_consequences_latex: One step produces at most \(|I_0|+|I_-||I_+|\) inequalities before redundancy removal.
The projection remains polyhedral.
boundary_notes: Generated inequalities may be duplicate or redundant.
Strict inequalities and integer quantifiers require different elimination rules.

children.title: Elimination Pathology Family
children.top_down_role: Representation explosion, redundancy, and intrinsic-dimension changes during elimination.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a polyhedral formulation \(P_k\) and projection \(Q_k=\pi_k(P_k)\), let \(m(P_k)\) denote the number of input inequalities, \(f(Q_k)\) the number of inequalities in an irredundant H-description, and \(g_j\) the number of inequalities present after elimination step \(j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition classifies representation behavior of exact real-variable elimination, independently of a particular implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An elimination pathology family is a sequence \((P_k,\pi_k)\) for which at least one of the following quantities is unbounded with \(k\): the output expansion ratio \(f(Q_k)/m(P_k)\); the intermediate expansion ratio \(\max_j g_j/f(Q_k)\); the redundancy ratio \(g_{\mathrm{final}}/f(Q_k)\); or the affine-dimension drop \(\dim P_k-\dim Q_k\). The first records intrinsically large projected descriptions, the next two distinguish transient or final redundancy, and the last records collapse under projection. These properties can coexist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elimination pathology family is a sequence of polyhedral projections exhibiting unbounded output growth, excessive intermediate growth, excessive redundancy, or increasing affine-dimension loss. The measures separate intrinsically large projections from blow-up caused by the chosen elimination process.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P_k,\pi_k)\) is pathological when at least one of \(f(Q_k)/m(P_k)\), \(\max_jg_j/f(Q_k)\), \(g_{\mathrm{final}}/f(Q_k)\), or \(\dim P_k-\dim Q_k\) is unbounded.
special_cases_latex: The cross-polytope extended formulation gives a family with linearly many extension facets and exponentially many projected facets.
Fourier–Motzkin pairing can cause large intermediate systems even when the final irredundant system is small.
immediate_consequences_latex: Redundancy removal can control transient size but cannot remove intrinsic output-size growth.
Elimination order can change the intermediate expansion ratio.
boundary_notes: This definition does not assert that every projection has pathological growth.
Counts depend on the chosen formulation and, for intermediate ratios, the elimination order.

children.top_down_role: Growth in intermediate or final descriptions during variable elimination.

assumptions_latex: One Fourier–Motzkin step eliminates a variable appearing positively in \(p\) inequalities and negatively in \(q\) inequalities.
No generated inequality is removed as duplicate or redundant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The step generates \(pq\) inequalities, which can be \(\lfloor m^2/4\rfloor\) when \(p+q=m\).

notation.meaning: Numbers of positive and negative occurrences of the eliminated variable.
Number of inequalities involving the eliminated variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case raw output size for one elimination step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fourier–Motzkin elimination forms one new inequality for each positive-negative pair, so the raw number generated is
\[
pq.
\]
If \(p+q=m\), then
\[
pq\le\left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor,
\]
and equality occurs when the positive and negative classes are as balanced as possible. Hence a single elimination step can cause quadratic representation growth, while repeated steps can compound the growth unless redundancy detection substantially reduces intermediate systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One elimination step can replace m variable-dependent inequalities by about m²/4 pairwise inequalities, and repeated steps can compound this growth.
knowledge_statements.title: Elimination Representation Blow-Up

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The raw pair count and the bound floor(m squared over 4) are correct for one elimination step under the stated assumptions. Complexity bound is the correct kind for this blow-up leaf, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Hidden Affine Equalities
children.top_down_role: Latent affine restrictions exposed by projection or elimination.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+m}:Ax+By\le b\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Elimination can convert inequalities into affine equalities defining \(\operatorname{aff}Q\).

notation.meaning: Projection of the lifted polyhedron onto the x-coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-hull constraints revealed by projection rather than explicit in the retained variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le b\}\) be nonempty and let \(Q=\operatorname{proj}_xP\). It may happen that \(Q\) is contained in a proper affine subspace although no equality involving only \(x\) occurs explicitly in the lifted description. Equivalently, there can exist \(c\ne0\) and \(\delta\in\mathbb R\) such that \(c^Tx=\delta\) for every \(x\in Q\). Such equalities are generated by compatible linear combinations of eliminated inequalities and must be identified to obtain the intrinsic affine description of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection can force affine equations among retained variables even when the lifted formulation contains no explicit equation involving only those variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Affine Equalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary classification fits the elimination-pathology leaf, and the statement is mathematically plausible and internally consistent. No cited source with an inspectable locator supports the projection-induced equality claim or its linear-combination characterization.

children.title: Elimination-Induced Redundancy
children.top_down_role: Superfluous inequalities created or revealed during elimination.

assumptions_latex: A valid inequality description \(Q=\{x:Cx\le d\}\) is produced by eliminating \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting system can contain inequalities implied by its remaining rows and affine equalities.

notation.meaning: The ith row of the eliminated inequality system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy introduced by projection-elimination, independently of redundancy in the input system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let elimination of \(y\) from \(Ax+By\le b\) produce \(Q=\{x:Cx\le d\}\). An output row \(C_i x\le d_i\) is elimination-induced redundant when removing it leaves \(Q\) unchanged, equivalently when \(C_i x\le d_i\) is implied by the other output rows together with the affine equalities of \(Q\). Such redundancy can occur even when the lifted description is irredundant, because distinct combinations of lifted inequalities may project to identical or dominated supporting inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elimination may create duplicate or dominated inequalities, so an irredundant lifted system need not yield an irredundant projected system.
knowledge_statements.title: Elimination-Induced Redundancy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement accurately identifies elimination-induced redundancy and fits a failure-boundary container. An authoritative source with a specific section, theorem, or page locator is required for the implication characterization and the claim that irredundant lifted systems can yield redundant projected systems.

children.title: Intrinsic-Dimension Changes
children.top_down_role: Dimension loss or affine-hull changes affecting projected representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection may strictly reduce intrinsic dimension, with \(\dim Q=\dim P-\dim(P\cap(\{x_0\}\times\mathbb R^m))\) on relative-interior fibers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine dimension under coordinate projection of a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\) and \(Q=\operatorname{proj}_xP\), one has \(0\le\dim Q\le\min\{n,\dim P\}\). If \(x_0\in\operatorname{ri}Q\), the fiber \(F_{x_0}=P\cap(\{x_0\}\times\mathbb R^m)\) has the generic fiber dimension and satisfies \(\dim P=\dim Q+\dim F_{x_0}\). Hence elimination can lower intrinsic dimension; the lost dimension is the dimension carried by a relative-interior fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection cannot increase affine dimension; over a relative-interior projected point, the lost dimension equals the dimension of the fiber.
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic-Dimension Changes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is locally appropriate and states a precise relative-interior fiber dimension formula. Because that exact formula is the substantive claim and no citation is supplied, its hypotheses and generic-fiber conclusion require an authoritative source.

children.title: Representation-Conversion Problems
children.top_down_role: Transformations between external, generator, and incidence descriptions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: A polyhedron may be represented externally as \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Ex=f\}\), internally as \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+\operatorname{span}(L)\), or combinatorially by its finite face-incidence structure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion means exact equality of represented sets or exact recovery of incidence data; it does not prescribe one algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A representation-conversion problem takes one finite representation \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{in}}\) of a polyhedron \(P\) and asks for a finite representation \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{out}}\) satisfying \(\operatorname{set}(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{out}})=\operatorname{set}(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{in}})=P\), or for the face-incidence relation determined by \(P\). The principal geometric conversions are H-to-V, V-to-H, and H/V-to-incidence. Minkowski–Weyl equivalence guarantees existence of finite H- and V-representations, while finiteness of the face lattice guarantees finite incidence output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral representation-conversion problem asks for a new finite description of exactly the same polyhedron, or for its finite face-incidence structure. The main directions are constraints to generators, generators to constraints, and geometric descriptions to incidence data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{set}(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{in}})=P\Longrightarrow\operatorname{set}(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{out}})=P\), with \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{out}}\) finite.
equivalent_formulations_latex: H-to-V seeks \(V,R,L\) with \(\{x:Ax\le b,Ex=f\}=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+\operatorname{span}(L)\).
V-to-H seeks \(A,b,E,f\) satisfying the reverse equality.
special_cases_latex: For a polytope, the V-description contains only points.
For a pointed cone, conversion reduces to inequalities versus extreme rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: Vertex enumeration and facet enumeration are dual conversion problems under polarity in suitable full-dimensional settings.
Conversion output can be exponentially larger than input.
boundary_notes: A valid output need not be irredundant unless minimality is explicitly required.
Bit complexity and enumeration order are separate algorithmic specifications.

notation.meaning: Polyhedron represented by finite data R.
