children.title: Geometric Diagnostic Query Family
children.top_down_role: Structural diagnostics preceding conversion and enumeration.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural Diagnostics of a Represented Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a rational polyhedron given by a finite \(H\)- or generator representation. Write \(\operatorname{aff}P\) for its affine hull and \(\operatorname{rec}P\) for its recession cone when \(P\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact structural queries used before representation conversion or face enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A geometric diagnostic query is a decision or search map returning one or more intrinsic invariants of \(P\): emptiness; \(\operatorname{aff}P\) and \(\dim P=\dim(\operatorname{aff}P)\); lineality \(\operatorname{lin}P=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P)\); pointedness, defined by \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{0\}\); and boundedness, defined for nonempty \(P\) by \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}\). A certificate-producing diagnostic returns data verifying the answer, such as a feasible point, an affine-hull system, a nonzero lineality vector, or a nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric diagnostic query computes or decides structural invariants of a represented polyhedron before conversion or enumeration. The core diagnostics are emptiness, affine hull, affine dimension, recession cone, lineality, pointedness, and boundedness. Search variants return explicit witnesses, such as a feasible point or a nonzero recession or lineality direction, rather than only a Boolean answer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{lin}P=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P),\qquad P\text{ pointed}\iff\operatorname{lin}P=\{0\},\qquad P\text{ bounded}\iff\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For nonempty closed convex \(P\), \(d\in\operatorname{rec}P\) exactly when \(x+td\in P\) for every \(x\in P\) and \(t\ge0\).
A nonempty polyhedron is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^d\) precisely when \(\dim P=d\).
special_cases_latex: For \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), every recession direction satisfies \(Ad\le0\), and every lineality direction satisfies \(Ad=0\).
For a polytope, the recession cone and lineality space are both \(\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A vertex can exist only when the polyhedron is pointed, although pointedness alone does not assert nonemptiness.
Dimension and lineality diagnostics determine whether subsequent computations should be performed in a lower-dimensional quotient or affine hull.
boundary_notes: The recession cone is conventionally diagnosed only after nonemptiness or with an explicitly stated convention for the empty set.
Facial enumeration, representation conversion, and optimization are downstream tasks rather than diagnostic invariants in this definition.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the nonempty polyhedron.
Largest linear subspace contained in the recession cone.

review_flags: Available sources separately support recession and normal-cone notions but not this complete diagnostic-query family at one exact locator.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Diagnostics of a Represented Polyhedron

children.title: Affine-Dimension Queries
children.top_down_role: Diagnostics for the dimension of a polyhedron relative to its affine hull.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}P)=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine dimension of a nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Affine Sets and Convex Sets p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine hull and affine dimension of \(P\) satisfy \[\operatorname{aff}P=x_0+\operatorname{span}\{x-x_0:x\in P\},\qquad \dim(\operatorname{aff}P)=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-x_0).\] Consequently, an affine-dimension query asks for the rank of the direction space generated by feasible-point differences. Equivalently, the dimension is one less than the maximum number of affinely independent points contained in \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine dimension equals the dimension of the span of all differences between feasible points and any fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Dimension Queries

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Affine Sets and Convex Sets p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rational computation from an inequality representation after feasibility has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each row \(a_i^Tx\le b_i\), solve \(\max\{b_i-a_i^Tx:x\in P\}\). The row belongs to \(I_=\) exactly when the optimal value is zero; a positive or unbounded value means it is not universally tight. After collecting \(I_=\), return \(n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{I_=})\). For rational input, polynomial-time linear programming and rational rank computation make this procedure polynomial in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test each inequality for universal tightness by linear programming, then compute the rank of the universally tight rows.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\text{ has rational binary data}.
Linear-programming calls use exact rational decision criteria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim P=n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{I_=})\text{ is computable in polynomial bit time}.

notation.meaning: Universally tight row indices found by the LP tests.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Dimension Algorithm for an H-Polyhedron

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided certificate for the claimed affine dimension of a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A claim \(\dim P=r\) is certified by feasible points \(x_0,\ldots,x_r\in P\) that are affinely independent together with valid affine equations \(Cx=d\) for all \(x\in P\) such that \(\operatorname{rank}C=n-r\). The points prove \(\dim P\ge r\), while the equations prove \(P\subseteq\{x:Cx=d\}\) and hence \(\dim P\le r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affinely independent feasible points give a lower bound on dimension, and enough independent valid equations give the matching upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim(\operatorname{aff}P)=r.

notation.meaning: Independent affine equations valid throughout the polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Affine-Dimension Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Hull from Universally Tight Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine dimension of a nonempty polyhedron supplied by an inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), with rows \(a_i^T\), and let \(I_=:=\{i:a_i^Tx=b_i\ \forall x\in P\}\). Then \[\operatorname{aff}P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_{I_=}x=b_{I_=}\},\qquad \dim P=n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{I_=}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull is cut out exactly by the input inequalities that are tight at every feasible point; affine dimension is ambient dimension minus their rank.
assumptions_latex: I_=\text{ indexes the inequalities tight throughout }P.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{aff}P=\{x:A_{I_=}x=b_{I_=}\},\quad \dim P=n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{I_=}).

notation.meaning: Submatrix consisting of universally tight rows.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Hull from Universally Tight Inequalities

children.title: Lineality-Space Queries
children.top_down_role: Diagnostics for reversible recession directions within a polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap(-\operatorname{rec}(P))=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lineality of a nonempty polyhedron in inequality form.

source_refs.locator: 6 Convex Cones and Generalized Interiors p. 111
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The recession cone of \(P\) is \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}\). Its lineality space is \[\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap\bigl(-\operatorname{rec}(P)\bigr)=\{d:Ad=0\}=\ker A.\] Therefore a lineality-space query for an inequality representation reduces to computing a basis of the null space of \(A\); its dimension is \(n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty inequality-defined polyhedron, the lineality space is exactly the null space of its constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Space Queries

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Convex Cones and Generalized Interiors p. 111
source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

children.title: Polyhedral Boundedness Queries
children.top_down_role: Diagnostics distinguishing polytopes from unbounded polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is bounded iff \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\), equivalently iff \(Ad\le0\) implies \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness of a nonempty polyhedron via its recession cone.

source_refs.locator: 6 Convex Cones and Generalized Interiors p. 111
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedron \(P\) is bounded exactly when it has no nonzero recession direction: \[P\ \text{is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}=\{0\}.\] Thus boundedness is a homogeneous linear-feasibility question. For example, it can be tested by deciding whether \(Ad\le0\) admits a nonzero solution after imposing a normalization that excludes \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is bounded exactly when its recession cone contains only the zero direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Boundedness Queries

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Convex Cones and Generalized Interiors p. 111
source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

children.title: Pointedness Queries
children.top_down_role: Diagnostics for the absence or presence of nontrivial lineality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is pointed iff \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\), equivalently iff \(\ker A=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Null space of the constraint matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness means absence of an affine line in a nonempty polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 6 Convex Cones and Generalized Interiors p. 111
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedron \(P\) is pointed when it contains no affine line. For a nonempty inequality representation, \[P\ \text{is pointed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ker A=\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rank}(A)=n.\] Hence pointedness can be decided by a rank or null-space computation on the constraint matrix, independently of \(b\), once nonemptiness has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty inequality-defined polyhedron is pointed exactly when its constraint matrix has trivial null space.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness Queries

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Convex Cones and Generalized Interiors p. 111
source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-point certificate for an inequality-defined nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), let \(x\in P\), and define \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^Tx=b_i\}\). If \(\operatorname{rank}(A_{I(x)})=n\), then \(x\) is a vertex and \(P\) is pointed. Conversely, when \(P\) is pointed, it has a vertex \(x\), and every vertex satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(A_{I(x)})=n\). Thus a feasible point with full-rank active normals is a complete existential certificate of pointedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointedness is certified by a feasible point whose active constraint normals span the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is pointed}\iff \exists x\in P:\operatorname{rank}(A_{I(x)})=n.

notation.meaning: Indices of inequalities active at the feasible point x.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Normal Pointedness Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonemptiness Boundary for the Rank Test

children.title: Enumeration-Sensitive Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity viewpoints accounting for potentially large outputs.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an instance \(I\) of encoded length \(L=L(I)\) have a finite output set \(Y(I)=\{y_1,8,\ldots,y_N\}\). Let \(K=K(I)=\sum_{j=1}^N|y_j|\) be the total encoded output length, and let \(T_j\) be the time at which the \(j\)-th distinct output is produced.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite enumeration with explicitly encoded outputs; the chosen output order need not be canonical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An enumeration algorithm is output-polynomial if its total time is bounded by a polynomial in \(L+K\). It is incremental-polynomial if the time to produce the first \(j\) outputs is bounded by a polynomial in \(L+\sum_{i=1}^j|y_i|\) for every \(1\le j\le N\). It has polynomial delay if preprocessing time, every gap \(T_{j+1}-T_j\), and termination time after the last output are bounded by a polynomial in \(L\). Polynomial-space enumeration additionally requires working storage polynomial in \(L\), excluding the write-only output stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumeration-sensitive complexity measures computation against both input and produced output. Output-polynomial time bounds the whole run by input plus total output length. Incremental-polynomial time bounds every prefix of the run by the input plus that prefix's encoded output. Polynomial delay bounds preprocessing, every inter-output pause, and final termination by an input polynomial. Space is measured separately and normally excludes the write-only output stream.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{\mathrm{total}}\le\operatorname{poly}(L+K),\qquad T_j\le\operatorname{poly}\!\left(L+\sum_{i=1}^j|y_i|\right),\qquad \max_j(T_{j+1}-T_j)\le\operatorname{poly}(L).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Polynomial delay is a uniform input-polynomial bound on the time between consecutive observable enumeration events, including start and termination.
Output-polynomiality permits long delays before an early output when the eventual output is large; polynomial delay does not.
special_cases_latex: If \(N\) and every \(|y_j|\) are polynomial in \(L\), an output-polynomial algorithm is an ordinary polynomial-total-time algorithm.
A reverse-search enumerator can have polynomial space even when \(N\) is exponential, provided local adjacency and parent operations use polynomial space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any explicit enumerator needs at least \(\Omega(K)\) total output-writing time in a bit model.
An exponential number of vertices or facets does not contradict output-polynomial complexity.
boundary_notes: Polynomial total time in \(L\) alone is impossible for explicitly written superpolynomial output.
Duplicate outputs, compressed output, and randomized expected delay require separate semantics not included here.

notation.meaning: Total encoded length of all distinct outputs.
Time at which the j-th distinct output is emitted.

review_flags: No inspected source supplied precise definitions of output-polynomial, incremental-polynomial, and polynomial-delay enumeration.

children.title: Dimension-Parameterized Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity distinctions controlled by whether dimension is fixed.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I\) be a rationally encoded polyhedral instance, let \(L=L(I)\) be its input length, and let \(d=d(I)\) denote an explicitly selected dimension parameter, such as ambient dimension, affine dimension, or codimension.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact parameterized resource bounds; the selected meaning of dimension is part of the problem specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dimension-parameterized complexity statement specifies the dependence of a resource \(T(I)\) on both \(L\) and \(d\). The problem is fixed-parameter tractable with parameter \(d\) when \(T(I)\le f(d)L^c\) for a computable \(f\) and a constant \(c\) independent of \(d\). It is in the slice-wise polynomial or \(\mathrm{XP}\) regime when \(T(I)\le L^{g(d)}\) for a computable \(g\). A fixed-dimension polynomial result means that for every constant \(d_0\), instances with \(d(I)=d_0\) admit a polynomial bound in \(L\), whose degree or coefficient may depend on \(d_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dimension-parameterized analysis records separately how running time depends on encoding length and a chosen notion of dimension. Fixed-parameter tractability permits arbitrary dependence on dimension only as a multiplicative factor, with an input exponent independent of dimension. XP permits the polynomial exponent to depend on dimension. Merely proving polynomial time for every fixed dimension does not by itself establish fixed-parameter tractability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathrm{FPT}:\ T(I)\le f(d(I))L(I)^c,\qquad \mathrm{XP}:\ T(I)\le L(I)^{g(d(I))}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: An \(L^{d+O(1)}\) algorithm is slice-wise polynomial but is not, from that bound alone, fixed-parameter tractable.
A fixed-dimension theorem is a family of input-polynomial bounds indexed by constants \(d_0\).
special_cases_latex: When \(d\) is globally bounded, both FPT and XP bounds reduce to polynomial bounds in \(L\).
Parameterizing by codimension may yield a different classification from parameterizing by ambient dimension.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any claim that suppresses dimension-dependent constants must state whether dimension is fixed or part of the input.
Output-sensitive parameterized enumeration may replace \(L\) by \(L+K\) while retaining the same distinction between \(f(d)(L+K)^c\) and \((L+K)^{g(d)}\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not claim that any particular conversion or enumeration problem is FPT or XP.
Arithmetic-operation bounds require a separate bit-length analysis when the input is rational.

notation.meaning: Declared dimension parameter of instance I.
Computable functions depending only on the parameter.

children.title: Rational Bit-Complexity Model
children.top_down_role: Finite-bit representations, exact arithmetic, and certificate size.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Rational Bit Model for Polyhedral Computation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Every rational scalar is stored in reduced form \(q=p/r\), where \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(r\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,r)=1\). Matrices, vectors, polyhedra, and certificates are encoded as finite strings of such integers plus structural metadata.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Turing-style bit complexity for finite rational input and output; unit-cost real arithmetic is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\ell(z)=1+\lceil\log_2(1+|z|)\rceil\) for \(z\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\ell(p/r)=\ell(p)+\ell(r)\) for a reduced rational. The encoding length \(L(I)\) is the sum of scalar lengths and dimension, sign, and incidence metadata. An exact algorithm's time is the number of bit operations on a Turing-equivalent machine, and its space is the maximum number of working bits. It is polynomial-bit-time when both the number of arithmetic operations and all intermediate operand lengths are bounded so that total bit operations are polynomial in \(L(I)+K(I)\). A certificate is polynomial-size when its encoded length is polynomial in \(L(I)\) and exact verification uses polynomially many bit operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rational bit-complexity model stores every rational as a reduced numerator-denominator pair and measures the entire binary encoding. Running time counts bit operations, so large intermediate numerators and denominators matter even if the arithmetic-operation count is small. Explicit output length is included for conversion and enumeration. Certificates must have polynomial binary length and be exactly verifiable in polynomial bit time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\ell(p/r)=\ell(p)+\ell(r),\qquad L(I)=\sum_{q\in I}\ell(q)+\ell(\text{structural data}),\qquad T_{\mathrm{bit}}=\#\text{ bit operations}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Clearing denominators gives an integer encoding only after the bit growth of the common multiplier is included.
A strongly polynomial arithmetic-operation bound and a polynomial bit bound are distinct properties.
special_cases_latex: For integral \(A,b\), the scalar contribution is \(\sum_{ij}\ell(A_{ij})+\sum_i\ell(b_i)\).
A rational feasibility witness has polynomial certificate size only when all numerator and denominator lengths are polynomially bounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: Unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers cannot establish polynomial bit complexity.
An output-polynomial conversion bound must count the binary lengths of output coordinates, not only the number of vertices, rays, or facets.
boundary_notes: Floating-point rounding, condition numbers, and approximate feasibility belong to a numerical model outside this definition.
The precise binary serialization may vary by polynomially equivalent conventions, but the convention must be fixed.

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of an integer or reduced rational.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact-arithmetic bit complexity of an algorithm is the number of Boolean operations required to execute it when integers are stored in binary and rationals are stored as reduced numerator-denominator pairs. children.title: Representation-Conversion Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial and numerical obstacles to reliable representation conversion.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure Boundary for Explicit Polyhedral Conversion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) map an input representation \(R_{\mathrm{in}}(I)\) of a rational polyhedron to a required explicit output representation \(R_{\mathrm{out}}(I)\). Write \(L(I)\) and \(K(I)\) for their respective bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact explicit representation conversion; compressed, approximate, and oracle outputs define different problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance family \(\mathcal F\) lies beyond the input-polynomial representation-conversion boundary when \(K(I)\) is not bounded by any polynomial in \(L(I)\) on \(\mathcal F\); no algorithm writing the full output can then run in time polynomial only in \(L(I)\). A conversion is also outside a claimed exact bit model if its representation semantics omit required lineality or recession data, or if intermediate or output coefficient lengths are not controlled by the stated resource bound. Numerical failure is separately present when a tolerance-based procedure does not guarantee a representation of exactly the same set under the declared input semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conversion failure boundary separates failures caused by unavoidable output size from failures of representation semantics or arithmetic. If a short input can require a superpolynomial explicit output, input-polynomial conversion is impossible because writing the answer already takes too long. Exact conversion also fails when recession or lineality information is lost or when coefficient growth is ignored. Approximate numerical conversion is a different problem unless exact set equality is guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bigl(\forall p\in\mathbb R[t]\ \exists I\in\mathcal F:\ K(I)>p(L(I))\bigr)\Longrightarrow T_C(I)\not\le\operatorname{poly}(L(I))\text{ for every explicit writer }C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The combinatorial output barrier may be expressed using the number of required facets, vertices, or rays when every output item needs at least one encoded bit.
Output-polynomial solvability is not ruled out by a superpolynomial relation between \(K\) and \(L\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal active-set degeneracy for inequality descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in P\), define the active set by \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\). The feasible point \(x\) is combinatorially degenerate when the active description contains more constraints than are needed to determine its local face; equivalently, \(|I(x)|>\operatorname{rank}A_{I(x)}\) after equations defining the affine hull are treated consistently. In particular, a full-dimensional polyhedron has a degenerate vertex when more than \(d\) inequalities are active there. Degeneracy is representation-dependent because redundant inequalities can create additional active constraints without changing \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is combinatorially degenerate when more constraints are active than the rank needed to describe its local face; redundant inequalities can create degeneracy.

children.title: Output-Size Explosion
children.top_down_role: Conversion instances whose target representations are combinatorially much larger than their inputs.

assumptions_latex: The input is the explicit inequality description of the cube \(Q_d=[0,1]^d\).
The required output is a complete explicit list of its vertices, and the ambient dimension \(d\) varies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any conversion algorithm that explicitly emits every vertex requires at least \(\Omega(2^d)\) output operations on this family.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit cube family directly establishes exponential output size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unavoidable output-sensitive boundary for explicit inequality-to-vertex conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_d=[0,1]^d\). Its inequality description consists of the \(2d\) inequalities \(0\le x_i\le 1\) for \(i=1,\ldots,d\), whereas its complete vertex description contains exactly the \(2^d\) vectors in \(\{0,1\}^d\). Therefore, any algorithm required to write every output vertex performs at least \(\Omega(2^d)\) output operations on this family. An explicit inequality-to-vertex conversion cannot consequently have running time polynomial only in the input length for variable \(d\); its complexity guarantee must account for output size or impose an additional restriction such as fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cube has only twice as many inequalities as dimensions but exponentially many vertices, so complete inequality-to-vertex conversion cannot always run in time polynomial only in its input size.
knowledge_statements.title: Output-Size Explosion

children.title: Numerical Reliability Failure
children.top_down_role: Incorrect structural decisions caused by finite-precision arithmetic or unstable predicates.

assumptions_latex: Geometric predicates are evaluated using finite-precision floating-point arithmetic.
The conversion procedure branches on signs of determinants or residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without separation bounds or certified arithmetic, sufficiently small perturbations can reverse combinatorial decisions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-precision sign tests fail when predicate magnitude approaches rounding error
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision failure of combinatorial predicate evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the two-dimensional row vectors \(a_1=(1,0)\) and \(a_2=(1,\varepsilon)\). The determinant deciding their independence equals \(\varepsilon\). If a floating-point evaluation incurs absolute error comparable to \(u\), then for \(|\varepsilon|\lesssim u\) the computed sign may be zero or incorrect. A representation-conversion algorithm using this predicate can consequently merge distinct facets, create spurious incidences, or omit vertices. Reliability therefore requires exact or certified predicates, adaptive precision, or an explicit lower separation bound keeping every decisive nonzero predicate safely above its error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near-zero determinant and residual tests can be misclassified by rounding, corrupting the face lattice unless predicates are certified or sufficiently separated.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Reliability Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaled two-dimensional determinant example supports the stated finite-precision failure mechanism, and failure_boundary fits the container. A source is required for the error model and the certified-predicate remedies.

children.title: Near-Degenerate Input Regimes
children.top_down_role: Inputs close to rank loss, incidence changes, or alternative combinatorial types.

assumptions_latex: The input is a parameterized rational inequality system \(A(t)x\le b(t)\).
A finite family \(\mathcal{P}\) of real-valued decisive predicates is fixed, and every map \(t\mapsto p(A(t),b(t))\) for \(p\in\mathcal{P}\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nondegenerate input is near-degenerate at tolerance \(\tau>0\) when its minimum absolute decisive-predicate margin satisfies \(0<\delta(t)\le\tau\).

notation.meaning: fixed finite family of decisive predicates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Procedure-relative predicate-margin condition for proximity to combinatorial degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite family \(\mathcal{P}\) of continuous determinant, slack, or multiplier predicates whose signs determine the relevant combinatorial decisions. At a parameter value \(t\) for which every decisive predicate is nonzero, define \(\delta(t)=\min_{p\in\mathcal{P}}|p(A(t),b(t))|\). For a declared tolerance \(\tau>0\), the input is near-degenerate when \(0<\delta(t)\le\tau\). It is exactly degenerate relative to \(\mathcal{P}\) when \(p(A(t),b(t))=0\) for at least one decisive predicate \(p\). Along a sequence of nondegenerate inputs with \(\delta(t)\to0\), perturbations of vanishing magnitude can reach a predicate-zero boundary and may change the inferred combinatorial representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a fixed finite collection of continuous decisive predicates, a nondegenerate input is near-degenerate when its smallest absolute predicate value is positive but below a declared tolerance.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P(u)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron depending on data or a parameter \(u\), and let \(f_u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be an objective whose polyhedral structure is explicitly represented.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A chapter-boundary object connecting polyhedral geometry to optimization models, solution maps, certificates, and sensitivity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral optimization interface is the set-valued and extended-value map generated by the family \(\inf\{f_u(x):x\in P(u)\}\): \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in P(u)}f_u(x)\) and \(S(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P(u)}f_u(x)\). The interface includes declared geometric data sufficient to express feasibility, recession behavior, optimal faces or active pieces, and exact optimality certificates. Values use the conventions \(v(u)=+\infty\) when \(P(u)=\varnothing\) and \(S(u)=\varnothing\) when the infimum is not attained. The interface does not prescribe a particular optimization algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimization interface packages a polyhedral feasible-set family and a structured objective into its value function and solution mapping. It also specifies which geometric objects carry feasibility, recession, active-set, optimal-face, and certificate information. Empty feasible sets and unattained or unbounded problems use explicit extended-value conventions. The interface describes the mathematical boundary between geometry and optimization algorithms, not an algorithm itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[v(u)=\inf\{f_u(x):x\in P(u)\},\qquad S(u)=\{x\in P(u):f_u(x)=v(u)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the indicator \(\delta_{P(u)}\), the same interface is \(v(u)=\inf_x(f_u+\delta_{P(u)})(x)\) and \(S(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_x(f_u+\delta_{P(u)})(x)\).
A certificate interface augments \((v,S)\) with a relation \(\mathcal C(u,x,z)\) whose satisfaction declares the status certified by \(z\).
special_cases_latex: Linear optimization uses \(f_u(x)=c(u)^Tx\).
Polyhedral nonsmooth optimization uses a max-affine objective plus a polyhedral indicator.
Parametric optimization permits the right-hand side, objective, or both to depend on \(u\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Different algorithms can implement the same mathematical interface.
Recession diagnostics are required to distinguish a finite optimum from an objective unbounded below.
boundary_notes: Integer restrictions and robust quantifiers alter the feasible-set semantics and must be stated explicitly.
Smooth nonpolyhedral objectives may be placed over a polyhedral feasible set, but their analytic theory is not supplied by this interface definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier Certificate for Polyhedral Linear Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: H-representation certificate under the minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Ex=f\}\ne\varnothing\). A feasible point \(x^*\) minimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) if and only if there exist \(\lambda\ge0\) and free \(\mu\) such that \(c+A^{\mathsf T}\lambda+E^{\mathsf T}\mu=0\) and \(\lambda_i(A_i x^*-b_i)=0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal feasibility, stationarity, multiplier signs, and complementary slackness exactly certify linear optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) is optimal if and only if the displayed multiplier certificate exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Optima Need Not Contain Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the vertex-optimum formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a nonempty polyhedron \(P\) is pointed and \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is finite, its optimal face contains a vertex of \(P\). Pointedness cannot be omitted: for \(P=\{(t,0):t\in\mathbb R\}\) and \(c=(0,1)\), every feasible point is optimal although \(P\) has no vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointed polyhedra admit vertex optima, whereas lineality can leave a finite optimal face with no vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vertex attainment holds under pointedness and fails without it.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Optima Need Not Contain Vertices

assumptions_latex: The feasible region \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizers form an exposed face; finite attainment is characterized by recession directions, and pointwise optimality is characterized by the normal cone.

notation.meaning: recession cone of the feasible polyhedron

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard exposed-face, recession-cone, and normal-cone characterization of linear optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention for linear objectives on nonempty polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the problem \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), the infimum is finite if and only if \(c^{\mathsf T}r\ge0\) for every \(r\in\operatorname{rec}P\). When it is finite, it is attained, and the solution set \(F_c=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=\min_{y\in P}c^{\mathsf T}y\}\) is a nonempty exposed face of \(P\). For \(x\in P\), define \(N_P(x)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^d:v^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\le0\ \text{for every }y\in P\}\). Then \(x\in F_c\) if and only if \(-c\in N_P(x)\). Objective vectors in the relative interior of the normal cone associated with a face select that face as the optimal face; these relatively open regions form the normal-fan stratification of objective space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-below linear objective on a nonempty polyhedron attains its minimum on an exposed face; recession and normal cones characterize boundedness, optimality, and the corresponding objective-space regions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal Faces, Recession Directions, and Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and consider \(v(c)=\inf_{x\in P}c^Tx\). Define \(N_P(x)=\{y:y^T(z-x)\le0\ \forall z\in P\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact geometry of linear minimization over a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear-optimization geometry of \((P,c)\) consists of the recession test, optimal face, and normal-cone region. The objective is bounded below precisely when \(c^Td\ge0\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{rec}P\). When the minimum is finite, the optimal set \(F_c=\{x\in P:c^Tx=v(c)\}\) is a nonempty exposed face of \(P\). For every \(x\in P\), \(x\in F_c\) exactly when \(-c\in N_P(x)\). Consequently, the cost vectors producing a fixed face \(F\) as part of the optimum are described by the negatives of normal cones along \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear optimization over a nonempty polyhedron is governed by three linked objects. Recession directions determine whether the objective can decrease without bound. If the value is finite, all minimizers form a nonempty exposed face. A feasible point is optimal exactly when the negative cost vector belongs to its normal cone, so normal cones partition cost space into regions sharing optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[v(c)>-\infty\iff c^Td\ge0\ \forall d\in\operatorname{rec}P,\qquad F_c=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^Tx,\qquad x\in F_c\iff-c\in N_P(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F_c=P\cap\{x:c^Tx=v(c)\}\) is the face exposed by the supporting hyperplane with normal \(-c\).
A direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}P\) with \(c^Td<0\) is an unboundedness direction for the minimization problem.
special_cases_latex: If \(P\) is a polytope, \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}\), so every linear objective has a finite attained minimum.
If \(-c\) lies in the relative interior of the normal cone of a face \(F\), then \(F8) is the exact optimal face.
immediate_consequences_latex: When \(F_c\) is a singleton, its point is an optimal vertex.
Costs on boundaries between normal-cone regions can expose a higher-dimensional optimal face.
boundary_notes: For the empty polyhedron, feasibility must be diagnosed before recession and optimal-face assertions are applied.
The statement concerns exact linear objectives and does not include numerical conditioning or a linear-programming algorithm.

notation.meaning: Optimal exposed face for cost c.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unboundedness and attainment alternative for the equation-defined generalized linear program, expressed through a homogeneous feasible improving direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the generalized linear program \((LP)\) be consistent. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the optimal set as the feasible set of the original inequalities augmented by the optimal-value inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*\neq\varnothing\) be the solution set of \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:\langle a^i,x\rangle\leq b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(f^*=\langle c,x^*\rangle\) for any \(x^*\in X^*\). children.title: Polyhedral Nonsmooth Modeling
children.top_down_role: Max-affine, minimax, composite, and exact-penalty models using polyhedral functions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear epigraph formulation of a domain-restricted max-affine function composed with an affine map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(z)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^{\mathsf T}z+\beta_i)+\delta_D(z)\), where \(D=\{z:Fz\le g\}\), and set \(z=Mx+q\). Then \[\operatorname{epi}(h\circ(M\cdot+q))=\{(x,t):F(Mx+q)\le g,\ t\ge a_i^{\mathsf T}(Mx+q)+\beta_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\}.\] Thus an affine objective plus this composite polyhedral term has a finite linear epigraph formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Substituting an affine map into a max-affine term's domain and epigraph inequalities yields an exact linear formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) has the displayed domain-restricted max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}(h\circ(M\cdot+q))\text{ has the displayed finite linear description}.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Composite Polyhedral Epigraph Formulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polyhedral formulation of weighted absolute-value losses and penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w_i\ge0\), affine residuals \(r_i(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i\), and a nonempty feasible set \(X\), \[\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m w_i|r_i(x)|=\inf_{x,t}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m w_it_i:x\in X,\ -t_i\le r_i(x)\le t_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\right\}.\] If \(X\) is polyhedral, the formulation is a linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted absolute-value objectives admit an exact linear formulation with one epigraph variable per residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_iw_i|r_i(x)|\text{ is represented exactly by }t_i\ge r_i(x),\ t_i\ge-r_i(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Value and Weighted L1 Linearization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex penalty result locally relevant to positive-part polyhedral modeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[v=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ h_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\},\] where \(X\) is convex and \(f,h_i\) are convex. Suppose the constrained problem attains \(v\) and admits an optimal multiplier \(\lambda^*\ge0\) with zero duality gap. Define \[P_\rho(x):=f(x)+\rho\sum_{i=1}^m\max\{0,h_i(x)\}.\] Every constrained optimizer minimizes \(P_\rho\) over \(X\) when \(\rho\ge\|\lambda^*\|_\infty\). If \(\rho>\|\lambda^*\|_\infty\), every minimizer of \(P_\rho\) is feasible and solves the constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-part penalty is exact at an optimal-multiplier bound, and strict excess forces every penalized minimizer to be feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda^*\ge0\) is dual optimal and the duality gap is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho\ge\|\lambda^*\|_\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{argmin}_{\mathrm{feas}}f\subseteq\operatorname{argmin}_XP_\rho,\quad \rho>\|\lambda^*\|_\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{argmin}_XP_\rho\subseteq\operatorname{argmin}_{\mathrm{feas}}f.

assumptions_latex: The model is a proper convex polyhedral function on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every such model has a finite max-affine representation on a polyhedral domain, enabling an epigraph formulation by linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued max-affine representation of convex polyhedral functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is polyhedral if and only if there exist a nonempty polyhedron \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) and finitely many pairs \((a_i,\beta_i)\) such that \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_i)+\delta_D(x)\). Consequently, minimizing \(f(x)+g(x)\) over any additional model represented by \(g\) can expose the polyhedral term through an epigraph variable \(t\) and inequalities \(t\ge a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_i\), together with \(x\in D\). Finite maxima, piecewise-linear losses, and weighted absolute-value penalties are instances of this representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex polyhedral function is a finite maximum of affine functions on a polyhedral domain, and its epigraph is modeled by linear inequalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical polyhedral nonsmooth model is the extended-real function \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^Tx+b_i)+\delta_P(x)\). Its epigraph is \(\{(x,t):Cx\le d,8 a_i^Tx+b_i\le t\ (i=1,8\ldots,m)\}\), hence a polyhedron. At \(x\in P\), the active affine-piece set is \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^Tx+b_i=8\max_j(a_j^Tx+b_j)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical polyhedral nonsmooth model is a finite maximum of affine functions restricted to a polyhedron by an extended-value indicator. Its epigraph has one linear inequality for each affine piece plus the constraints describing the domain. Therefore its minimization can be written as a linear epigraph problem. Nonsmoothness occurs where two or more affine pieces are simultaneously active or where the polyhedral domain contributes a normal cone.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(u\in U\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) and define \(P(u)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b+Bu\}\). Let \(c(u)=c_0+Cu\), \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in P(u)}c(u)^Tx\), and \(S(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P(u)}c(u)^Tx\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional parametric linear optimization with affine data dependence; global regularity is not asserted without additional feasibility and nondegeneracy hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The parametric sensitivity interface is the pair \((v,S)\) together with its feasibility domain \(\mathcal D=\{u:P(u)\ne\varnothing\}\), optimal active-set correspondence, and critical-region decomposition. For \(x\in S(u)\), define \(I(x,u)=\{i:A_ix=b_i+B_i u\}\). A critical region associated with an optimal active pattern \(J\) is a maximal connected polyhedral subset \(R_J\subseteq\mathcal D\) on which there exists an optimal selection having the same declared active or basis pattern \(J\). A transition occurs at a parameter belonging to the boundaries of two or more such regions or where feasibility, boundedness, or attainment status changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parametric sensitivity interface records the optimal value, minimizer set, feasible parameter domain, and optimal active patterns of a polyhedral optimization family. A critical region is a maximal connected polyhedral parameter set on which a selected optimal basis or active pattern remains unchanged. Region boundaries mark active-set transitions or changes in feasibility, boundedness, or attainment. This definition does not assume that every parameter has a unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal D=\{u:P(u)\ne\varnothing\},\qquad v(u)=\inf_{x\in P(u)}c(u)^Tx,8\qquad S(u)=\{x\in P(u):c(u)^Tx=v(u)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The value function is the marginal function obtained by partially minimizing the jointly parameterized objective plus the indicator of the polyhedral graph \(\{(u,x):Ax-Bu\le b\}\).
When an optimal basis is fixed and nonsingular, the associated primal and dual candidates are affine functions of the parameter, and its validity inequalities describe a polyhedral region.
special_cases_latex: Right-hand-side sensitivity has \(C=0\) and varies only \(b+Bu\).
Objective sensitivity has \(B=0\) and varies only \(c_0+Cu\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Set-valued \(S\) is required at degenerate parameters where several optimal faces or bases coexist.
Critical-region boundaries identify candidate locations for changes in directional derivatives of the value function.
boundary_notes: Piecewise-affineness and finiteness of a global critical-region partition require hypotheses not included in the bare interface definition.
Nonlinear parameter dependence or integer variables can destroy the stated polyhedral critical-region structure.

children.title: Parametric Polyhedral Models
children.top_down_role: Optimization models whose objectives, constraints, or right-hand sides depend on parameters.

assumptions_latex: The parameter and decision spaces are finite-dimensional: \(p\in\mathbb R^q\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
The matrices and vectors \(A,B,b,c\) are fixed and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functions \(v\) and \(S\) define the value and solution maps of a parametric polyhedral optimization model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional right-hand-side-parametric linear programs with extended-real value convention.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times q}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
F(p):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b+Bp\},\qquad v(p):=\inf_{x\in F(p)}c^{\mathsf T}x,
\]
with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). The associated solution map is
\[
S(p):=\{x\in F(p):c^{\mathsf T}x=v(p)\}
\]
when \(v(p)\in\mathbb R\), and \(S(p):=\varnothing\) otherwise. This quadruple \((F,v,S,p)\) is a parametric polyhedral model because the joint feasible set \(\{(p,x):Ax-Bp\le b\}\) is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parametric polyhedral model is a linear program whose polyhedral feasible set depends affinely on a parameter, together with its value and minimizer mappings.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Polyhedral Models

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lower-unboundedness alternative for fixed \(A\) and \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(D\ne\varnothing\). If some \(d\) satisfies \(Ad\le0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(v(p)=-\infty\) for every \(p\in D\). If no such direction exists, every nonempty fiber has a finite attained minimum. Thus lower unboundedness cannot occur for only some feasible parameters in this fixed-\(A,c\) model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The common recession cone makes all feasible instances unbounded below or none of them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A direction \(d\) with \(Ad\le0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) exists if and only if every feasible parameter has value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: All-or-None Lower Unboundedness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible Parameter Domain and Common Recession Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural facts for the fixed-matrix right-hand-side model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(p)=\{x:Ax\le b+Bp\}\), the feasible parameter domain \(D:=\{p:F(p)\ne\varnothing\}\) is the projection of \(\{(p,x):Ax-Bp\le b\}\), hence is a polyhedron. For every \(p\in D\), \(\operatorname{rec}F(p)=\{d:Ad\le0\}\), independently of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible parameters form a polyhedron, and all nonempty fibers share one recession cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is polyhedral and \(\operatorname{rec}F(p)=\{d:Ad\le0\}\) for every \(p\in D\).
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Parameter Domain and Common Recession Cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lower-unboundedness boundary for the fixed objective and constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\ne\varnothing\). If there exists \(d\) with \(Ad\le0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(v(p)=-\infty\) for every \(p\in D\). If no such direction exists, every feasible fiber has a finite attained minimum. Thus, in this fixed-\(A,c\) right-hand-side model, lower unboundedness cannot occur for only some feasible parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because every fiber has the same recession cone, either all feasible parameter instances are unbounded below or none are.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of \(d\) with \(Ad\le0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) is equivalent to \(v(p)=-\infty\) for all \(p\in D\).
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Independent Unboundedness Alternative

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
v(p):=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b+Bp\}.
\]
If \(v(p)>-\infty\) for every \(p\) and \(\operatorname{dom}v:=\{p:v(p)<+\infty\}\ne\varnothing\), then
\[
\operatorname{epi}v=\{(p,t):\exists x,\ Ax\le b+Bp,\ c^{\mathsf T}x\le t\}
\]
is a polyhedron. Consequently, \(v\) is a proper closed convex polyhedral function. In particular, \(\operatorname{dom}v\) admits a finite polyhedral subdivision such that the restriction of \(v\) to every cell is affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper value function obtained by partially minimizing a linear objective over affine polyhedral constraints is closed, convex, polyhedral, and piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Value Functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation for the fixed right-hand-side-parametric linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y:=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:y\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y=-c\}\). If the value function is proper, then \(Y\ne\varnothing\) and, in the extended-real sense, \[v(p)=\sup_{y\in Y}-(b+Bp)^{\mathsf T}y.\] For every \(p\in\operatorname{dom}v\), the supremum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value is an attained supremum of affine parameter functions indexed by a parameter-independent dual polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: The primal value function is proper.
\(F(p)=\{x:Ax\le b+Bp\}\) and the objective is \(c^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(p)=\sup_{y\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y=-c}-(b+Bp)^{\mathsf T}y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Max-Affine Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Properness Boundary for the Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separation of infeasibility and lower unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed-\(A,c\) model, \(v(p)=+\infty\) exactly when \(F(p)=\varnothing\). If some \(d\) satisfies \(Ad\le0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(v(p)=-\infty\) for every feasible \(p\). Hence \(v\) is proper exactly when the feasible parameter domain is nonempty and no such direction exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Properness requires a feasible parameter and excludes a common negative-cost recession direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is proper if and only if \(\{p:F(p)\ne\varnothing\}\ne\varnothing\) and no \(d\) satisfies \(Ad\le0\), \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Properness Boundary for the Value Function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order value sensitivity, including domain-boundary normals through the dual optimal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in\operatorname{dom}v\), define \(Y^*(p):=\arg\max_{y\in Y}-(b+Bp)^{\mathsf T}y\). Then \[\partial v(p)=\{-B^{\mathsf T}y:y\in Y^*(p)\}.\] In particular, when \(p\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}v)\), \(v\) is differentiable at \(p\) exactly when this image is a singleton, and its sole element is \(\nabla v(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value subgradients are images of optimal dual multipliers; at interior parameters, a unique image characterizes differentiability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial v(p)=-B^{\mathsf T}Y^*(p)\), with the stated interior differentiability criterion.

notation.meaning: Optimal dual multiplier set at parameter \(p\)

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradients as Shadow-Price Images

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a finite polyhedral subdivision \(\{C_j\}_{j=1}^N\) satisfies \(v(p)=\alpha_j^{\mathsf T}p+\beta_j\) on \(C_j\). Then
\[
\operatorname{gph}S\cap(C_j\times\mathbb R^n)
=\{(p,x):p\in C_j,\ Ax\le b+Bp,\ c^{\mathsf T}x=\alpha_j^{\mathsf T}p+\beta_j\}
\]
is a polyhedron for every \(j\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{gph}S=\bigcup_{j=1}^N\bigl(\operatorname{gph}S\cap(C_j\times\mathbb R^n)\bigr)
\]
is a finite union of polyhedra. Thus solution sensitivity is governed by finitely many polyhedral regimes, although \(S(p)\) may be empty, multivalued, or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimizer map of a parametric linear program has a graph assembled from finitely many polyhedra, one for each affine regime of the value function.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Map Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Sensitivity Under a Stable Nondegenerate Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local single-valued sensitivity for a right-hand-side-parametric linear program under a fixed nonsingular active basis with strictly positive multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b+Bp\}\). Let \(I\) contain \(n\) indices, let \(A_I\) be nonsingular, and suppose \(\lambda_I:=-(A_I^{\mathsf T})^{-1}c>0\). On \[R_I:=\{p:A A_I^{-1}(b_I+B_Ip)\le b+Bp\},\] one has \[S(p)=\{x_I(p)\},\qquad x_I(p):=A_I^{-1}(b_I+B_Ip).\] Hence \(S\) is affine and Lipschitz on \(R_I\), with derivative \(A_I^{-1}B_I\) along directions remaining in that region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular active basis with strictly positive multipliers makes the optimizer unique and affine throughout its critical region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(p)=\{A_I^{-1}(b_I+B_Ip)\}\quad(p\in R_I).

notation.meaning: Parameter region on which the basis solution is feasible

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Sensitivity Under a Stable Nondegenerate Basis

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Continuous Selection at an Optimal-Face Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that a finite-union polyhedral graph does not imply local single-valuedness or a continuous selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[S(p):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le x\le1}px,\] one has \[S(p)=\begin{cases}\{1\},&p<0,\\ [0,1],&p=0,\\ \{0\},&p>0.\end{cases}\] Its graph is a finite union of polyhedra, but \(S(0)\) is multivalued and no continuous single-valued selection exists on a neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an optimal-face transition, a polyhedral solution multifunction may become multivalued and admit no continuous local selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gph}S\text{ is a finite union of polyhedra, but no continuous selection exists near }0.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Continuous Selection at an Optimal-Face Transition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient hypotheses for a genuine constant-active-set critical region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the unique optimizer \(x_0\) at \(p_0\) has exactly \(n\) active inequalities indexed by \(I\), the square matrix \(A_I\) is nonsingular, every inactive slack is strictly positive, and the unique multipliers associated with \(I\) are strictly positive. Then a neighborhood of \(p_0\) exists on which the same basis is primal and dual feasible, the optimizer is unique and affine in \(p\), and its exact active set is \(I\). The boundary is reached when basis nonsingularity, an inactive strict slack, or a positive basic multiplier is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular, strictly feasible and strictly complementary optimal basis persists locally.
assumptions_latex: Exactly \(n\) constraints are active, \(A_I\) is nonsingular, inactive slacks are positive, and basic multipliers are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimizer is locally unique and affine, with exact active set \(I\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(p\in\mathbb R\), consider \(\min 0\) subject to \(0\le x\le1\), with parameter-independent constraints. Every feasible point is optimal. The optimizers \(x=0\), \(x=1\), and \(x=1/2\) realize three different exact active sets throughout the same full-dimensional parameter region \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonunique optimizers can realize multiple exact active sets on the same open parameter region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact realizable active-set regions need not be disjoint or meet only on lower-dimensional boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General set-valued active-set geometry without uniqueness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a polyhedral cell \(C\) on which the finite value function is affine, \(v(p)=a^{\mathsf T}p+\gamma\). The pairs \((p,x)\) satisfying \(p\in C\), \(Ax\le b+Bp\), \(c^{\mathsf T}x=a^{\mathsf T}p+\gamma\), and \(A_i x=b_i+B_i p\) for every \(i\in I\) form a polyhedron. Its parameter projection is therefore polyhedral and consists of parameters admitting an optimizer at which every constraint in \(I\) is active. Regions for different \(I\) may overlap and need not form a partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameters admitting an optimizer with a prescribed included active set form polyhedral regions that may overlap.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a polyhedral cell on which \(v\) is finite and affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The included-active-set realizability region is polyhedral, without any disjointness conclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in S(p)\), define
\[
I(p,x):=\{i:A_i x=b_i+B_i p\}.
\]
For each \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let
\[
R_I:=\{p:\exists x\in S(p),\ A_i x=b_i+B_i p\ (i\in I),\ A_i x<b_i+B_i p\ (i\notin I)\}.
\]
After intersecting with each affine cell of \(v\), the set \(R_I\) is the projection of a relatively open polyhedron; its closure is polyhedral. There are finitely many such closures, and an exact active set is locally constant away from their relative boundaries. Consequently, every active-set transition occurs on a finite union of lower-dimensional polyhedral faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameters split into finitely many polyhedral regimes with fixed realizable active sets; changes occur only on regime boundaries.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Transition Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The supplied source locator does not reliably support the exact-active-set projection claim, and the mathematical statement is overstated. Because R_I records active sets realizable by some optimizer, several distinct R_I may overlap on full-dimensional parameter regions when optimal solutions are nonunique or degenerate. Thus an exact active set need not be locally constant away from regime boundaries, and transitions need not be confined to lower-dimensional faces without additional uniqueness or nondegeneracy hypotheses. A source and corrected hypotheses are required.

Then there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(p_0\) on which the same basis remains primal and dual feasible, the optimizer is unique and affine in \(p\), and its active set is exactly \(I\). Loss of one of the strict inequalities or basis nonsingularity marks the boundary of this stability region.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Robust Feasibility and Discrete Relaxation Interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal U\) be a nonempty polyhedral uncertainty set of data realizations \(\xi\), with constraint system \(A(8\xi)x\le b(8\xi)\). Let \(D=\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^{n-p}\) encode designated integer variables, and let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a deterministic polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static robust linear decisions and polyhedral relaxations of mixed-integer feasible sets; adjustable decisions and nonpolyhedral uncertainty are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The robust feasible set is \(R=\{x\in X:A(8\xi)x\le b(8\xi)\ \forall\xi\in\mathcal U\}\). The robust-discrete feasible set is \(S=R\cap D\). A polyhedral relaxation is any polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(S\subseteq P\); it is ideal when \(P=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S\). The modeling boundary consists of the two operations that change semantics: universal quantification over \(\mathcal U\) creates robust feasibility, whereas replacing \(S\) by a containing polyhedron \(P\) removes or relaxes integrality. Neither operation may be omitted when interpreting the resulting optimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the robust-discrete boundary, uncertainty and integrality are separate mathematical operations. Static robust feasibility requires one fixed decision to satisfy every constraint realization in the uncertainty set. Discrete feasibility then intersects that robust set with the required integer lattice. A polyhedral relaxation contains the discrete feasible set, and it is ideal when it equals the closed convex hull. Solving the relaxation does not by itself solve the discrete problem unless an integral optimum is recovered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R=X\cap\bigcap_{\xi\in\mathcal U}\{x:A(8\xi)x\le b(8\xi)\},\qquad S=R\cap(8\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^{n-p}),\qquad S\subseteq P.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For rowwise uncertainty, robust feasibility is equivalent to \(\sup_{\xi\in\mathcal U}(a_i(8\xi)^Tx-b_i(8\xi))\le0\) for every constraint row \(i\).
The natural continuous relaxation is obtained by replacing \(\mathbb Z^p\) by \(\mathbb R^p\) while retaining the robust constraints.
